en: (Ṭīkā 4972) (Nāma-tārāsahasranāmavyākhyā-abhidhārthacintāmaṇiḥ) (Author: Śrī Viśveśvara)
(Folio number - 121) (Saṃvat - 1941) (Subject - Tantra)
The Mirror of Secret Meanings: A Commentary on the Thousand Names of Tārā.
Composed by the highly wise Viśveśvara for the delight of men.

Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Om. May that Lord—who possesses limbs as beautiful as a cluster of blue lotus petals, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of the gods, who is overflowing with bliss, who is the non-dual infinite consciousness, and who shines with pure teeth—always shine radiantly within the heart of the wise. (1)
Having bowed with great devotion to the pair of feet of the one who bears the glory that is the crest-jewel of the wise,

Viśveśvara composed this commentary on the *Tārā-nāma-daśa-śata*— which accords with his own understanding— for his daughter Tārā. (2) Therein, this first verse, which sets forth the subject matter, begins with "Kailāse" [and continues with] "kela..."

Between the two, water and earth, there is Mount Kailāsa; because it is made of crystal (*sphaṭika*), it is called "Kailāsa. In the reading *tasyāyaṃ kailāsaḥ śikharāsīnam*, the meaning is that [the Lord] is seated upon its peak. Even in the reading *śikhare devam*, the sense of service is implied. The word *mahādeva* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) in its application to consciousness as delimited by specific attributes. Thus, in the Skandhapurāṇa...
In the *Rāṇa*, it is said: "I am greater than even the great gods; there is none higher than me, for I am Mahādeva.

Here, the connection [of the text] has been stated because it is clear. By the phrase "seated there," his state of well-being (*svasthatva*) is indicated, which implies the presence of Brahma at that time.
These qualities—conformity with time and possession of intuitive brilliance—are like wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadughā*) in all actions. Thus it is said.

By the word *kteḥ*, the state of being hidden (*gopyatva*) is indicated; therein, because dwelling together with another is not appropriate, the term *Bhavānī* is used for the purpose of establishing her connection as the wife of Bhava.

By the rule, "One should not speak to anyone without being asked, nor should one answer one who asks improperly," the word *prītyā* (with affection) is used for the sake of providing an answer. By the term *Parameśvara*, his capacity to explain the matter to be inquired about is indicated due to his omniscience.

The word *cana* likewise [indicates] the supreme state of the Lord (*īśvara*), which possesses knowledge and other qualities, and is the eternal, ultimate reality. There is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between that [supreme state] and the knowledge which is a single part of its object. The term *maheśvara*, setting aside its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and prioritizing only its etymological meaning (*yoga-artha*), signifies the one who governs the entire universe; thus, everything is consistent. "The venerable Goddess said" (*śrī-devy uvāca*): the word *śrī* is used here in the sense of excellence.

The application [of the rule] is as follows: regarding the root *vac* (to speak) with the suffix *paribhāṣaṇa*, when the *liṭ* (perfect tense) affix is applied, there is the substitution of *vikhaṃpi*;

thus, how is the form *uvāca* derived? It is through the Lord (*īśāna*), whose status as the controller of all has been stated; and by being "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*), he is fit for the definitive explanation of the objects to be questioned.
Those who accomplish the mantra desired by the practitioner attain the highest, world-transcending perfection (*siddhi*) of the mantra and so forth, which is well-known to all.
When a mantra-practitioner places his hand upon the head of even a fool and commands him, he immediately causes that person to rise up from the world;
this is according to the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra*. [The questioner asks: "In what way (*katham*) and by what means (*kena prakāreṇa*) do they obtain [the results]?"—thus the one who has asked.

He asks me, the Great Lord, to explain that other method (*prakārāntaram*) by which and how they obtain them; the verb is in the imperative (*loṭ*) as a request for me to speak. [He addresses] others as well, O Lord.
In order to exclude that [possibility], the word *su* is used; likewise, by the expression *su iti*, the absence of inferiority attributed by another master is obtained.

This is understood from the rule *kathayeti* and from the rule *dedasi parepi*. Just as, according to the *Chāndasa-rūpāpakarṣa*, there is application even in the case of the years [of study], so it is clearly stated in the *Śabda-kaustubha* and other works. Even though the means for attaining perfection is mine...

Although the fact that Brahman is the object of inquiry is understood from the very statement regarding Brahman by virtue of its beginningless intention (*anādi-tātparya*), nevertheless, the statement "it must be explained for the sake of clarity" was spoken by Śrī Śaṅkara; this is clear from the phrase "without [further] explanation. Worship is fivefold, as stated in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa*: "Worship is declared to be fivefold in the five [systems] beginning with Pañcarātra," and these are described...
The five limbs [of worship] consist of *abhigamana*, *upādāna*, *ijyā*, *svādhyāya*, and *yoga*. Among these, *abhigamana* refers to approaching [the deity] accompanied by ministers;
it consists of the purification of the temple through sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other such consecrations. *Upādāna* would be the gathering of the materials for the worship of the deity.

Furthermore, there should be the offering of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) and the worship of the deity along with his limbs (*sāṅga*) and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).

The recitation of a mantra preceded by the contemplation of its meaning is declared to be the "recitation" (japa) of that mantra; the thorough study of its scripture is traditionally known as "study" (adhyāya) by the experts in mantras. Yoga is said to be the contemplation of the identity between the Guru, the Deity, and the Self; this form of meditation is described in the *Prapañcasāra*: "That state of the deity which belongs to the mantra-practitioner should be properly established within that [Self]"—thus is meditation (dhyāna).

Those who know the truth say that [the suffix] *ya* is applied after the word *japa* in the sense of "that which is" (*tad-artha*), according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*. That [recitation] is of three kinds; thus it is stated in the *Viśuddheśvara-tantra*:
"That which is beyond the range of one's own ears is known as mental (*mānasa*) recitation; that which is within the range of one's own ears is proclaimed as whispered (*upāṃśu*) recitation;

and that which is perceptible to people is called audible (*nigada*) recitation—thus recitation is said to be of three types. Regarding the different types of offerings (*bali*), the *Tantra* states: "The offering is of two kinds..."

The *rājasa* [offering] is described by the wise as being rich in meat and blood, adorned with the three fruits (*phalatraya*), combined with honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and drenched in the three sweets (*madhuratra*). The *sāttvika* [offering] is devoid of meat; the rest is as previously stated. Here, in the phrase "they obtain," since the object of the action (*karman*) was not explicitly mentioned, it is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) from the preceding verse. In this context, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is one who desires success (*siddhi*).

First, the fact that you are the means for attaining the fruit follows by way of the *rātrisatra* principle; for, having determined that "the Goddess is always to be recited" as an injunction (*vidhi*), since no specific [result] is mentioned, there exists a requirement for one. Alternatively, it might be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fruit of worship and so forth, which is established by the qualification for the primary act already determined, because it is impossible to postulate a result through a subsidiary (*aṅga*) when the primary is already established; otherwise, [this would apply] even to the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

Because it would result in the fallacy of assuming a distinct ritual procedure (*kalpanā*), the statement regarding the attainment of success (*siddhi*) apart from worship and other such acts is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), since it serves another purpose;

this is according to the maxim that "the mention of a fruit in relation to auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) is merely explanatory praise. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the injunction for those [auxiliaries] being rendered futile. Thus, this is merely an injunction of the quality consisting of the form of a hymn (*stotra*), and it is the means of apprehending its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*).

How can there be accomplishment through non-existence? How [can it be] when, even though the recitation and other such aids are accomplished through the operation of this [text] in dependence upon its existence, the injunction for the recitation of the hymn (*stotra*) is directly perceived due to the desire for manifold fruits? By the principle of the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, even this mere recitation should be understood as the primary act; for it is not the case that "one should cause him who desires food to sacrifice with this [sacrifice]."

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice is heard of as having a separate injunction, it is an independent rite; yet, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is also a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *Rājasūya*. In the present case, however, the injunction "it should be recited" is appropriate as a subsidiary rule. As for [the statements] such as "this hymn (*stotra*) is to be recited," since they are subordinate to the relative pronoun *yat*, they cannot be injunctions; rather, the injunction "it should be recited" establishes the subsidiary rule.

If it is argued that this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that very [obligation], we reply: True; yet here too, because the connection with a fruit is heard in the recitation by way of specifying particular locations—such as "in a place of Śiva" or "on a bed"—and because of the association with an injunction for one who has not yet undertaken the practice (*aniśrita-vidhi*) in the phrase "whoever should hear," there is nothing whatsoever that indicates hearing is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*). Nor is there an attainment of it through natural inclination (*rāga*), since it is not something already established.

Even though the word *yat* (which) is employed in the phrase "one should hear [this]," because it refers to something not otherwise established (*aprāptārthatvāt*), the necessity is twofold; thus, by the force of the word *eva* (indeed), the injunction for recitation must necessarily be accepted. Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence that even one who is uninitiated (*adīkṣita*) would have the entitlement to recite this, for such is indeed desired. For this very reason, all learned men (*sarvaśiṣṭāḥ*) practice accordingly even with respect to other hymns (*sūktāntareṣu*). Thus it is said: "Of the names... (*nāmnām iti*).

Based on the statement in the Bhāṣya, "From one up to ten, [the suffix] tasi is used after both numerals and non-numerals," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is treated as non-remaining (*aśeṣa*). Alternatively, the suffix *tasil* has the sense of the accusative;

or rather, it has the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), since the word is primarily expressive of an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Or else, the point of departure (*apādāna*) is understood through the ellipsis of an implied action, according to the maxim of "all systems" (*sarvatantra*), as in the expression "skilled in [crossing] over" (*kuśalātyavatīti*). Although the Bhāṣya does not mention the dative case (*caturthī*) in connection with this rule, [it is still applicable] in the case of "of the devotees" (*bhaktānām*).
Because it is the sixth [chapter] remaining from the *Trayodaśānanda*, and because the Blessed One began [this work] by saying "Listen" (*śṛṇu*), one should not say [it is redundant];

for likewise, it is for the purpose of indicating that this [work] must necessarily be accepted, just as in the case of [the statement] "I shall speak to you" (*tattvām asmivacyīti*). Thus, there are four preliminary adjuncts (*anubandhas*): the desire for success (*siddhikāma*) is the qualification (*adhikārin*), success (*siddhi*) is the purpose (*prayojana*), and the Thousand Names (*nāmasahasra*) is the subject matter (*pratipādya*) of the text.

The relationship characterized by the means of realization (*pratipādadaka-lakṣaṇa-sambandha*) must be stated at the beginning of the treatise; for it is logical that the relationship, along with its purpose (*saprayojana*), must be stated at the beginning of the treatise. [Regarding the phrase] "without" (*vinā*): if this particle is used in the sense of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārthe*), then that by which one obtains the fruit is the fruit; there is non-difference between the fruit and the cause of the fruit (*hetu-hetumat-abheda*).

It should be noted that if one were to act otherwise, there would be an inconsistency because the fruit resulting from the performance of worship, offerings, and so forth—distinct from [the aforementioned]—is not mentioned here. Now, having revealed the great purpose of this [work], he begins to state the sages (*ṛṣi*) and other [components] with the prose passage beginning with "asya," since knowledge of them is necessary. Thus says Hemādri, citing Yājñavalkya:

The seer, the meter, the deity, and likewise the application (viniyoga), as well as the Brāhmaṇa and the Viśeṣa, should be understood with effort. However, for one who performs officiating at sacrifices, teaching, recitation, burnt offerings, or rites such as those performed within water without knowing these, the fruit shall be meager. But he who knows the seer, the meter, the deity, the application, and the Brāhmaṇa according to their true nature—

Furthermore, one who knows the meaning of the mantras and even of each individual *ṛc* should be honored like a guest; he attains union (*sāyujya*) with the deity—of this there is no doubt. Moreover, the deluded person who, according to the previously mentioned method, knows the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, shall possess the qualification for the secret rites and other practices, by means of which the seer through whom [the mantra] was seen attained perfection.
The state of that mantra’s seer is declared to be its *ārṣa* (seer-portion). Because it covers [the self], it is designated as *chandas*;

for in ancient times, the Self was covered by the gods out of fear of death, and it was raised up by the Ādityas and the Vasus—those indeed are the *chandas*. Whatever deity is specified for whichever mantra, that is its *daivata* (deity-portion). Its form...
He shall indeed attain divinity; he is called a god. In a former kalpa, this mantra arose for the purpose of fulfilling desires.
This must not be performed [arbitrarily]; its specific application (viniyoga) is now declared. There is also a Vedic revelation (śruti) which serves as the root of this:
"Whosoever, having learned a mantra together with its meter and deity, teaches or causes it to be recited by a Brahmin who lacks the Brāhmaṇa-explanation, he falls into a pillar."

"...or falls into a pit," and so forth. Then Kātyāyana says: "He who studies, recites, mutters, offers oblations, sacrifices, or officiates at sacrifices without knowing these [Vedic meters], his Veda becomes devoid of vigor and exhausted; moreover, he falls into a pit or a chasm, strikes against a stump, dies, or becomes worse off. But he who studies after having understood these, for him [the Veda] possesses vigor..."
The knowledge of the meaning of the *Ṛgveda* becomes more powerful after one has performed the recitation (*japa*). In the *Prapañcasāra*, it is said:

"By means of the seer (*ṛṣi*), the letters (*varṇa*), and so forth, and by means of the root (*dhātu*) through its attainment and application, that which expresses the nature of the mantra is the Guru; it is the designator of the seer. The roots *chand* (to desire) and *dā* (to give) belong to the *tudādi* class; since it gives the desire of those two, 'Chanda' is the designator of the ocean of mantra-syllables, [and] Ātman..."

The learned have proclaimed in all the Tantras that the term *devatā* is a compound consisting of *a-devatā-bhāva-pradāna* (the bestowing of the state of being a deity). The root *ṛdh* signifies both "attainment" and "going"; the root *ṣidh* signifies "knowledge. Because he bestows knowledge, the Guru is designated by the term *ṛṣi*. The root *chand* signifies "desire," and the root *dā* signifies "giving. Thus, the word *icchā* (desire) is the meaning of the word *chanda*; such is the etymological derivation according to the Nairukta school.

This is the meaning. Thus it has been stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "The verbal root beginning with the letter *ṛ* has the sense of 'going' (*gati*), while that beginning with *śam* has the sense of 'restraint' (*śama*).

The letter *ṣi* signifies 'knowledge' (*vijñāna*), and *sa* is the 'attainer' (*prāpaka*). Through the union of these two forms, one is called a *ṛṣi*, a teacher (*guru*). The root *chand* signifies 'desire' (*icchā'), while *dā* and others have the sense of 'giving' (*dāna*). *Chandas* refers to the speech of the mind; from both [roots] comes the sense of desire."

From the root *div*, meaning "to play," the word *deva* (god) is derived; it is so called because he bestows (*dadāti*) the state of divinity upon the practitioner, granting his own nature to him. This is the intended meaning of the aforementioned term. In the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Ātmataraṅga-bhāga* of the *Hṛdayabodha*, it is said:
"Then there was a certain Ṛṣi who, assuming the guise of a sage, took refuge in the one named Akṣobhya."
The word *uṣṇik* is grammatically correct due to its inclusion in the *ṛtvig-ādi* list of sūtras; according to Amara, *jaṭā* refers to hair attached to the head;

and one should meditate on the tawny, fierce Ekajaṭā—thus it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*. This concludes the *Girijābhidhārthacintāmaṇi*, composed by Viśveśvara, the son of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who had crossed the ocean of words and authoritative statements.

The first ray of light has arrived, like the solar radiance consisting of a thousand beams that pierces the darkness of delusion; the thousand names of Tārā shine forth with supreme excellence. In this regard, although other [goddesses] are also possessed of femininity, their names will be mentioned here for the purpose of indicating the all-pervading nature (*sarvātmakatva*) of the Blessed Lady. And it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa: "Those names which are gentle..."

O fair-faced one, those [powers] arising from the knowledge of Māninī are to be beheld by that large-eyed lady. Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "The Goddess Girijā is Śakti, and Śaṅkara is the possessor of Śakti. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, there is the speech of Dakṣa: "There is nothing whatsoever in this universe, whether moving or unmoving, that has been created without you. And in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, the sciences...

All the Vidyās, such as the goddesses Stā, Stavā, Devī, Bhedā, Vidya, Samastā, Sakalā, Jagat, and so forth, are mentioned there. Furthermore, in that very same place, when Śumbha says, "O excessively proud one, you fight by relying on the strength of others," and [the Goddess replies] with this passage beginning, "When I exist through my own majesty in many forms of myself," it is consistent with the statement that the Vaiṣṇavī and other [Śaktis] belong to the Blessed Lady alone. (Liṅga Purāṇa)

All men are Śaṅkaras, and all women are Maheśvarī. Those denoted by masculine words are proclaimed to be Rudras, and those denoted by feminine words are all the manifestations of Gaurī. All men and women are said to be the very manifestations of those two. Whatever power is ascribed to any given object, that too is the Goddess Śivā, the Sovereign.

Śarva is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) of all; these objects that possess power are the manifestations of Śarva. The wise know Gaurī to be the power inherent in those objects. The eight primary natures (prakṛtis) are celebrated as the forms (mūrtis) of the Goddess, and likewise her transformations (vikṛtis) are her manifestations pervading the body, just as sparks are remembered as being manifold within fire. [These are] the individual souls (jīvas).

All things, from Śarva down to the dualities, have attained the state of truth; all the bodies of embodied beings are forms of Gaurī, and likewise all embodied beings are established as Śaṅkaras. Maheśvara, the Lord, assumes the nature of the enjoyer (the subject), while Umā assumes the nature of the object of enjoyment. Śaṅkara sustains the entire collection of created things that are to be produced and destroyed.

The beloved, the Creator, the servant, the Soul of the Universe, and the one whose crest is the crescent of the young moon—the Sovereign of the Earth bears the form of the objects of sight as her subjects; the Lord of the Universe, the Divine One, is the seer, the wielder of power, the staff, and the crest-jewel of his disciples. The entire collection of flavors is the form of Umā, and the entire collection of fragrances is likewise so. Śambhu is the father who provides nourishment, and the Lord of the World is the brother. The Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, assumes the state of the object of thought.
The Great Lord Maheśvara, the Soul of the Universe, is the mantra; the object to be known is the form of the world, and Pārvatī, the beloved of Hara, is its activity.
The Lord, the Blessed One whose crest is the young moon, is the worshipper; the goddess Umā is the form of the pedestal (pīṭha), and Śaṅkara is the form of the liṅga.
Having installed [the liṅga] according to the prescribed rites, the gods and demons worship it. Whatever objects bear the mark of the liṅga, they are all manifestations of Śarva.

Whatever manifestations exist, marked by the portions of objects—extending from heaven to the netherworld (pātāla), up to the end of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) within the eight spheres—it is to be known that everything is the form of Umā; the Knower is the Lord Maheśvara. The Goddess, the beloved of the Destroyer of Tripura, maintains the state of the field (kṣetra);
the Blessed One, the slayer of Death, assumes the state of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). These two remain established in every form.

Those seeking the highest good should always worship, prostrate to, and contemplate them at all times. It is stated in the *Samayācāra*: "The female form is everywhere considered to be the offering (*āhuti*) for all; she is to be known as the embodiment of Śakti, while the male is the embodiment of Śiva.
In this manner, the nature of other names should also be understood; therefore, by the utterance of those [names], that very deity [is invoked].

Because there is no difference in the result produced by the mere utterance of the name, and because the injunction for the utterance of the name includes only those things that convey [the deity], these [names] should be recited in the dative case during worship;
in *homa* and worship they are followed by *svāhā*, while in *nyāsa* and *tarpaṇa* they are followed by *namaḥ*. Thus it is declared that one's own name is the mantra for all beings.

Since the *Brahmapurāṇa* itself is an authoritative source for this, it cannot be argued that these [names] do not possess the status of names at all; for, by being recited within this context, there is no obstacle to their being names—just as with technical designations such as *vṛddhi*—as their status as names is established through their inherent power (*śakti*) within that specific textual arrangement. Furthermore, it has already been stated that because they are excluded from the *stotra*, there is no separate performance of them for the purpose of destroying sins.

Otherwise, there would result the loss of the designation "Thousand Names" (*sahasranāma*). Since this meaning is thus established by logic, it also follows that in the *Sahasranāmastotras* mentioned in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* and other texts, there is an injunction for worship by means of the names explicitly uttered aloud.
And in this regard [it is said]: "With these thousand names he praised the Bull-bannered Lord; the All-pervading One bathed him and worshipped him with lotus-fragrance."

The passage beginning with "jairiti" is from the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, which states: "Then he praised the Supreme Lord with a thousand names, having worshipped the Bull-bannered One (Śiva) with lotuses for each name. Furthermore, the narrative from the *Ādityapurāṇa* also serves as corroborating evidence;

this is the general direction [of the argument]. Since the dative case is prescribed for the words "namaḥ," "svasti," and "svāhā," the determination of their forms is provided here for the sake of convenience.

We shall explain the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). In the case of words ending in *ā*, when the fourth-case singular suffix *ṅe* is applied and the augment *āṭ* is added, there is *vṛddhi*. In the case of words ending in *ī*, when the augment *āṭ* is added, there is *vṛddhi*. In the case of words ending in *o*, according to the rule "when a suffix beginning with a *ṅit* follows, there is shortening," the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* applies; however, because of the rule "there is *guṇa* [before a suffix beginning with a vowel]," *guṇa* occurs. Otherwise, it is the same as in the case of *ānandī*; the difference in form therein is merely occasional (*kāryika*). This is the procedure for those ending in consonants.

Thus it is said that [the name] is like the form of a husband's brother (*devara*). In this context, because she is the primary one and the abode of all auspiciousness, he first introduces the names of the deities:

*Oṃ Tārā*. Here, the etymology is according to the Great Atharvaṇa Śruti: "She who saves (*trāyati*) is Tārā. Thus, the suffix *ac* is indicated by the rule beginning with *pañci* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). The *Bhairavī Tantra* also states: *Tā...*

Because she is red (rakta), she is the one who always bestows liberation through happiness; and when considering her as the protector (tāra) within saṃsāra, she likewise culminates in that very state.

Thus, her status as the cause for the supreme human goal in the form of liberation is revealed, and this will become clear in the subsequent passages. Alternatively, "tāra" refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om); because she is associated with mantras joined with that [syllable], she is endowed with the mouth of the Vedas and so forth.

She is called *Tārā* because she enables one to cross over the three worlds (*tribhuvana*). She is *Phetkāriṇī* because of her practice of incantation (*phetkara*). She is *Praṇava* because she is of the nature of Brahman, or because she causes the attainment of *svadhā*; for the scripture states: "The designation of Brahman is remembered as threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*.

Alternatively, she is *Praṇava* because she is the form of the wife of Sugrīva; thus it is said in the *Matsya Purāṇa* in the speech of the Goddess to Dakṣa: "O Tārā, [the one on] Kiṣkindha... [and so forth].
The word *rātrī* refers to the Goddess Buddhidevī; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, it means "mother," "Tārā," "Sugrīvā," or "the wife of a teacher.

It is called "night" because she possesses that form, according to the statement: "The Goddess is of the nature of night, while Maheśvara is of the nature of day. Furthermore, regarding the time for her worship, it is said: "How can one who wanders at night, having failed to perform the worship of Śakti during the night, be a devotee of Īśāna or a Kaulika? Thus, she is the time for worship.

Because of such Smṛti passages as "At night, spirits and powers wander about," and because she has been made dark by the Blessed Lady who entered his belly through the word *brahma*—or because she is a specific form of Power (*śakti*), or because she is a specific form of Yoginī, or because she is propitious during her worship at this time—it is called *mahārātri*. And it is said in the Vīra... [text ends].

In the *Ratnatantra*, it is stated: "That which follows midnight for two *muhūrtas* is designated as the 'Great Night' (*mahārātri*). Thus, the second and third *praharas* of the night constitute the "Great Night," according to the statement of Devala cited in the *Hemādri*: "The Great Night should be known as the two *praharas* situated in the middle.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "O Maheśānī, when one *prahara* of the night has passed, [perform] the worship of the heroes (*vīra-pūjā*). (3)

Regarding "Kālarātri," it is stated in the *Varāha Purāṇa*: "She whom they know as the goddess Kālarātri, the cause of dissolution—that goddess is celebrated as Saṃhāriṇī (the Dissolver), [known as] Kālarātri. Likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O fair-faced one, Rudra is the supreme reality, while Śiva is indeed motionless; yet the power of Rudra, which devours [all], is of the nature of *Namā* (the Bowing One). By this, [she is established] as the Lord (*Īśvara*) through her capacity to destroy the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)."

The proof for that [conclusion] has also been indicated there; likewise, in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*: "Indeed, the entire world, from the cosmic egg down to the binary atomic dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), is perishable by means of an agent possessing effort, like a jar being destroyed before our eyes. O Kunteya, at the end of a kalpa, all beings go to my own nature (*prakṛti*); then, at the beginning of a new kalpa, I emit them forth once again."

Thus, because she is the presiding deity (*prādhidevatā*) of external objects, Śaunaka has stated that there are many such treasures mentioned in the *Śruti*. One should diligently perform here as well the previously described procedure for worship, for which Kālarātri is the presiding deity. Regarding the term "Kapālinī," Amara states that *kapāla* means a skull or a potsherd (*karpara*). She who possesses the skull [is Kapālinī]. She who [protects] the root...

The master Rddhoddhāṃsthitin says that it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra*: "She who possesses a pair of hands joined with a skull and a blue lotus. Regarding the word *Kālikā*, Amara states: "Kāla means dark, black, or deep blue. From the form ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (*kālikā*), the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of "belonging to" (*tasyedam*). Indeed, it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "O Pārvatī, when she had emerged, she too became black (*kṛṣṇā*)."
Likewise, in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, it is stated that she who is known as Kālī and has made her abode on the Himālaya is Mahātārā;
thus, Tārā is remembered as Kālikā. Through the perception of difference between these two, the loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises.
As it is said in the *Kālītantra*: "As is Kālī, so is Tārā; as is Tārā, so is Unmukhī. The meaning is that Unmukhī is Śilamastā.

Therefore, because of the extension [of the rule] to that subject, the identity of the object should be understood; as it is said in the *Gandharva Tantra*: "As is Kālī, so is Tārā; she who is Tārā is indeed Kālikā. There is no difference between the two. Alternatively, according to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *kaṃ* means 'mouth' (*mukha*) or 'head' (*śīrṣa*) in the sense of water"; and according to the *Amara* lexicon: "*Alīkam* means the forehead (*lalāṭa*) or the temple (*goha*)"; thus, those whose temples (*alikāni*) are on their heads (*ke*).

Because of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the word] ending in the seventh case [is placed] first when it is a qualifier," this very injunction serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a *bahuvrīhi* compound may occur even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vya-dhikaraṇatva*). Thus, in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, it is said: "She who desires the state of a *phetkāriṇī* [should meditate on her] adorned with five skulls joined by white bone-slabs, and embellished with the five mudrās. Here, the word "desire" (*kāma*) refers to the god of love (*smara*).

The word *lākha* means "the universe" (*viśva*), according to the *Viśva-prakāśa* lexicon. He gives that [universe]; thus he is the *Ātitika*, one whose intent is the giving of objects that have become the objects of desire.

And it has been said in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Having attained [this state], great-souled poets of pure intellect consider nothing whatsoever to be unattainable for the sake of dharma, action, wealth, and liberation. Regarding *māyā*, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "The power (*śakti*) of that all-pervading Progenitor is called *māyā*."

By her, the Lord, the master of illusion (māyāvī), the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), causes this world to revolve; for it has been stated therein: "O Śarva, you are the power of all illusions. Thus says the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā (māyin). In that context, according to the Sāṃkhya school, "Māyā" refers to the root-prakṛti, which is the state of equilibrium among the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; however, the Vedāntins [regard it] as concealment (āvaraṇa).

The *Liṅga Purāṇa* states: "The wise say that Śiva alone is the Lord (Īśvara), and they know Māyā to be Gaurī. This description of [Māyā] as having the same nature as Him is because the Lord is the perceiver of Prakṛti, while Brahman is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, it is because [Māyā] is a mantra whose essence is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Māyā; for since each individual seed-syllable is also heard to be a mantra, these seed-mantras (*bījamantra*) are independent.

The [mantras] of Syāmarī grant all accomplishments. Regarding the term *Mahāmāyā*, as in the case of Maheśvara and others, it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "By this Mahāmāyā, the world is deluded. Furthermore, according to the root *māy* meaning "to know," *māyā* is knowledge; moreover, from the observation of the *Nighaṇṭu*, the word *māyā* refers to supreme knowledge. This is clearly evident at the outset.

Upon its establishment, it should be understood that the term *mahāmāyā* refers to the supreme consciousness (*caitanya*) which arises inevitably through its own functional activity (*vṛtti*). (9) Regarding the word *mahotsava*: according to Amara, "that which has a great festival (*utsava*) is a *mahotsava*"; thus, this is an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) known as *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the appearance of a tautology). Alternatively, [the word] *mahaḥ* means splendor (*tejaḥ*). And that [splendor], by virtue of the meaning, belongs to the opponents; therefore, from the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *kvip*, [the form *mahaḥ* is derived].
Such is this sacrifice (*sava*), consisting of fame, worship, and so forth; according to Amara, *sava*, *adhvara*, and *yāga* are synonyms for sacrifice. It is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"In the assembly or debate, it is a speech that paralyzes opponents and causes the loss of knowledge for rival scholars through the offering of a *bali*.
In the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*: "By the mere knowledge of the mantra, two powers arise... [the text continues with *tātkā*].

It should be spoken of by those devoted to poetry and the arts as being "delighted in great giving" (*mahādānaratā*). Regarding this, the *Āditya Purāṇa* states that the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*) is the supreme gift, and no other gift is heard to be superior to it. Likewise, it is said in the *Kālī Tantra*: "Sanskrit words, Prakrit words, as well as worldly and Vedic ones—all these come under the control of the practitioner and bow down before them."

In the Rudrayāmala, it is said: "He whose intellect is unimpeded regarding the scriptures is victorious even in debate; if a man knows the Matsyasūkta, he shines like another Vācaspati. Regarding the word *yajña*: it is that which is worshipped (*ijyate*) or honored (*pūjyate*). Furthermore, in the mantra "The gods sacrificed with sacrifice" (*yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ*), the authors of the Mantra-bhāṣya have also explained it as referring to ritual action (*karman*). Alternatively, the meaning is that "sacrifice" (*yajña*) exists in her because she is the intended object (*uddeśyabhūta*) of that [action].

Since sacrifice (*yajña*) consists precisely in the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity, [the text says] "adorned with all sacrifices" (*sarvayajñopabhuṣitā*). This means she is adorned—meaning satisfied—by the practitioner's state of being free from doubt and so forth, which constitutes a sacrifice. And it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "A mantrin who is full of doubt becomes one who has violated the Guru’s bed; therefore, O Great Goddess, one should always remain free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). (12-13)

In the term *candravaktrā*, the comparison is conveyed through a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose face is like the moon. As stated by the teacher Daṇḍin: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound [is used] in cases such as *śaśāṅkavadanā* (*moon-faced*), with the remainder [of the meaning] being the indicator of similarity" (Kāvyādarśa 2.65). (14) In *cakorākṣī*, the term means "she whose eyes are like those of a *cakora* bird. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the first member is the object of comparison (*upamāna*), followed by the elision of the final member of the compound. Much...

Regarding the term *brīhausavapya-kṣṇoḥ*: the suffix *ṣac* is applied [to form *akṣi*], and by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Thus, *cāru-netrā* means "one who has beautiful eyes. According to the *Amara-kośa*, *cāru* means "beautiful," "lovely," or "charming"; alternatively, it may mean "a lovely garment. This is because it is stated in the *Mantra-bheda* that the Goddess possesses a pair of garments illuminated like camphor and the moon. Regarding *sa-locanā*: this is a *nitya-samāsa* (invariable compound), and its analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose eyes (*locanāni*) are beautiful (*somanāni*). 3. Tri.

"Netrā" means she whose eyes consist of the moon, the sun, and fire—this is the intended sense. Likewise, in the *Nīlatantra*: "Adorned with three eyes like the orb of the rising sun and so forth. (18) "Calapadmākṣī": the word "cala" (moving) is an epithet intended to indicate the flickering nature of her eyes; the rest is clear. (19) "Kuraṅgākṣī": according to Halāyudha, "eṇa," "kuraṅga," "hāraṇa," and "mṛga" all mean deer. (20) "Manoharā" means beautiful—this is the intended sense.

Or [she is called Vāmā] because she removes ignorance (*avidyā*), or because she possesses passion for that which is the remover of *vāma* (evil). (21) She is *Brāhmī*: by the rule of *nipātana* stating "born from Brahmā" (*brahma-ja*), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Thus, in the Varāha Purāṇa, after describing the three forms of the Goddess, it says:
"That which is the form of Śiva as Brāhmī, by her she indeed creates progeny; with a gentle form, O fair-hipped one, Brāhmī is the ordainer of creation."

Next, (22) it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* that she is "Nārāyaṇī," and in the *Varāha Purāṇa*: "O Supārśva, that goddess of beautiful form and slender waist, who bears the conch and discus and is of a red complexion, became Vaiṣṇavī; this Vidyā, worshipped by Nārāyaṇa, bestows all prosperity. Or, according to the mention of her specific forms, (22) she is "Jyotsnā," and the moon is the Vidyā.

In that [context], there is an over-extension [of the term] by such expressions as "moonlight" (*jyotsnā*) and "darkness" (*tamisra*). Alternatively, it may mean "that which is supreme among the purifiers"; here, *ślā* means purity, and the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of existence. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose *jyā* (bowstring) is supreme. According to Śāśvata, *jyā* refers to the bowstring (*maurvī*), the earth (*vasundharā*), and so on. In the sense of "supreme on the earth," it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. The meaning is that she is superior to other causes of purification, being the cause for the excellence of purification for her devotees. (24)

"Cārukeśī" [is formed] from "svāṅga" with the suffix *ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.54). "Sulocanā": "sulocaḥ" means that which can be easily seen (*locayitum śakyaḥ*); she whose salutation (*namaskāra*) is not [otherwise]—the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *nam* because it is so observed in the *Ekākṣarakośa*. This amounts to saying she is "easily propitiated.
She is "Vārāhī" because she is a specific form of Śakti; as stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*: "There are other [forms] in Kāśī, such as Vārāhī and Kratu-vā."

A man who bows with devotion to her in the presence of Rāhu does not sink into calamities; or rather, he is carried away by the serpent—the best of serpents, for according to the *Abhidhāna*, "ahi" denotes both Vṛtrāsura and a snake—and she is his [consort], Vārāhī. Akṣobhya is the one upon whose head all reside, the three-fold form (Trimūrti) who assumes the form of a Nāga, according to the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Akṣobhya is the Ṛṣi of this [mantra], and its metre is said to be Bṛhatī."
Furthermore, from the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "She who bestows boons, whose matted locks possess the excellence of the Naga Akṣobhya," and from the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
"The fierce Vārāhī, terrible with a pestle and fangs, who supports the earth, was born from the back [of Varāha] and stands upon all the Nagas"—she is Vārāhī in this division of the Mothers.
Also, according to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *vārāhī* refers to a type of tree, water, and also to a medicinal herb named *gṛṣṭi*. (27) *Vāruṇī* refers to a specific tree and to water.

The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The west, the army, and the sun. Alternatively, she is *Vāsiṣṭhī*, because she belongs to Vasiṣṭha, who is her worshipper; for it has been stated in such passages as "the Goddess worshipped by Vasiṣṭha does not grant swift results" (*Tāsa-ṭīkā*). (28) She is *Vidyā* because she is the cause of liberation; thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "That eternal supreme Vidyā is the cause of liberation; [it should be] recited... (*japyā*).

In the *Anuvṛtti*, it is stated that "among the worlds, the world of the gods is the best by virtue of knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, based on this scriptural testimony (*śruti*), or because [the deity] possesses that nature, or because in the *Samayācāra* it is said: "Some mantras are proclaimed as male, while others are celebrated as *vidyās*; mantras whose deities have masculine names are [male], whereas those with feminine names are remembered as *vidyās*. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*: "The distinction between mantra and *vidyā*..."

There are two types of mantra families: mantras are to be known as having male deities, while vidyās have female deities. Furthermore, regarding the Mahāvidyās, it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Dhimastā, Vidyā, Bhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and she whose essence is Kamalā—these [are the Mahāvidyās]."

She is proclaimed as the Great Knowledge (*Mahāvidyā*) and the Supreme Great Knowledge (*Mahāvidyā*); she is extremely difficult to attain in the worlds and is saluted by the six-faced one (*Ṣaḍānana*). (30) She is called *Maheśvarī*; here the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for feminine derivation from a masculine term (*puṃyoga-lakṣaṇa*). From the *Matsyapurāṇa*, [the form] is *Mahākālī Maheśvarī*. (31) Regarding the phrase "she whose hair is tawny and curled" (*piṅgā-kuñcita-keśā*), the particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*hu-tu-ci-smaha vai pādapūraṇe*), according to the *Amara-kośa*, and thus the letter *ca* is redundant. It is likewise so.

The term *piṅgākucitāvakracakreśā* is a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose hair is tawny, curly, and wavy. Being characterized by *ūrmimatva* (the state of having waves) implies limitation by time; thus, the meaning is that she is the nature of the non-dual reality (*advaitātmatattva*). As it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Know me to be the supreme power (*paramā śakti*) resting upon Maheśvara—non-different, imperishable, and unique, whom those seeking liberation behold" (40). She is eternal.

Because of the Vedic revelation that "Brahman is eternal bliss, while everything else is suffering," the meaning is that [the Goddess] is of His very nature. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, it is said: "In the ultimate sense, those who contemplate reality—the yogis—declare a difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), yet they perceive their non-difference.

The word "ultimately" (*paramārthataḥ*) connects with the second half of this verse. (41) She is called *Nandā* because she gladdens her devotees; for the *Matsya Purāṇa* states, "Nandā is on the ridge of Himavat."

"Bhadrā" is derived from the root *bhadr* (to make auspicious) with the suffix *ṇya*, followed by the *pacādyac* suffix; it is a specific ritual act (*karaṇa-viśeṣa*) or a specific lunar day (*tithi-viśeṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "I am Bhadrā, and Bhadrā is I," [it refers to] the *viṣṭi* yoga being excluded on the Great Eighth (*mahā-aṣṭamī*). A statement cited in all authoritative treatises (*sarva-nibandha*) within the section on Navarātri states: "If anyone performs my worship on the Great Eighth when the *viṣṭi* has been abandoned, the fruit of that worship shall not belong to him; by that, I have been insulted."

Regarding "Nīlasarasvatī," Amara states that *gīḥ*, *vāk*, *vāṇī*, and *sarasvatī* are synonyms. It is stated in the *Candrikā* that she descended to the world from the lake in the realm of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) after becoming a river due to a curse. Furthermore, it is said in the *Śrīrudrayāmala*:
"At this very time, having reached the summit of Mount Meru and performed my recitation (*japa*) for three yugas, I remained there. My [face] was turned upward...

Formerly, she emerged from the mass of light and splendor of the mouth of the bee-like [Brahmā] and, having been restrained by the *colā* (garment) in the lake, became blue-colored; thus she was first called *Gāyatrī*.

Because she protects (*trāyate*) one who sings (*gāyan*), she is remembered as *Gāyatrī*. This is stated in the *Niprapañcasāra* and other texts. Regarding the suffix *-ī*, the *Padacandrikā* states that it is formed with the suffix *ka* after the prefix *anu-* (though here applied to *gā-*) and the suffix *ṅīṣ* due to her belonging to the *gaura*-class. Thus it is said in the *Vrāhma Purāṇa*. She is indeed that.

Because she protects those who sing (*gāyat*), she is therefore remembered as *Gāyatrī*; and because she protects the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which are the *gayas*, she is for that reason called *Gāyatrī*.

Both of these etymologies are recorded in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Since she protects one who sings, she is therefore remembered as Gāyatrī; the *gayas* are remembered as the vital breaths by those who have seen the further shore of the Vedas. Or rather, she is remembered as Gāyatrī because she protects the vital breaths of one who recites her. This is also stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.

"Gāyatrī is the mouth of the Vedas"—this is the statement of the Goddess. "Gāyatrī indeed is all this, whatever exists here"—such is the Vedic passage; the Vedāntins maintain that the word Gāyatrī refers to the Supreme Brahman. (45) *Sucaritri*: she whose conduct (*caritra*) is beautiful; from the root *car*, the suffix *kadṛtra* is applied according to the Uṇādi rules. (46) *Kaulavrata-parāyaṇā*: because it pertains to the lineage (*kula*), there is the Kaula vow as taught in their scriptures; she is devoted (*parāyaṇā*) to that.

The meaning is "unattached. According to Śāśvata, the word *paṇya* is understood as that which is desired by those who rely [on it]. In the Mahācīna-krama, she is said to be the one who bestows the fruit of the tree of liberation; this is from the Kālītantra (47). Regarding the term *Hiraṇyagarbha*, the word *hiraṇya* refers to the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) because he is born from it, as stated in the Purāṇa: "Thus the golden egg came into being. This has been said in the Jñānārṇava regarding Brahmā.

O Supreme Sovereign, the form of the creation of the Mothers is to be understood as the power of Vāmā; there is no doubt that Brahmā is a preta. According to the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, it is stated: "One should meditate on the goddess with a single tawny and fierce matted lock, her body slightly bent"—and this state of being slightly bent (*kuñcita*) is mentioned in the *Sāmudrika* [treatise on physiognomy].
She is "the embodiment of the Great Sacrifice" because she is the embodiment of the Vedas; or else, because she made Dakṣa’s sacrifice her own.

The meaning is that when one forms a mental image (*rūpayati*) and perceives [the deity] as such, then even though that Being is invoked by the name "I," it is understood as being one's own; this is well-known from the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* and other texts. Alternatively, He makes Himself—the Self—possessing form (*rūpavantam*) for the sake of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*);
likewise, there is the propitiation of the deities who fulfill the causality defined by the desire for heaven as the desired effect.

The sense is that [the deity] is the substratum for the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the ritual form (*rūpa*). According to the Vedic text, "Indra satiates him with progeny and cattle because he has been satiated," the Vedāntins maintain that the propitiation of the deity is indeed the operation of sacrifices and other rites which are otherwise quickly perishable. Even in the Nyāya view, it is so because [the deity] is the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Alternatively, [the term *svārūpā* may mean] she whose own form (*svarūpa*)—that is, her essential nature—is present in the sacrifices through the substances and deities.
The Mīmāṃsaka tradition holds that the form of a sacrifice consists of its constituent parts (*vatehiyajña*); by this, there is an indication that she embodies all the deities.

(33) Regarding "Gaurī": according to Amara, *gaura* means "ruddy," "white," or "yellow. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, [it says]: "O Lotus-born One, I shall behold the divine body of the Goddess, resembling gold; and I shall become renowned in the world as Gaurī. Kāny...

*Kubjā-tathā-gaurī-matsya-purāṇam* (34). Regarding *campakavarṇā*, Amara states that *campaka* is a golden flower (*hemapuṣpaka*). Alternatively, it may refer to the red flower with bitter leaves, as stated by Muṇḍamāla: "The *campaka* is the red flower and the *nāgakesara*. Or else, it refers to the red stone (*raktopala*), for Vīracūḍāmaṇi states in the section on oblations (*homaprakaraṇa*) that "the *puṣpaka* is the Lakṣmī-stone (*mahīlakṣmī*). (35) Regarding *kṛśāṅgī*, it is as prescribed [in the texts]. *Ava*.

The meaning is that she is so called because she has reduced [the world] from the ascendant onwards; or, it is due to the meditation on Bhadrakālī as "the one with hollow eyes" (*koṭarākṣī*) who devours hunger (*kṣut*).

(36) She is "worshipped by the *kula*" (*kulapūjitā*); the word *kula* refers to specific substances as defined in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*) of the Āgamas, and this is stated in the *Kālītantra* and other texts.

(37) She is "the embodiment of all bliss" (*sarvānandasvarūpā*), because liberation-bliss (*mokṣānanda*) and the others are included within it; for all [other forms of] bliss are but a fraction of this bliss.

For it is stated in the Śruti: "They subsist on [the remains of] food that has been offered"; and as spoken by the Blessed One: "As much benefit as there is in a well for one who drinks from it when water is overflowing everywhere, so much benefit is there for a Brāhmaṇa who knows in all the gods. (38) She is the savior from all distress; thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti: "Now, she is the savior from fear, the savior from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the savior from great sins..."

"O Takatāriṇī!"—thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "Wherever there are fierce Rākṣasas, venomous serpents, enemies, robbers, or armies; wherever there is a forest fire or even in the midst of a battle—there, abiding, you protect the universe. (39) Regarding the word *nitya*, Amarasimha states: "In the neuter, *nitya* means 'constant' (*śīghra*) and so forth; when it denotes a quality among these [three genders], it is applied according to the specific object. Thus, she is devoid of limitation (*pariccheda*) caused by substance, space, or time.

The nature of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) to a distinction is the delimitation of the object (*vastu-pariccheda*); the nature of being the counter-positive to absolute non-existence is the delimitation of space (*deśa-pariccheda*).
[She] creates everything; this entire world is her effect. It is the teaching of the Wise One that for the Lord there is neither effect nor instrument.
(48) "Bhūgarbhā" means she whose womb is the earth, because [the world] arises from her; in reality, however, it is because the *yantra* is situated within a triangle.

"One should draw a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus with cow dung, surrounded by a city-gate (*bhūpura*) rich with excellent petals; this is the *yantra* consisting of a single womb," according to the words of the *Phetkāriṇī*. Regarding the phrase "with cow dung," there is an alternative reading, "with sandalwood. The ultimate truth is that, as in the *Kaulāvatī* and other texts, the intention is the superimposition of non-duality, such that just as there is no difference between the body and the self, so too is there none between the *yantra* and the deity. (45) vi.

Because it is the withdrawer [of all things] into the womb of Śiva, and because it is woven through everything as its true nature, there exists the fivefold aspect consisting of "Being," "Shining," "Pleasant," "Form," and "Name. Of these, the first three are the form of Brahman, while the latter two are the form of the world. In ether, air, fire, water, and earth, and among gods, animals, humans, and so forth, Being, Consciousness, and Bliss are undivided; only Form and Name are differentiated, according to the statement: "He who knows a hundred Vedas... (Śata-veda).
The suffix *vin* in the word *yaśasvinī* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *asyāyām* etc., in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*), constant connection (*nityayoga*), or excellence (*atiśāyana*).

Furthermore, "glory" (*yaśas*) here consists in being the subject matter of the purport of all the Vedāntas by virtue of being the Self of Brahman; this is clearly established in the first chapter of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā. She is called "the daughter of Himavat," for *Himavat* is a mountain distinct from the *Niṣadha* and *Vindhya* mountains.

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, Nārada says to the Lord of Himācala: "O Śivā, you who are the mother of all the worlds and the source of the past and future, have been born upon your field with the brilliance of fire for the sake of purification. In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "I was indeed begotten by the gods from the Supreme Lord (Maheśvara) after they had censured my father Dakṣa, a reviler of Maheśvara, for the purpose of establishing Dharma through the propitiation of Him."

Because she was born from the body of Menā, she has taken refuge in you as her father. (52) "Divya" is used here because it belongs to the class beginning with "diś" (directions), as the *Viśva* lexicon states:
"Divyam refers to cloves (*lavaṅga*), to the divine (*valau*), and to that which exists in heaven (*divi-bhave*). The meaning is that she is fond of the conduct of heroes (*vīra*).

Since there is little difference between a hero and the divine, there is no distinction between the divine and the hero; whatever difference there is, that is now being stated: even though he is peaceful (*śānta*), he is also... [the text continues].

[He] is sweet-voiced, endowed with arts and beauty, and generally heroic like the sun; he is the crest-jewel of those whose minds are uplifted, according to the *Bhāvaprakāśana*. (53) Regarding "divine garments and ornaments," the meaning is already implied; it is stated in the Purāṇa: "Having worshipped the Daughter of the Mountain with either silk or cotton garments, and having adorned her with ornaments, one shall attain the status of Indra. Silk (*aṇḍaja*) means [garment made of] cotton."

Alternatively, that which is the supreme divine garment is the space in the form of the *brahmarandhra*; [she is so called] because she dwells therein. As it is stated in the *Nīlatantra*: "Having arisen during the northern watch (*uttarayāma*), one should meditate upon Ugratāriṇī, whose nature is like a thread, entering from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*. (54) Regarding the word *jagat*, it is a nipātana in the *uṇādi* group according to the rule beginning with *pṛṣan mahat*. O all you, Brahmā and the others!

Because of the statement in the *Iti-kula-cūḍāmaṇi*, "born from the non-existence of a portion of Me" (mamaṃśābhāvasaṃbhavā), [the term] "Jagaddhātrī" (the Sustainer of the World) is formed with a genitive compound ending in a word derived from the root *dhṛ* (to sustain). This is because the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.2.15)—which prohibits such compounds when the agent is expressed by a word ending in *-tṛ* or *-aka*—is understood to be an exception (*jñāpana*) due to the inclusion of the word *kartṛ* (agent) there. Thus, a genitive compound is formed with that suffix. And so says the Śruti: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, heaven and earth are held apart. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9)

"Standing thus" (56) means she is the benefactor of the worlds; the meaning is that she benefits [them] by bestowing sound and so forth. According to the Bhāṣya school, since the inclusion of the suffix *su* is not for the purpose of excluding prefixes (*upasarga*), the formation of the *ṇini* suffix is established. The meaning of "of the worlds" (*jagatām*) is that, by referring to the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*), she is the giver of liberation to all beings. (57) Regarding "Aindrī": the word *indra* is a nipāta according to the rule beginning with *ṛjyeṃdra*.

"Vajrapāṇi, Mahādeva, Śacī, and the daughter of the Lord of Mountains"—thus says the *Liṅgapurāṇa* (58). "Saumyā": this is derived from Soma; [the suffix] *sauma-* is formed with the feminine suffix *ī*, which is absent due to the Vedic usage [of the rule] *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85) (59). "Yāmyā": this is derived from Yama; according to the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* and the statement of Vāmana that it applies to Yama and others, the suffix *ṇya* is used. According to the opinion of the *Bhāṣya*, Dīkṣita states that the suffix *tṣyac* is applied. Furthermore, "Yāmyāḥ"... [text continues].

"The [place of] torments," so say the teachers beginning with Udayana. "Yama himself is the god Hara; his beloved is the Daughter of the Mountain"—thus says the *Liṅga Purāṇa*. Regarding the name Vāruṇī: "Varuṇa is the mountain-dweller, the wielder of the noose"—so says the *Amara-kośa*. "They choose a boon (*vara*); he is the giver of boons (*varada*) to those seeking boons. Because he is declared to be the one who causes the flow (*varaṇa*) of the elements (*dhātu*), he is remembered as Varuṇa"—thus from the *Sāmba Purāṇa*. Varuṇa is the Lord Rudra, the bull... [text ends].

The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (61) states: "She who bestows all goals" (*sarvārthadāyinī*). Regarding the term *Vāyavī*: although one would expect the suffix *ya* (yielding *vāyavya*) by the rule *vāyvṛtupitruṣaso yaḥ*, nevertheless, when there is a desire to express a mere relationship (*saṃbandha*), the suffix *ṇya* (yielding *vāyava*) should be applied. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (62) further states: "She is the moon-crested Lord Vāyu, Śiva, the beautiful Śivā. Regarding the term *Āgneyī*: [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after the word *agni*, resulting in *āgneyī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (63) states: "She is the daughter of Agni. Regarding the term *Māheśvarī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *maheśvara*, resulting in *māheśvarī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (64) states: "She is the mother of the world, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Maheśvara. Regarding the term *Kaumārī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *kumāra*, resulting in *kaumārī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (65) states: "She is the mother of Kumāra, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Kumāra. Regarding the term *Cāmuṇḍā*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *caṇḍamuṇḍa*, resulting in *cāmuṇḍā*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (66) states: "She is the one who destroyed Caṇḍamuṇḍa, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Caṇḍamuṇḍa. Regarding the term *Mahāmāyā*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *mahāmāyā*, resulting in *māhāmāyī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (67) states: "She is the great illusion, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Mahāmāyā. Regarding the term *Vārāhī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *varāha*, resulting in *vārāhī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (68) states: "She is the one who slew the boar, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Varāha. Regarding the term *Nārasiṃhī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *nṛsiṃha*, resulting in *nārasiṃhī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (69) states: "She is the one who slew the man-lion, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Nṛsiṃha. Regarding the term *Vaināyakī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *vināyaka*, resulting in *vaināyakī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (70) states: "She is the one who slew Vināyaka, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Vināyaka. Regarding the term *Sārasvatī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *sarasvat*, resulting in *sārasvatī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (71) states: "She is the daughter of Sarasvat, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Sarasvat. Regarding the term *Brahmāṇī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *brahman*, resulting in *brāhmī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (72) states: "She is the wife of Brahmā, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Brahmā. Regarding the term *Raudrī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *rudra*, resulting in *raudrī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (73) states: "She is the wife of Rudra, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Rudra. Regarding the term *Indrāṇī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *indra*, resulting in *aindrī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (74) states: "She is the wife of Indra, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Indra. Regarding the term *Yāmyā*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *yama*, resulting in *yāmyā*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (75) states: "She is the wife of Yama, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Yama. Regarding the term *Kauverī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *kuvera*, resulting in *kauberī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (76) states: "She is the wife of Kuvera, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Kuvera. Regarding the term *Vāruṇī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *varuṇa*, resulting in *vāruṇī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (77) states: "She is the wife of Varuṇa, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Varuṇa. Regarding the term *Vaiṣṇavī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *viṣṇu*, resulting in *vaiṣṇavī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (78) states: "She is the wife of Viṣṇu, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Viṣṇu. Regarding the term *Gāndharvī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *gandharva*, resulting in *gāndharvī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (79) states: "She is the wife of Gandharva, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Gandharva. Regarding the term *Yakṣiṇī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *yakṣa*, resulting in *yākṣī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (80) states: "She is the wife of Yakṣa, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Yakṣa. Regarding the term *Rākṣasī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *rākṣasa*, resulting in *rākṣasī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (81) states: "She is the wife of Rākṣasa, the supreme goddess, the beloved of Rākṣasa. Regarding the term *Paitṛṣvasrī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*, resulting in *paitṛṣvasrī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (82) states: "She is the sister of the father, the supreme goddess, the beloved of the father's sister. Regarding the term *Mātulī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *mātula*, resulting in *mātulī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (83) states: "She is the wife of the maternal uncle, the supreme goddess, the beloved of the maternal uncle. Regarding the term *Sāpatnī*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the word *sapatna*, resulting in *sāpatnī*. The *Liṅgapurāṇa* (84) states: "She is the wife of the co-wife, the supreme goddess, the

By [the words] beginning with "tyādi," the footless one is described; Svāhā is said to be the self of that Agni, who is Paśupati, while the Lord Ṣaṇmukha is called "Putra" by the wise—thus says the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. "Jātavedas is Rudra himself, and Svāhā is the one whose body is half of all"—thus says the *Liṅgapurāṇa* (63). Regarding "Nairṛtī": Nairṛta is "Karvura" and "Kravyād"—thus says the *Śabdārṇava* (64).

The word *daśānī* is derived from the root *daś*, meaning "sovereignty," with the suffix *anaś* according to the rule *tācchīlyavayovacana...* etc., and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* due to its connection with a masculine noun (*puṃyoga*).

Thus, her nature as the embodiment of the powers (*śakti*) of the eight guardians of the directions has been explained. (65) Regarding *Caṇḍikā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *caṇḍa* because it belongs to the *vahv-ādi* group;
furthermore, according to the *Narasimha Purāṇa*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is used for names [of deities]. (67) Regarding "from Sumeru": *meruḥ* refers to *Sumeru*. *Heṃ*.

"Mādrī" is [an epithet of] Amarā, because she is a portion (*ekadeśa*) of that [lake] which is the *utpala* (blue lotus). And it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "On the western slope of Meru, there is a lake known by the name Cola; therein, the goddess herself, Nīlasarasvatī, [is present]. (68) "Beneficial to all" means that, as the cause of every action, she acts as a collaborator (*sahakārin*) for everyone. (69) "Vandyā" (to be saluted): he who is to be known... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete].
The Naiyāyikas maintain that *namaskāra* (salutation) is a specific activity conducive to making oneself known as inferior for the sake of honoring another.

(70) Regarding "with a lolling tongue" (*lalajjihvā*): the root *lal* means "to dangle"; thus, she has four arms and a lolling tongue, according to the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*. In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, it says: "she whose tongue is lolling and who is most terrifying. (71) Regarding "lotus-eyed" (*sarojākṣī*): the meaning is clear; she has eyes like full-blown blue lotuses.

From the statement "tivacanāt" (72): regarding the term *muṇḍasrajavibhūṣaṇā*, according to the opinion of Bhāguri, the suffix *ṭāp* is added after the word *sraj*; furthermore, there is a neuter gender by way of Vedic anomaly (*chāndasavyatyaya*), or else there is a shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *aṅ māpoḥ saṃjñāchandasoh*. Thus, it means "adorned with a garland of shaven heads," as stated in the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra* (73). Regarding the term *sarvānandamayī*: the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of "consisting of that" (*tatprakṛtavacana*). Since the bliss of the Lord (*īśvara*) is eternal, it cannot be produced by means such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).

Although multiplicity is established through the absence of bliss due to the denial of the intermediate species that serve as delimiters, nevertheless, it is stated "all" because the intended meaning is identity with that which possesses abundant bliss—specifically, the state of being devoid of any deficiency relative to other forms of bliss. (74) Regarding the word "all," the *Mahābhārata* states: "In the three worlds, there is nothing anywhere that exists without you. In this context, the term [is used] to denote all things.

The nature of the entire phenomenal world (*jagat-prapañca*) is to be known as *bhāvena* (by way of being), because, according to the ultimate philosophical view (*advaṃtima-mata*), it has the Lord (*Īśvara*) as its material cause (*upādāna*) and is non-different from the Lord. This is supported by the Vedic scripture (*śruti*): "There is no diversity whatsoever here; he goes from death to death who perceives diversity here. Alternatively, from the root *sarva* meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*), the sense is that He "injures all" (*sarva-hiṃsā*) because He possesses the form of Rudra. (75)

"Of the nature of universal bliss" (*sarvānandasvarūpiṇī*): according to the etymology previously stated, the commentators on the *Amara-kośa* explain that "Śiva" means "the corpse" (*śava*). She manifests—that is, she makes manifest as her own nature or brings into being—the bliss of that [corpse]. Alternatively, this is a statement of identity through metaphorical attribution (*bhedopacāra*). (76) Regarding "destruction" (*kṣati*): it is the absence of falling even for the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which possesses weight; it is the support of the palāśa [leaf] which acts as an obstacle to its falling.
"Thus, *dhṛti* [is used] in the sense of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) and fortitude (*dhairya*)," according to the *Viśva-kośa*. "Also, *dhṛti* [refers to] *piṇḍāraka*," according to the *Mātsya-purāṇa*.

(77) Because she is the very nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) capable of retention (*dhāraṇā*) regarding knowledge (*medhā*), [she is called *Medhā*]. "The syllable *maḥ* [denotes] Śiva, Māra, and Māyā," according to the *Viśva-kośa*. She who bestows (*dadhati*) desire (*kāma*) upon that [Śiva] is *Medhā*; the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *dhā*. Because she has the form of *Kālikā*, she is situated above Mahākāla; thus [says] the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
From the *Nidarśana* (78): "Lakṣmī" [is so called]; likewise, from the *Matsyapurāṇa*, it is stated that between Viṣṇu and Rudra there is the *Śrīrudrāntara*.

Regarding this, the *Kalpataru* quotes the *Varāhapurāṇa* (79): "The poetic work (*kāvyam*) concerning mortals that exists between [the sections on] Śrī and Rudra is censured by the scriptures. "Faith" (*śraddhā*) is the certainty regarding the non-occurrence of a result; faith is devotion (*bhakti*).

Some maintain that [the two] are specific sub-classes of the genus *aśraddhātva* (non-faith) and *ajñānatva* (ignorance). By this, their utility for both the path of action (*karma*) and the path of liberation (*mokṣa*) is stated;

for there is the Vedic revelation: "By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered," and from the Vedic revelation: "Having become one whose mind is faith, one should see the Self in the self. Furthermore, [the word *ṛṣi*] is derived as "one who moves through the forest" (*vana-gāmin*), meaning "one who traverses the forest with his feet" (*vana-gatī*); thus, he is a seer (*ṛṣi*).

The status of being *darādi* (beginning with *dṛ*) is stated in the *Kaumudī*; however, in the sense of *yoga* (union), the meaning must be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The root *śī* signifies mere staying, as in the case of "a reservoir of water" (*jalāśaya*). Likewise, in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "She who causes Mahādeva, who is white-complexioned, to lie upon the pure seat of the heart, or who causes Nārāyaṇa to sleep on the serpent"—here, the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root. This is because she is the very nature of *yoganidrā* (the sleep of yoga). This is the intended meaning.

"Even He who created the world, who transcends the world, and who is beyond the world, was brought under the power of sleep by you; O Lord, who is able to praise you?"—thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. (81) Regarding "Rukmiṇī": according to the *Matsya Purāṇa*, "O Rukmiṇī, [you were born] in Dvāravatī. Because she is non-different from Lakṣmī, there is non-difference from Rukmiṇī. In the state of being Rādhā, she becomes Sītā; in the birth of Kṛṣṇa, she is Rukmiṇī.

According to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (82), she is called Jānakī because she is the female offspring (*apatyam*) of Janaka; likewise, she is called Sītā at Citrakūṭa, as explained previously from the Matsya Purāṇa (83). She is called Durgā because she is approached or known with difficulty, according to the Candrikā;
and according to the Mādhavī [commentary] on the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, it is said that she can be reached with difficulty, and in that very same place, he says: "I shall slay the one named Durga."

"The demoness shall become famous as Durgādevī; that very one shall be Mine. Also, in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa: "From this day forward, she shall attain the name 'Durgā' because she was exceedingly difficult to overcome (durga) by the Daitya Durga in battle due to her fierce nature (dhātu). 'Durgamā' is another name for Durgā [derived from] the difficulty of being approached.
When the seeker (mārgaṇa) met with failure against him, she became known as 'Durgamāsurī'—meaning she whose nature is truly invincible. Vedāṃsi.

Because the existence of objects is a property belonging solely to Brahman, the conventional usage of "existence" is applied to things such as jars; for it is said: "Existence, manifestation, pleasure, form, and name—this fivefold aspect is [perceived]. The first three are the nature of Brahman, while the latter two are the nature of the world. (85) *Satyavatī*: she who possesses the eternal truth, knowledge, and so forth, hence the suffix *matup*. (86) *Rati*: the Viśva lexicon states, "The word *rati* is declared to mean a woman beloved by Kāma."

Alternatively, because she is the specific form of the power (*śakti*) of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), [she is called] "Rati" and likewise "Prīti," according to the *Siddhasārasvata* (87). Because she resides on a particular mountain, Kāmākṣa, [she is called] "Kāmākṣa" and "Citrakūṭa," according to the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. For this very reason, there is the wording of the mantra for the worship of the Virgin (*kumārī*): "I worship Kāmākṣā, who is accompanied by many powers."—[from the] *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Therefore, it is said that the *kāmākṣā-yonimaṇḍala* possesses a hundredfold merit compared to that [other] jewel; O Mahādeva, what can be said of its fruit?

(88) It bestows liberation (*mokṣada*), and liberation is non-return (*apunar-nivṛtti*); this is the supreme truth of all doctrines. As it is stated in the *Kiraṇāvalī*: "No one accepts that suffering falls upon one who is liberated. Thus, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, from that...

Seeking the two-fold liberation, one should take refuge in Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess, the supreme Śivā who is the self of all beings; by the grace of this mantra, a Brāhmaṇa attains liberation, according to the Rudrayāmala. From the Kūrma Purāṇa, it is said "Anantā": her sovereignty is beginningless, established, incomparable, and great; through connection with that [Rudra], she is called Anantā by Rudra.

"Paramātmanā" (90). "Nārasiṃhī" because she is the form of the power (*śakti*) of Nṛsiṃha; for it is stated in the *Vāmanapurāṇa*: "Scattering the planets, lunar mansions, and stars with the falling of her mane, the exceedingly fierce Nārasiṃhī was born from the heart of the Clawed One (*nakhinī*).
(91). "Sarasvatī": according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *sarasvatī* refers to a specific river, the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*), and the mountain (*girī*). (92). "Mahādevaratā" [is the reading].

(93) Because she is intensely attached to that [wrath] due to its severity, she is called Caṇḍī; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "Caṇḍī, Kātyāyanī, Hiṃsrā, and Koyanī are recognized as names for women. (94) She is "the one who shatters the staff-like arms of Caṇḍa," meaning she is of a nature that breaks the staff-like arms—which are thick and firm—of Caṇḍa, a particular type of demon. (95) She is "long-haired" because this is a mark of auspicious physical characteristics according to the *Sāmudrika* treatises. (96) Su... [text fragment]

*Keśī-piṅgakeśā*—the meaning is clear. (97–98) *Mahākaca*—the absence of the *t* sound is due to Vedic usage. (99) *Bhavānī*: that from whom everything comes into being (*bhavati*) is *bhava*; his wife is *bhavānī*. By the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. According to the rule *indre varuṇe...* and so forth, the augment *anuk* is added. Regarding the form *sthāneśvare bhavānī*, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states: (100) "Of Lakṣmīdhara, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of words, authoritative statements, and [grammatical] rules..."

In this *Arthacintāmaṇi* composed by Viśveśvara, the son of Rābhidhayudha, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem for the sake of the meaning [of the text], this second chapter—which is not devoid of joy—now begins. Even though it is established that all branches of knowledge reside within the atoms of the first day, here the atoms of the lotus-feet of the Guru manifest themselves; now follows the commentary on the second hundred [verses], beginning with "The wife of Bhava... (bhavapatnī).

Regarding the term *patnī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule *patyurno yajñasaṃyoge*; the letter *n* is enjoined by that rule, as Amara states: "A *patnī* is one whose hand has been taken [in marriage].

Alternatively, through the etymology *pāti* ("she protects"), it means she who is the protectress of the world of existence (*bhava*). This is because Bharata, Vimalabodha, and others have explained it thus in the verse: "May the Aśvins, the lords of the *dāsas*, vanish... (1). [She is called] "the remover of the fear of existence" (*bhavabhītihārā*).

*Bhava* is Śiva, who is attached to the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*); according to the *Viśva* lexicon, it means "one whose birth is dear. According to the *Vārttika*, the compound is formed with the sense of "fear" and "terror" (*bhaya-bhītibhiḥ*). The suffix *ac* is applied to the root *hṛ* (to take away), meaning "she who bestows liberation" (*mokṣadāyinī*). (2) *Śacī* refers to Pulomajā; according to Amara, she is Indrāṇī. The *Mātsya Purāṇa* states that *śac* and *śvac* mean "to go," and likewise that she is Indrāṇī in the world of the gods. (3) She is called *Pauraṃdarī*; according to the rule "vācaṃyama-puraṃdarau ca," this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation).

*Tātsādhuḥ* means "she who is virtuous toward him"; because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, meaning "she who is to be honored by him. Regarding *viṣṇorjāyā*: the word *viṣṇu* is derived from the root *viṣ* with the *uṇādi* suffix *nu*, which is *kit*. He is called *Viṣṇu* because he "pervades" (*viśati*) everything; as stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "Because he pervades the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, he was himself declared to be Viṣṇu by the Self-born One. Regarding the wife: she is called *jāyā* because she "gives birth" (*janayati*).
"May I be born again"—thus says Manu. "This very one, when red with *rajas*, is proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavī," according to the Varāha Purāṇa.
