(5) Regarding "Māheśvarī," the word *maheśvara* has been explained; from it, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. "This very one, when dark like *tamas*, is proclaimed as the goddess Raudrī," based on the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of the Varāha [Purāṇa]. Māheśvarī is three-eyed, mounted upon a bull, and bears a trident; she possesses the great power of the serpent...

"She was born from the glance of Raudrī, [specifically] Kuṇḍalinī"—thus says the *Vāmana Purāṇa*. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that she was born from the "glance" (*īkṣaṇāt*), meaning from the eye, of Māheśvarī.

(6) The word "supreme" (*parā*) means "most excellent. Furthermore, since the term *Parā* is used for Tripurā in works such as the *Prapañcasāra*, she should be understood as the foremost (*agrā*). Regarding the first [interpretation], because it is a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), the form *parasmai* occurs in the dative case; why? As Bhāravi and others state: "In the supreme Person (*parasmin puruṣe*) or in passion (*raje*)" [and so on]. Others [hold the second view].
The distinction regarding the supreme [cause] is as follows: (7) the meaning of "the mother of all" is extremely clear; the word "all" refers to everything other than eternal entities.

(8) The Naiyāyikas define eternality (*nityatva*) as being a non-counterpositive of destruction while being a counterpositive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). By this [definition], it is established that [the supreme cause] is not a substratum of an effectness characterized by an instrumentality residing in something else, while possessing an effectness residing in anything other than itself.

The state of being the substratum of the determined causality has been stated; otherwise, the [scriptural] statement "she is the progenitor of all" would be untenable. Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the nature of the sixteen Nityās, such as Lalitā, Kāmeśvarī, and so forth. (9) Regarding the term *cārvaṅgī*: her limbs (*aṅgāni*) are beautiful (*cārūṇi*), that is, lovely. By the rule *svāṅgāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.54), which serves as an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule *ayogopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.53), [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after the words *aṅga*, *gātra*, and *kaṇṭha*.

According to the statement of the author of the *Ṭīkā* on the *Śiśupālavadha*, and because this meaning is included by the particle *ca* used for the purpose of collecting what has not been explicitly mentioned—as well as from the explanations in the *Dhātupradīpa* and other works—the suffix *chaṅīṣ* [is applied]. In the word *daityanāśinī*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of "offspring" according to the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*;
and the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *naś* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). Thus, whenever there shall be an arising of affliction caused by the Dānavas...

"Descending at such and such times, I shall effect the destruction of my enemies"—thus it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the destroyer of the Daityas, heaven, and so forth, because she bestows liberation (*mokṣa*); for in the commentary on the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*, the Teachers have explained it thus: "The worlds of the Asuras are those which lead to the dense darkness. (11) Regarding the term *ghorarūpā*: the *Viśva* lexicon states, "Ghora means terrible or fearsome."

According to the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, "She whose tongue is lolling and who is most terrifying," the meaning is that she is the very nature of Śiva; or, it may mean she is the one who grasps the aforementioned power.

(12) Regarding "Maheśānī," the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is used here to indicate a connection with a male, as in "the Great Sovereign" (*mahatī cāsau īśānī ca*). (13) Regarding "Kāminī," it is derived from the root *kam* with the suffix *ini* in the sense of "one who desires," or it means "she in whom the desire to love exists."

The suffix *ini* denotes a constant connection (*nityayoga*), because the eternality of the Lord’s will (*īśvarecchā*) is accepted. (14) Regarding the term *varavarṇinī*: Amara states in the section on women that it means "an excellent woman" (*uttamā varavarṇinī*). Svāmī explains it as "she who possesses an excellent complexion" (*vara-varṇo 'syā asti*). Alternatively, it may mean "she whose complexion is excellent" (*varā śreṣṭhā varṇinī yasyāḥ*); due to its being a Vedic [or archaic] form, there is no compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). Or, by intending non-difference (*abhedavivakṣayā*), it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. And this refers to the *ḍākinī* in the form of Chinnamastā.
(15) "Endowed with the movement of left and right" is because it is stated therein that she possesses the movement of both the left and the right.
(16) "Mahāvidyā" means she in whom great, eternal ignorance—meaning she who possesses eternal knowledge—is found.
(17) "Mahāmāyā" means she whose locus and object are the great Māyā, which is manifold due to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts, beginningless, and indefinable, as is well-known in Vedānta.
The meaning is that she is of the nature of Brahman because Brahman is the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), according to the Vedāntic statement: "Brahman alone remains as the ground of all parts.

Although ignorance is one, its manifoldness is accepted due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as per such scriptural passages as: "Indra appears in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*). Alternatively, it refers to her connection with being the support for the practice of mantras during the lunar day (*tithi*) of the new moon (*amāvāsya*).

She is called *amāyākā* because she is free from *māyā*, which consists of false knowledge (*viparīta-jñāna*), doubt (*saṃśaya-jñāna*), and absence [of knowledge]. She is "great" (*mahatī*) because she is the substratum of all knowledge while being devoid of error and doubt; thus, the term *mahatī* forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with *amāyākā*. Since her worship is specifically prescribed therein, she is referred to as such. Alternatively, *amāyāka* refers to that in which *māyā*—in the form of false knowledge, doubt, and absence [of knowledge]—does not exist; the word "great" (*mahat*) then forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with it, meaning she is the locus of all knowledge while possessing the state of being free from delusion and doubt.

The meaning is as follows: "In that regard, delusion (*moha*) is threefold; it is the source of all evils, consisting of the triad of ignorance (*ajñāna*), doubt (*saṃśaya-jñāna*), and false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*)," according to the Smṛti. Alternatively, *mahatīm* means the Great One (*Mahat*), which is characterized by both the qualities of being the object of all things and impermanence; the meaning is that he goes to that [state of] ignorance. Or else, *mahatīm* refers to Mā Lakṣmī; he goes to her, for the Śruti says, "He is the ruler of all. (17)

"Mahāmedhā" means one who possesses great *dhāraṇā* (retentive memory), according to Amara; or it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose *medhā* (intellect) is great," in the sense of the fifth case (*ablative*), meaning that from her [the Goddess] there arises the attainment of great intelligence for those to whom she has spoken. This is because of the previously cited statements from the *Yāmala* and other texts, such as "one whose intellect is unimpeded regarding the scriptures. Alternatively, it may mean "one whose *medha*—derived from the root *medh*, meaning 'to strike' or 'to injure'—is great."

The meanings of *sādi* are stated in the *Kalpadruma* and other works; therefore, the sense is that the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) because it is dear to Bali. Thus, the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states: "The wise practitioner should satisfy Caṇḍikā by the offering of a *bali*. Regarding the term *mahotsava*: according to Amara, *utsa* means a spring, a flow, or a primary stream, and *nirjhara* means a waterfall. [The word *mahotsava*] is derived from the root *gam*, meaning "to go" or "to smell," with the prefix *ati* and the suffix *ap*. It refers to that which greatly exceeds or surpasses a great festival (*mahān utsavaḥ*).

(19) Because the location of the means [of worship] is stated in the Vedic text, "Who [is there] on the riverbank at the edge of the mountain? (19). "Virūpā" means she whose form is transformed (*vikṛta*) due to her terrifying nature; or, she whose form is distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*) because she is supreme among all; or, she whose form has departed (*vigata-rūpa*) because her nature is Brahman—according to such Vedic texts as, "This very imperishable, O Gārgī, which the Brāhmaṇas declare is neither gross nor fine, neither short... (20). Vi...
Regarding her own nature (*svarūpa*), it is stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "She is always to be seen in all beings, everywhere on earth; whatever exists among all beings is not without me.

(21) The word *mṛḍānī* is derived from the root *mṛḍ*, which means "to give happiness," with the suffixes *yac* and *ādyac*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. According to Halāyudha, the form is established by the rule beginning with *drava-ruṇa* etc., as in: "Āryā, Ambikā, and Mṛḍānī. (22) The word *dayita* is derived from the root *mṛḍ* with the suffix *valkabh*.

*Vallabham* means "beloved" according to Amara; *valleti* is a Vedic root meaning "to love," according to Svāmī. Alternatively, by taking the suffix *ka* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), it refers to that which possesses *mṛḍam* (happiness), being connected to it as its producer. *Labhā* is that which has attainment in the form of devotion and so forth; from the root *ḍulabhaṣ* meaning "attainment," the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyaḥ aṅ*. *Kāmarūpā* means "one whose form is at will," because she is endowed with the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*). [The remainder of the compound concerns] the body...

For Udayanācārya has stated that [the term] refers to "action" (karma) at the beginning of creation and so forth, or because the body is grasped for action accomplished by the body; and it is said in the Bhagavadgītā: "Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and a rise of adharma, then I manifest Myself. [The name] Kāmarūpa is a sacred seat (pīṭha); it possesses this [quality], according to the rule regarding words beginning with *arśas*.
Having offered [this], it is said in the *Tathāca-Ḍaṇḍamālā*: "In the Kṛta age, Jālandhara-pīṭha; in the Tretā, Pūrṇagiri; in the Dvāpara, Uḍḍiyāna;

but in the Kali age, Kāmarūpa—bestowing great fruit in the world, that place grants immense accomplishment through its mere sight. Among the fifty pīṭhas, Kāmarūpa is of supreme fruit; there, recitation, worship, and offerings become a hundred thousand times more effective. Thus it is described in many ways by the Lord.

The description of the qualities of Vikintasa is that where [the Goddess] herself exists in the form of the Yoni as ten million-fold attributes. In the *Samayācāra*, it is said: "O Subhaga, those four seats (*pīṭhas*) which exist within the bodies of Śakti, I shall describe them, for they are more secret than the secret.
The entire body of Śakti is considered the seat of Pūrṇagiri; O Subhaga, Uḍḍiyāṇa is proclaimed to be upon her head."

"That which has breasts is to be known as Oḍḍiyāṇa, and the bhaga is remembered as Kāmapīṭha," and furthermore, from the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Or else, the vision of Kāmarūpa occurs through good fortune," and so forth. (24) Regarding the term *Maheśānī*: *Maha* means worship; she is the one who brings about great worship (*mahā-pūjakā*). [Alternatively,] it is a *dvandva* compound of *Mahā-lakṣmī* and *Samāhāra*. By the word *maha*, she brings the Great Lord (*maheśa*)—the husband of the living soul—as her lord; thus she is *Maheśānī*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in *karmaṇya*. Because she is the cause of the devotees' [attainment], she is "ever-energetic" (*nityotsāhā*). This means that she is always intent upon granting the desired objects to her devotees; or rather, because the effort of the Lord is eternal, the word "energy" (*utsāha*) denotes "effort" (*yatna*), or because it is her very nature. Alternatively, she is "high-minded" (*manasvinī*) according to the rule: "In cases of abundance, censure, or praise... (*bhūmaniṃdāpraśaṃsāsu*).

The meaning is that she is "praśastamanas" (of excellent mind) because of her quick graciousness; for this very reason, there is the statement of Vīra: "In this world, who among those who bow down to her has not instantly obtained their desired object? and also the saying: "Because of her quick graciousness, she is always the Nīlasarasvatī of the worlds. (27) Regarding the phrase "the consort of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha," the word "Vaikuṇṭha" [is used] in the Bhāgavata and other texts...

It is well known for the sake of the world of Vaiṣṇavas; the rest is clear. (28) The two words "śaṃkaravallabha" have been explained. (29) Regarding "koṭicandrapratīkāśa," the compound is "koṭicandra. According to Amarasimha, "twenty and so forth always [function] in the singular. In the word "pratīkāśa," there is a lengthening of the vowel according to the rule "upasargasya dhatvi. Furthermore, this word "pratīkāśa" has the meaning of "resembling," as stated by the teacher Daṇḍin: "The words *pratīkāśa*, *upama*, and so forth [denote similarity]."

"Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons"—thus says the *Nīlatantra* (30). Regarding the phrase "possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns," the word *sūrya* is grammatically correct due to its formation by *nipātana* (irregular derivation) according to rules such as those governing *rājasūya*. In both instances, the words "ten million" (*koṭi*) and "hundred" (*śata*) intend merely a large number. Alternatively, "hundred" (*śata*) may mean many; thus, it refers to that which is protected (*āsya*) from harm (*akṣema*) by many learned scholars (*sūri*).

The compound *tādṛśīmājñānam* is a *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of the fifth case (*tatpuruṣa*), meaning "one whose knowledge is such. Then, *śatasūryasamaprakṛṣṭabhājānam yasyāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of the sixth case (*tatpuruṣa*) denoting the object of the action (*viṣayatva*), meaning "one whose object of knowledge is superior like a hundred suns. The meaning is that she is the object of devotion which generates the knowledge that causes the disparagement of many scholars; since knowledge resides in the devotee, this [objectivity] is obtained by implication. (31) *Jahukanyā* refers to the daughter of the sage Jahnu. The word *bhedasya* [is used].

Because it has been accepted as suchness (*tathātva*) in both the *Skanda-purāṇa* and the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa*: "As is Gaurī, so is Gaṅgā; therefore, whatever ritual procedure is prescribed for the complete worship of the Goddess, that same [procedure] applies to the worship of Gaṅgā. Furthermore, in that very Purāṇa: "He who speaks of a difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra, or likewise a difference between Śrī and Gaurī, or a difference between Gaṅgā and Gaurī—he is indeed a person of deluded intellect. (32) [The word] *manojñā* means "pleasing" (*manojña*).
"Matulām" means "mother" according to Amara; alternatively, it means she whose mind is like [his] own, for the Śruti states, "It is to be perceived by the mind alone.

(33) "Pārvatī": that which has joints (*parva*) is a mountain (*parvata*); the suffix *ta* is applied according to the rule "from *parvan* and *marut*" (*parvamarudbhyām*). Furthermore, the *Mātsya Purāṇa* states, "She who possesses joints (*parvavatī*) is Pārvatī. Her offspring is formed with the suffix *aṇ*, hence "Pārvatī. The *Mātsya Purāṇa* also states, "Pārvatī is in the presence of Śiva. (34) Harav...

He clearly obtained the Earth (Kāśyapī); for Amara states: "The earth is called Kāśyapī because she was protected by Kaśyapa. In the *Bhārata*, in the section on the Dharma of Giving (*Dānadharma*), it is said: "O King, for thirty thousand divine years, Kaśyapa of vast vows remained unwearied as the lord of the earth.
Then, O great king, the Earth, having approached and paid homage to Kaśyapa, became his daughter. Thus was the Earth born as the daughter of that [sage].

Because [the earth] was bestowed upon Kaśyapa by Bhārgava at the conclusion of the sacrifice—so says Svāmīpāda—and because of the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya: "Since you alone exist as the very form of the Earth, serving as the support of the universe";
or else, because she resides in the *mūlādhāra*, according to the teacher's saying: "This Earth is in the *mūlādhāra*"; or else, *Kāśyapi* refers to the Sun.
The relationship characterized by the worshiper and the object of worship is expressed as "this is mine" (*syeyam*). This is likewise the case with the Śrīvidyā mantra.

Thus it is stated in the Jñānārṇava regarding the second Vidyā known as Lopāmudrā, O Maheśvarī: "In the Kāmarāja [part], having removed Bhṛgu from the third [syllable], there is 'Saka' and 'Ga', which is Śiva.
O Varārohā, this Vidyā is worshipped by the Sun-god Tripura. Alternatively, [the term] *kaśyapaḥ* may refer to the sage; for the Viśva lexicon states: "*mītabhede iti kaśyapaḥ*."

She is called *Sostyasyāvālale* because she is so described; likewise, it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "The fish and the blood from her own limbs are considered the *avalaya* (ornamental girdle) of Caṇḍikā.

Alternatively, the meaning is that she belongs to Kaśyapa through the relationship of being his daughter (*janaki*). For it is said in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "The venerable Marīci is Rudra, and Saṃbhūti is his beloved, O Lord. (36) Regarding the word *kamaleti*, it ends in the suffix *yac* according to the *Arśa-ādi* group; likewise, it is the space between Śrī and Gaurī.

Because of the stated words; or because she has the form of Padmāvatī, as indicated by the meditation: "Seated upon a lotus throne, holding two red lotuses with her lotus-like hands, and possessing three eyes"; or because her hair-knot (*jūṭa*) is bound with a garland of lotuses, as stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "Her hair-knot is adorned with a shimmering garland of blue lotuses, and she is formidable. (37) "Entire" (*kṛtsnā*) means all-pervading; it does not mean...

"Whatever exists in this Brahmāṇḍa, whether moving or unmoving, is devoid [of intrinsic nature]"—according to this statement by Dakṣa in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. Alternatively, [the term] "Kṛt" is a specific technical designation for a suffix (*pratyaya*) according to Pāṇini’s sūtra *kartari kṛt* ("kṛt-suffixes denote the agent"). For them, there is the suffix *añ* in the sense of "not being," and the feminine form is *Kṛtsnā* because it belongs to the *kṛtsna-ādi* group. Or else, Kāśakṛtsna is a particular sage; Indra, Candra, and Kāśakṛtsna... [and so forth].
Tsuṇāpiśali, Śākaṭāyana, Pāṇini, Amara, Jaineṃdra, Ajayaṃta, Ṭa, and others are the grammarians (śābdika), according to Vopadeva.

The term "Tsuṇā" here is a partial designation (*ekadeśaprayoga*), like the word "Bhīma" [standing for Bhīmasena]. Its meaning is twofold: it refers to that which causes one to know the entire science of grammar (*kṛtsna-vyākaraṇa-śāna-hetu*); or alternatively, it means it is the cause of the knowledge of the non-difference (*abheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. Thus, the Vedānta Sūtra states: *avasthiteḥ*.

The meaning is that the teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that because of the absolute non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—as expressed in the passage, "having entered with this living self"—the characteristic mark of the individual soul, namely, "but for the sake of the self's desire, everything becomes dear," is not contradictory. (38) Regarding the phrase "whose eyes are like the petals of a *kaṃja*": *kaṃ* is an indeclinable used in the sense of water; because it is born from that, *kaṃja* refers to a lotus.

She whose eyes are as long and wide as lotus petals—this [compound] should be understood as having its *vācaka* (denotative element) elided—or rather, she whose eye is as broad as a lotus petal and is joined with another of its own kind; for thus says the Śruti: "It [the Self] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and it emitted heat. That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and it emitted water. And from that...
"In the beginning, [Brahman] thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and He created them," and so forth. Here, the word "here" (*atra*) refers to the earth;
"vision" (*īkṣaṇa*) is a specific modification of *māyā*. Just as other instances of vision would be redundant for you, so it is clearly stated in the Vedānta texts.
(39) The syllable *ra* is Brahmā, the form of Viṣṇu; the syllable *ha* is Śiva; *ma* is Śiva and the Moon, the Creator; and the syllable *a* is Vāsudeva.

There may be a *Nānārthamañjarī* [composed] by Śūlinī, who is celebrated as the mistress of these [deities], because she is the presiding deity over them; this is the intended meaning. (40) Regarding "mounted upon a bull": because she is attached to half the body of Śiva, Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, holds a trident and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), wears great serpent-bracelets, and has attained the ornament of the crescent moon; thus it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*.

The meaning is that [the Lord] is mounted upon the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), which is like a bull (*vṛṣa*), because [He] is accessible solely through that; for the *Bhāṣya* states, beginning with "The bull roars loudly in three ways," that "the bull is so called because of his pouring forth (*varṣaṇa*) [of rain]" (41). Regarding the phrase "with a face resembling the full moon" (*pūrṇacandranibhānanā*):

"resembling the full moon" (*pūrṇacandranibham*) means equal to the full moon; this is an irregular analysis of the compound (*asvapadavigraha*) because it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), and from that, it is a *bahuvrīhi*. (42) [End of section] Mānye.

(43) Thus, because she is worthy of honor by all, the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of "worthiness" (*arha*). (44) "Possessing pride" (*mānavatī*) means possessing various types of pride, such as jealousy and arrogance; or else, it means having the nature of all women, or possessing an unlimited measure.

(45) "Fortunate" (*dhanyā*) means one who has obtained a mass of wealth; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "fortunate" (*dhanya*) refers to one who possesses merit (*puṇyavant*). On what part of the Snow Mountain?

Thus, because snow (*hima*) predominates there, it is clearly called the Snowy Mountain (*Himagiri*). (46) Regarding "Aparṇā": according to the Puranic account, she was called Aparṇā because she performed ascetic penance (*tapasyantī*) by subsisting on withered leaves (*parṇa*). This is also stated in the *Kumārasambhava*: "She who subsisted on the leaves of trees that had fallen of their own accord, and who [endured] the heat of the sun during the afternoon; and again, she who tormented herself—[the gods] call her Aparṇā, speaking thus to Priyamvadā. Thus he spoke of her.
Those who know the past say that his sister should be taken; thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "To Menā were born auspicious daughters endowed with yogic power:
Umā, Ekaparṇā, and Aparṇā, all devoted to rigorous vows. One was given to Hṛdika, another to Dvita, and another to Ājaigaṣavya.
These young women, superior in asceticism to all the world, were bestowed by Himavat. Or rather, the debt has been discharged and lost in the three worlds."

The word *dhaṇyā* is derived from the root *ṛṇ* (to owe) with the suffix *ṇic* followed by *yat*, meaning "that which causes one to discharge a debt. Alternatively, it is a *pañcamī-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one from whom the debt has departed. According to the Śruti: "As soon as he is born, the son of a Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by means of sacrifice, to the sages by means of Vedic study, and to the ancestors by means of *svadhā* (funeral offerings). Such [a mother] is so called because she provides the means for the fulfillment of that [debt], which is the cause for its removal.

The word *tribhāvaḥ* indicates the necessity of serving him; for in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, his [duty] is understood to be obligatory based on the scriptural injunction regarding the debts of Soma, Vedic study, and progeny, according to the principle of the sixth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], "Because of the connection" (*saṃyogāt*). (47) The term *padmapatrākṣī* is for the sake of clarity;

one should understand the specific distinction that this [word] has lost its [usual] expression of dharma because it has arrived as a compound. Alternatively, it follows the well-known usage of the term *śatapatra*.

The meaning of "Śatākṣī" (the hundred-eyed one) is that the word *padma* (lotus) refers to a hundred petals; thus, she will look upon the sages with a hundred eyes, and men will praise me as "Śatākṣī"—so it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (48). Regarding the phrase "having a serpent as her sacred thread (*nāgayajñopavītinī*)," by the word *nāga*, Karkoṭaka is intended; this is an instance where a general term is restricted to a specific individual.

Because it is not restricted [to humans], and because the *Upaniṣad* shows that she has a sacred thread (*upavītikā*) made of *karkoṭaka* snakes, Manu says: "When the right hand is raised, one is called 'sacred-threaded' (*upavītī*). [The term] *yajñopavīta* is derived from the *karmadhāraya* compound "the snake itself is the sacrificial thread," which takes the suffix *-in*. Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "one who possesses a sacrificial thread consisting of snakes. (49)
Regarding the term *mahāśaṅkhadhvara*: the *Viśva* lexicon states that it refers to the conch-like bone located between the eyebrows (*dāṃkho-nibhyantara-ekambu-lalāṭāsprisakhīṣu*).
Another tantra also declares: "The bone situated between the head and the eyes is proclaimed as the *mahāśaṅkha*. Its wearing is due to [the Goddess] holding a skull in her hand.

This rosary is to be understood as being made of *mahāśaṅkha* bones, either by means of the recitation of this mantra or according to the rules for constructing a rosary; thus says the *Nīlasarasvatī-tantra*.

*Troktaḥ* (50): According to Amara, *kānta* means "beloved," "delightful," or "pleasing. Alternatively, according to Viśva: *kaḥ* [denotes] Brahmā, fire, wind, the sun, Śamana, a pronoun, fire, a peacock, mouth, head, and water; *aṃtaḥ* signifies her own nature (*svarūpa*). Thus, she whose nature consists of Brahmā and the others is [described]. It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the word *aṃta* has the sense of "own nature" (*svarūpa*). (51) *Kamanīyā*: from the root *kam*, meaning "to desire."

The meaning is "extremely delightful" (*anīyararamyā*) from this [root], or else "the object of the desire of all" (*sarveṣām icchā-viṣayībhūtā*). (52) Regarding the term *vagātmajā*, it is not [the case that] the word *na* [is used] because of [the rule] *bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām*; thus the remainder is clear through the negative particle (*nañ*). (53) Regarding *brahmāṇī*: "Those who censure this [world] shall thereafter become *brahmāṇīs*," according to the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "She resides in a celestial chariot yoked with swans, holding a rosary and a water-pot. Or else:

The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form the word *brahmāṇī*] in the sense of "one who performs the work of a Brahmin" (*brahmaṇaḥ karmaṇi aṇ*). According to the view of the Naiyāyikas, the Vedas have God as their author, based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating:
"From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus were born"; and likewise from such Vedic passages as: "Verily, O Maitreyī, this is the breath of this Great Being:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgiras. This is also supported by the grammatical rule beginning with *indravaruṇa*.

Haradatta and others maintain that the word *anu* is mentioned here for the sake of brevity (*lāghavārtham*), even though it is already understood from the preceding rule, in order to prescribe that specific [suffix] even when [the root] is preceded by *anu*.

Dīkṣita, however, says that this form [of the word *brahmāṇīm*] occurs because of the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) in the phrase "he brings the Brahman priest" (*brahmāṇam ānayati jīvati*), with the *ṇatva* [nasalization] applied by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.3). Regarding the word *vaiṣṇavī*, she is the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*); just as the one God becomes threefold among the deities, she is indeed the Goddess (*devī*) herself according to the requirements of the purpose.

From the *Varāha Purāṇa*, it is said that she became threefold from him; and from the *Dhāman Purāṇa*: "The wonderful Vaiṣṇavī Śakti was born mounted upon Garuḍa, bearing a conch, discus, mace, and sword, and holding the Śārṅga bow and arrows. (55) Regarding the name *Śambhoḥ-jāyā*:
some say *Śambhu* is so called because happiness (*śam*) arises from him; Mādhava, however, [explains it] on the basis of the rule for the suffix *ḍu* after the root *pad*.

That which is to be thought upon means that he lives in the form of bliss; or rather, having internalized the purpose of the physician (*vaidya*), he contemplates bliss. Regarding the word *śamayatīti* (he pacifies): from the root *śam* with the suffix *ṇic*, according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well," the meaning is that he becomes the pacifier of diseases. "I invoke you, the best of physicians, O Physician"—thus [the text] begins, "The divine physician, the first speaker, has spoken... and so forth.
Regarding the word "śravaṇāt," the remainder has been explained [in verse 56]. As for "Gangajaleśvarī": she goes to the Ganges (*gaṅgā*), and she goes to the limbs (*aṅga*);

thus, according to Svāmī, the meaning is that she is the presiding deity (*svāminī*) because this is her place of practice (*sādhanasthāna*). Accordingly, it is said in the *Vīratantra*: "Whether in an empty house, a cremation ground, a solitary linga, a pond, or in the waters of the Ganges, the dull-witted one who recites [the mantra] should always be pure, of stainless mind, and endowed with devotion."

The Lord of the world, who knows the meaning of all scriptures, having mastered the sciences through the illustrious Blue Speech (*Śrīnīlavāṇī*), attains at the end of the body the state of supreme bliss, the Brahma-nirvāṇa, as a foremost among yogis. (57) She is called *Bhāgīrathī* because she was accepted as a daughter by King Bhagīratha; or else, based on the etymology that *bhā* is intellect and *gī* is speech in the form of sound, those whose chariot is the body are *bhāgīra*.

This is a statement of the summarized meaning (*phalitārtha*). Regarding the compound *tad-ubhaya-yukta-avadya-deha-yeṣām*, there is no room for the suspicion that the word *ratha* (chariot) should appear as the first member [of the compound]; for even the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "word" (*śabda*) reside in the body by way of the delimiting relation (*avacchedaka-sambandha*).

The form [of the compound] is derived from the suffix *aṇ* (as in *tadīya*), signifying the relationship of being served by them. By this, [the author] indicates the disputants of those who worship this [deity].
The manifestation of the capacity for victory (58) means that [the intellect] acts as a cooperative factor for the mental, cognitive, and sensory organs. Thus say the Sāṃkhyas:

"The internal organ is of a dual nature; it is the mind (*manas*), the deliberative faculty (*saṃkalpaka*), because it shares the common characteristics of the five senses. Furthermore, it is traditionally recorded that the Great One (*mahat*), the Intellect (*mati*), Brahman, the Intellect (*buddhi*), *yūḥ*, renown (*khyāti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), wisdom (*prajñā*), consciousness (*citi*), memory (*smṛti*), the junction (*saṃdhi*), and the Lord of All (*viśveśa*) are synonyms. It is called the "mind" (*manas*) because it thinks of all beings.

Because the fruit of action arises from that [mind], and because it is divided by its destruction—as stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "Those who know the mind as the mind" (Manu 12.5)—or because it is the motivator of the mental function (*manovṛtti*), it is called "mind. (59) "Intellect" (*buddhi*) means having the nature of the principle of Mahat.

Here, the Sāṃkhyas [hold] that intellect is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which, because it penetrates every object, is therefore threefold. [The text continues: "The instrument... (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 33).

Like lamps, these remaining gateways—the specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣas) which are mutually distinct—illuminate the purpose of the entire Puruṣa and present it to the intellect (buddhi). According to that view, because the effect merges with its cause, or because the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) has the nature of the productive primordial matter (prakṛti), all states (bhāvas) are here considered as being within the Puruṣas; for they are [objects] of cognition.

And because the intellect (*buddhi*) is thus restrained, it is so designated; this is from the *Liṅga Purāṇa* (60). It is called "Eternal Bliss" (*nityānanda*) because, while pleasure produced by sacrifices and the like belongs to others as well, this bliss is eternal. In the view where bliss is the Self (*ātman*), the suffix *-mayaṭ* is used in the sense of its essential nature (*svarūpa*);

however, in the view where there is a distinction between the two, it is used in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). (61) "Beloved of Hara" (*harapriyā*) is clear; [it refers to] both the letter *ha* and the letter *ra*.

Or, because the mantra has been joined [with it], she is called "Girisutā" (Daughter of the Mountain); for Amara states that *adri*, *gotra*, *giri*, and *grāvan* all mean "mountain. Alternatively, it is simply "giri."
The form *gīḥ* is the locative singular of the word *gī* (speech). Therein, [the term] *sutājananīśvarī* follows the rule *suprasavaiśvaryayoḥ*;

by the rule *halantāt*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. [The compound] *pṛthak-padeva-āharat-palī* means "a wife who brings [pleasure] separately"; it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. According to the previously mentioned method, the word *palī* has the meaning of "protector" (*rakṣaka*). [The term] *tapasvinī* [denotes] one who endures austerity (*tapaḥ-saha*).

"From the two [roots] *srā* and *viniḥ-ṛl* [comes] *ṅīp*"; "Austerity (*tapas*) is the observance of vows, fasts, and restraints, as well as the scorching of the body"—thus says Devala. Furthermore, this should be understood as being for the sake of attaining Śiva; or else, austerity is the specific act of contemplation, "May I become many," according to the Śruti: "He thought, 'May I be many,'" and "Of whom this austerity is born. (65) Regarding the phrase "remover of great diseases," they have been described in the aforementioned texts.

By her, the eight great diseases—wind-disorders, urinary calculi, leprosy, urinary disorders, abdominal dropsy, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and chronic diarrhea—are overcome; she is "Sudāruṇī" (the very formidable).
She is called "Devī" because she plays (*dīvyati*), according to the grammatical rule *pacādyac* and the reading *devaṭi*; thus, by the suffix *ṅīp*, the meaning is "the form of the Lord. It is said:
"Neither the lotus-eyed one (Viṣṇu) nor the three-eyed one (Śiva) is 'Deva'; rather, that certain deity who is the beginning and end of food and so forth is called 'Deva'."
The term *śumbhāsuraniṣṭadanī* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "she who utterly destroys the demon Śumbha.
By the word *nitarām* ("utterly"), it is indicated that even though he was slain by her as a solitary hero (*ekavīra*), his [karmic] consequences persist in other births.

This is understood from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, starting from the passage "attained by others at the time of Vaivasvata" up to "the dweller on the Vindhya mountain" (68), and from the phrase "bestower of great merit" (*mahāpuṇyapradā*). Thus, she is the one who bestows righteousness (*dharma*).

The meaning is that it brings merit because it is meritorious, auspicious, blissful, and virtuous through worship and other such acts. Thus, it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Rituals such as the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) and sacrifices to the gods accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of Caṇḍikā.
Likewise, a hero who is constantly devoted to the worship of Durgā is not stained by the defects arising from great sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water."

"By saying 'vām bhasā chityām' and so forth, having struck all these elements and this entire world, one who bows with their head to the Goddess is liberated from all sins. (69) "I am Bhīmā, O Goddess; indeed, on the Himavat mountain, I assumed the form of a fish to protect the sages. Thus it is said again in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "And when I, having assumed a terrible form on the Himavat mountain, shall destroy the Rākṣasas for the protection of the sages, then all the sages [shall worship me]."

With their forms bowed low in reverence, they shall say, "She shall be known as Bhīmādevī. (70) Regarding the name "Madhukaiṭabhanāśinī," the explanation is derived from the Harivaṃśa: "The lotus-born Lord, the All-pervading One, gave two names to those two: one was 'Mṛdu' and the other was 'Kaṭhina. This soft one was named Madhu, and the hard one became Kaiṭabha. In this regard, that...
It should be understood that she is the destroyer of the gates of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), because the separation from life was brought about by Viṣṇu.

For this very reason, her power is enumerated among the glories of Viṣṇu in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* in such passages as "the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha" and "the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura.

(71) Furthermore, she should be known as *Śaṅkhinī* because she is a form of Vaiṣṇavī; or else, because she possesses the *pañcakapāla-mudrā*; or else, because she is a specific type of female deity (*strībheda*). Likewise...

In the ocean of knowledge regarding the distinctions of castes among the *dūtīs*, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, it begins with "Hastinī" and "Śaṅkhinī," and thereafter the "Madhyamā-Śaṅkhinī" arises. O auspicious one, that Śaṅkhinī is indeed pure and free from sin; she is dear to all the gods and adorned with peaceful fragrance. According to the *Kāmaśāstra* as well, [the sequence is] Padminī, then Citriṇī, and then Śaṅkhinī.

The Danuhastinī-vidyā is the foremost; thereafter, each succeeding young woman is inferior to the one previously mentioned. (72) Thus, one should meditate upon Cakriṇī Mahiṣamardinī and present [to her] a fish, a trident, a sword, and likewise a discus in the right [hands]. Or, according to Amara, *cakrī* means a serpent or a reptile—that is to say, she is of the nature of Kuṇḍalinī. And so says the Śāradā:

There, the supreme deity, whose form is like a full-blown *tilaka* flower, was asleep; she who is the soul of all, whose nature is pure, and who is the mother of the world. Regarding the word *dhātrī*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The term *dhātrī* applies to a nurse, the *āmalakī* tree, the earth, and a mother. Alternatively, the *Amara* lexicon states that the flowers of the *dhātrī* tree, such as the *jātī* and others, are called *svālaṅgā*. Or rather, the leaf may be understood [as the meaning], for it is dear to her; thus, *āmala*... [text fragment].

"Is Pārvatī pleased by a leaf or by a flower?"—from the *Muṇḍamālā*; "holding a book in her hand"—because she has the form of Sarasvatī; "I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who bestows a mudrā, a rosary, a jar full of nectar, and knowledge with her lotus-hands, who possesses brilliant luster and three eyes"—from the *Śāradātilaka*. Furthermore, "pusta" refers to that which is to be written in a book.

According to the *Viśva* lexicon, [the goddess] is also known as *Karma* and *Vijñāna*. Alternatively, she is to be understood in the form of the youthful Tripurā; for it is stated in that same context in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O fair-faced one, she grants a book with her left hand and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the other to the practitioners; or, in the form of Bhairavī who bestows prosperity, she holds a book in the left and a rosary (*akṣamālikā*) in the right. (75)

Regarding the name "Cāmuṇḍā," the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states: "Because you have come here having seized Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, you shall therefore become famous in the world as the goddess Cāmuṇḍā. However, in the *Varāha Purāṇa*, it is said that the goddess struck that Daitya with a trident; when he was struck by her, his two auspicious eyes and four heads fell right behind him. Then Hara [spoke].
Because she carried away the four heads of the lord of serpents (Vāsuki) from Kṣaṇa and others, O Goddess, she became Cāmuṇḍā by that act. However, in the Vāmana Purāṇa it is said:
"Having approached, O Goddess, seize these two best of serpents; they shall be bound with the heads of the Daityas and encircled by the king of serpents.
Taking those two heads and placing them upon the broad head of Caṇḍī, he—having witnessed her most terrible deed—bound them and spoke to her. Śe... [text fragment]

"O auspicious one, because you hold Khaṛa, Caṇḍa, and Muṇḍa, therefore your fame in the world shall be 'Cāmuṇḍā'. (76) Regarding the word *capalā*: "The word *capala* [denotes] mercury, a fish, a thief, and a particular stone; *capalā* [denotes] the lotus, lightning, an unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*), and the *pippalī* plant," according to the *Viśva*. Here, "unchaste woman" (*puṃścalī*) is to be understood, as it has been mentioned in the context of the worship of the family (*kula*). Thus, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*...

"In the case of the *maṇi* [jewel], there are courtesans, barbers' daughters, washerwomen, and yoginīs; all of them are indeed women of noble family (*kulāṅganā*) endowed with exceptional cleverness. (77) "Exalted" (*tuṅga*) means being the most excellent of all; or else, because of its pervasiveness and its connection with the upper region, according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman alone extends below and above. (78) "Auspicious" (*bhadra*): the Viśva lexicon states that *bhadrā*, *mandākinī*, and *rāsnā* [are synonyms].

In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, it says "Bhadrābhadreśvara" and likewise "nikṛtanīti. It is so called because of its habit (*tacchīlāt*) of cutting down (*nikṛntati*) or severing (*chinatti*) the Daityas. Regarding the root *kṛtī* in the sense of cutting, there is no application of the augment *num* in this case; for the suffix *śa* is prescribed for roots beginning with *śamu*, and since that suffix is prescribed only when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows, whereas the *ṇic* suffix occurs when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix follows.

If it is argued thus, it is true; for this is justified by its being Vedic (*chāndasa*). By this, the usage in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*—"Just as, O Somya, when a fig is cut, all its parts are perceived"—is explained. (80) Regarding "śānti":

the *Viśva* lexicon states that *śānti* means both tranquility (*śama*) and auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*). Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, it is stated that four powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of the Goddess abide as her very nature (*svarūpa*).
O best of sages, listen to its basis: they are known as Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti.

Alternatively, the destruction of diseases, malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*), planetary afflictions (*graha*), and so forth, is declared to be *Śānti*; thus, the definition stated in other Tantras should be understood as falling within the scope of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*). (81) Regarding "sleep" (*nidrā*): it is the reclining of consciousness; Amara states that *svāpa* means sleep. Likewise, in the *Harivaṃśa*, Kṛṣṇa...

*Ktiḥ* means sleep that deludes all beings and is likewise inexhaustible (82). *Mahānidrā* means "the great sleep"; the meaning is that she is the cause of dissolution (*saṃhāraka*). It is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing a *bahuvrīhi*: she is both "great" (*mahatī*) and "sleepless" (*anidrā*), meaning she is devoid of [ordinary] sleep because she possesses eternal knowledge (83).
*Guhyanidrā*: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "guhya" refers to the secret or the private parts; the meaning here is that she resides in the *mūlādhāra*.

"O Lord, as long as Kuṇḍalinī has not been awakened within the root-lotus, the worship of the yantra, mantras, and so forth will not achieve even a slight success"—so it is stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra* (84). Regarding "Reṇukā": according to the *Viśva-kośa*, "Reṇukā" refers to the wife of Yājñavalkya;
or else, "reṇu" means vermilion (*sindūra*), and thus she is one whose head (*ka*) is adorned with that—meaning she has the form of such a woman. [The word] *cāmara*... [refers to] the sun.

"Biṃba" is according to the *Nīlatantra*; by the term "ravi-bimba" (the solar disc), it is explained as the forehead adorned with vermilion (*siṃdūra*). The meaning is that one should perform recitation (*japa*) after seeing this place. (85) Regarding "Kaumārī": she is the power (*śakti*) associated with Kumāra; she is the Śakti Kaumārī, who has a peacock as her vehicle and approaches the Daityas to fight, appearing in the form of Guha, the Mother (*Ambikā*)—according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya* [Purāṇa] and the *Skanda* [Purāṇa].

From the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "The Vāhika, Kaumārī, Varhipatrā, Asa, and Śaktinī emerged; they approached those two gods and sages to fight. Thus, she is called Kaubhūmārī, or Mārī. According to the *Viśva* lexicon, *mārī* means the destruction of a clan (*kula*). She herself, at that time, was the great Mārī. [Regarding the term] *kulajā* (born of a family): it is because she originated from a great lineage (*mahāvaṃśa*), or else because she is accessible through the conduct of the family (*kulācāra*).

The word *tajjāntatvam* (87) refers to *kuṃtī*; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *kuṃtī* means "the beloved wife of Pāṇḍu" or "the five-fingered lady" (*pāñcaśallakī*), as well as the *guggulu* tree. Alternatively, from the root *kunt*, meaning "to go toward oneself" or "to fall upon," with the suffix *kyac* and then *kvip*, the form *kuṃtī* is derived; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is both that [weapon] and Lakṣmī. The meaning is that she possesses those weapons. As stated in the *Bhaviṣya*: "She who bears the trident, the discus, the staff, the spear, the thunderbolt, and the bow."

From the statement: "O son, listen to my secret [teaching], which is devoted to the Kaula tradition and conjoined with the practice of the samaya, by means of which even those of low birth attain success"—according to the words of the *Kulecūḍāmaṇi* (88). From the statement: "O Vanadurgā," because of worship performed with flowers and other offerings related to her; likewise, there is the word of the Blessed One in the *Harivaṃśa*: "The great goddess Vāsastava [resides] in forests and groves."
Worshipped by Śabaras, Varvaras, and Pulindas, she whose banner bears the peacock feather traverses all worlds in every direction.
Furthermore, according to the *Prapañcasāra*: "She is to be grasped [as] this very one, who is surrounded by Kairātas, resplendent with flowers of wealth, and whose emblem is the peacock-umbrella.
Thus, she always acts; her conduct consists of the auspiciously praised southern form, which is prescribed in this system as the family tradition (*kulācāra*).

Therefore, it is stated in the *Samayācāra*: "O Goddess, conduct (*ācāra*) is of two kinds, distinguished as Vāma and Dakṣiṇa. That which is accompanied by the five mudrās and so forth is proclaimed as Vāma-conduct;

that which is devoid of the five mudrās and so forth is designated as Dakṣiṇa-conduct. She whose conduct is always constant is the one who goes everywhere—this is the meaning. (92) Regarding *Draupadī*: *Drupada* is a specific king; the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of offspring [to form *Draupadī*, meaning daughter of Drupada]. (92) *Drupadātmajā*.
Thus it is explained in the *Tathācakāśī-khaṇḍa*: "And Umā, the sustainer of the world, created from the fire-pit of King Drupada, who was performing sacrifice, a most beautiful daughter.
This has been explained previously. Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the daughter of the *drūṇām*—that is, of trees (*druma*), meaning the mountain.
(93) Regarding the term *sṛṣṭi* (creation): although she is the agent of creation, she is called "creation" itself through the metaphorical attribution of identity. She herself becomes the creation.

Regarding the statement in the *Jaiminīya-Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, "She exists at the primordial time of creation" (94): because she exists at the primordial time of creation—that is, at the time prior to [the world's] manifestation—her status as *prakṛti* (primordial material cause) is thereby affirmed, since at that time no effect whatsoever exists. By this, it is established that she is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) therein, by virtue of being the initiator of worldly activity and so forth at the time of creation.

Like the expression "occurring at the same time" (*samānakālīna*), [the term] *ravaḥ* [is explained as follows]: alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is both the beginning of creation (*sargādi*) and coextensive with heaven (*svargādi*) and so forth," because she is identical with them through her delight in them. (95) Regarding "the destroyer of Niśumbha’s life" (*niśuṃbhaprāṇanāśinī*): *Niśumbha* is a specific *daitya*, the younger brother of Śumbha; the rest is clear. (96) *Pa*.

The word *padminī* refers to a particular type of woman, a lotus pond, and a lotus flower—according to the *Viśva* lexicon—and it also denotes "one who bears a blue lotus," as seen in the *Cūḍāmaṇi*. (97) Regarding *vasudhā*: she is so called because, in her form as the earth (*pṛthvī*), she holds wealth (*vasu*, meaning "substance"); or alternatively, because she holds the fire (*vasu*) [as the third eye] upon her forehead; or else, because the root *vas* is taught with the sense of "burning" (*vai śoṣaṇe*) in the *Ātmanepada*... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete].

She is called *Tikā* because of the established grammatical rule that prohibits the suffix *ṭit* after the root *śvit*. She is called *Dharaṇī* because she supports those tormented by the heat of suffering with nectar (*sudhā*), just as the earth supports all beings. She is called *Pṛthvī* because she possesses great magnitude;
for the *Liṅga Purāṇa* states: "The Lord Śaṅkara is Ākāśa, and Pṛthivī is dear to Śaṅkara. She is called *Rohiṇī* because she... [text fragment ends].

The word *rohiṇī* occurs in the sense of the plant *hiṅgīkaṭurohiṇī*, the constellation Rohiṇī, the red goat (*lohitāga*), a particular disease of the throat, a rhinoceros, and the bark of the *soma* tree; thus says the *Viśva-kośa*. Because Padmāvatī is red, her crimson hue should be understood as being in the form of that [color], for it is stated therein: "wearing ornaments that were red. Alternatively, it refers to the specific constellation Rohiṇī, because she (Padmāvatī) is a portion of it; and so it is said in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
At the time of his renunciation of the body, he spoke these true words to Dakṣa: "O Lord of the Mountains, sixty daughters shall become your limbs (wives).
And regarding the sequence of that gift, it is said: "The Lord gave [them] starting from the one named Soma-ayanakṣatra, the twenty-seventh.
Among those sixty maidens, the one mentioned as the first in the procession (*yātrā*) is to be understood as this very one; specifically, she is not [the one] therein.

We shall demonstrate this through the *Mānitraca*. Alternatively, according to the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, it is stated: "By the sages, Rohiṇī was declared to be the consort of the Great God Mahādeva, whose essence is Soma, and Budha is his son. For that very reason, it is said there: "The Moon is the remnant of half the moon; Rohiṇī is the beloved of Rudra. Or else, because Rohiṇī shares the same asterism (*nakṣatra*), she is [to be honored] first in worship and so forth.

This [verse] is to be understood as being due to the arrangement of the sixty [syllables], or else because it represents the form of Baladeva’s mother. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Girijārthacintāmaṇi* composed by Viśveśvara, the son of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who has crossed the ocean of words, authoritative statements, and grammatical categories.
Now follows the commentary on the three hundred verses beginning with "Vindhyavāsinī. Here, the word *vāsa* is used in the sense of [dwelling].

When the blue-complexioned goddess Navabrahmaṇī had abandoned her body, she became Matsyapurāṇī, naked, fierce, with a bell in her hand, three-eyed, her limbs adorned with various ornaments, and clothed in yellow silk. Then Brahmā spoke to that goddess, who possessed the luster of a blue lotus: "O Daughter of the Mountain, by my command you have attained fulfillment through contact with the body of Niśā; for you were formerly Ekānaṃśā, O Siṃhī."

"O Goddess, from your wrath has arisen a very powerful Yakṣa named Pāñcāla, who is the vehicle of Varānana and whose followers are lakhs upon lakhs; he has been given to you as a servant, O Goddess, who is distressed by hundreds of great ailments. Having been addressed thus, the goddess Kauśikī went to Mount Vindhya. (1) Regarding the word *śivā*, the lexicon of Śāśvata states: "The auspicious one is called Śivā, Gaurī, and Śivā-kroṣṭrī. Among the meanings of *śivā*...

Because she bestows supreme bliss, Īśvara [states] in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "If one does not worship the Goddess who assumes the form of a beast (*paśu*) in a secluded place, it is certain that everything belonging to that person will quickly perish through the howling of the Śivā. Regarding the term *śakti*, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states: "The Goddess Girijā is Śakti, and those possessed of Śakti are Śaṅkaras. Thus, depending on the distinctions between beasts, birds, and humans, Śakti is classified as *paśu-śakti*, *pakṣi-śakti*, or *nara-śakti*.
According to the statement in the *Cūḍāmaṇi*, "Śakti is Śiva; Śiva is Śakti," and as it is also said in the *Śivāgama*:

"Śakti is Brahmā, Janārdana, Indra, Ravi, Candra, and the planets are certainly Śakti; he who does not see the entire world as having the form of Śakti is a mere observer of stars. [The term] "Mahāśakti" is either a *karmadhāraya* or a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its greatness (*mahattva*) is unimpeded.

You are *Yadvāśakti*, a specific weapon, whose form is that of Śivā and who is ungraspable. Thus, it is said in the *Ākulacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Bhairava, where Śivā is enjoyed by one [deity], there alone is the supreme, most difficult-to-attain delight of all the *Śaktis*; the meaning is that there arises an excellent joy. (4) Regarding *Śāṅkarī*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to Śaṅkara. (5) Regarding *Śaktidurlabhā*: there are three *Śaktis*, namely Prabhā... [and so forth].

"Born from the mantra of resolve" (*votsāha-mantra-jā*)—so says Amara. Because it is attainable through devotion alone, it is difficult to reach. Thus, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, there is this statement by the Blessed One: "That which is partless, consisting of pure consciousness, absolute, auspicious, liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), infinite, immortal, and supreme—that highest state is to be attained through knowledge alone, without hardship. (6) "O destroyer of the life-force of the Daityas"—this has a clear meaning; or else:

She protects the Daityas; from the root *prāti-pāl* (to protect), the suffix *ka* is applied, and by the rule "of that [root], the word *āṇa*"—as seen in examples such as *āṇa-raṇa*—the suffix *ghañ* is added to the verbal root meaning "protection. Because she removes the pride (*garva*) of Śumbha and others, she is called *dātrī* (the giver/remover); this refers to all those who possess desires, and for this reason, no specific object of the action is mentioned. Furthermore, from the root *day* (meaning giving, going, protecting, and harming), [the form *dayā* arises].

Regarding the term *dayitā*: because of the statement in the *Dāhasya* [text], "She who protects from all calamities (*sarvāpadbhyas*) is called *dayitā*," it is proclaimed that she must always protect those who are like kinsmen, those who are not kinsmen, and even enemies. (9) Regarding *Dāmodarapriyā*: according to the *Harivaṃśa* and other texts, she is named *Dāmodara* because of her binding to the mortar (*ulūkhala*). (10) Regarding *Kānti*: *Kānti* is beauty and desire.
Alternatively, because she is the nature of the power of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*), she is *Kṣemaṃkarī*. According to Amara, "kṣema" means welfare (*kuśalam*) and is not feminine;

by the rule beginning with "kṣemapriya," the suffix *aṇ* is applied and the augment *mum* is inserted. She is, in other words, the form of a particular bird. Thus, it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, following the phrase "one should pay homage": "Having likewise beheld Kṣemaṃkarī, the jackal messenger of Śiva," and so forth. (12)

He is called *Buddhi* because He brings about excellence for His devotees, or because, according to the Vedāntins, His essential nature is knowledge (*jñāna-svarūpa*). (13) He is *Bauddhācāraparāyaṇa*: "Bauddha" is derived from *buddhi* with the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthe*), meaning "the Wise One" (*buddha*); as stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* regarding the series of the Lord's incarnations, "Kalkī is [called] Buddha. He is devoted to his conduct (*ācāra*) in the form of the Kula, because He is dear to that [conduct]. As it has been said: Ma...
In the *Hācīnakrama*, she is called Nīlasarasvatī; the word "Śrī" is employed for the sake of praise as in "Śrīvidyā.

This is because it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, this sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā cannot be fully described. She is Bhairavī; thus, there are three [names]: Bālā, Bhairavī, and Sundarī.

The divisions of Tripurā are threefold, as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "In that very place, there is the venerable Tripurābālā, and likewise Tripurabhairavī. Or, she may be a specific Yoginī; for according to the *Ātharvaṇa*, "Bhairavī is proclaimed to be eightfold; one should worship those Yoginīs. Alternatively, she is called Bhairavī because she is connected with the women (*abheda-sambandhena*) of the Bhīrūs (fearful ones). The specific [forms] are the women (*aṅganā-bhī*).

"Rū" [is defined] by Amara (16). "Bhavya" is an irregular formation (*nipāta*) according to the rule *bhavya-geya-pravacanīya-* etc.; through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) from the root *bhū*, the sense of being eternally present is obtained. Alternatively, it is so called because it is the cause of the welfare (*kalyāṇa*) of devotees (17). "Bhāratī": she possesses the *bhārata* [epic], because she is its instigator. This is based on the *Phetkārīya* [Tantra], which states: "Having acquired what knowledge did the poets compose the *Mahābhārata* and other works? [The answer is: "The armor... (*kavaca*)... [etc.]
In the *Saṅga*, the sages such as Vyāsa and others composed the *Mahābhārata* and other works; and from the *Gandharva-tantra*, it is said that she is "the destroyer of fear.

Likewise, in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*: "Whether on a mountain, or in a thicket, or in a desolate place, at a crossroads, in a whirlpool of water, in a city, when the fear of fanged beasts arises, or when the fear of thieves and the like has come, whether in a town, in a great cemetery, on the banks of a river, or when there is fear of serpents, scorpions, and so forth..."

One should recite these [mantras] according to the prescribed method during times of distress; they will swiftly destroy all fear. In the *Harivaṃśa*, it is said: "In battles, in terrible fires that have flared up, on riverbanks, among thieves, in wildernesses, and in times of danger; while traveling abroad, in captivity by kings, in the crushing of enemies, and in all situations where life is at stake—you indeed provide protection, without a doubt. (19) [The word] *tāpasī* is formed with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to" (*amatrārthīya*). It ends in the suffix *ama*.

Because the injunction "by the thousandfold power of penance" [is understood] through the hearing of the *Śruti* and other sources as indicating the simultaneous occurrence [of these powers], and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "Her who is fire-colored, blazing with penance" (20); "Tāriṇī" means she who delivers one from *saṃsāra* (21);

"Tīkṣṇakṣī" is so called because of her extreme ferocity; or this should be understood as referring to a specific visualization (*bhāvanāviśeṣa*) from the *Matsyasūkta*, namely, "she whose mouth is wide open" (22).

"She who destroys the fierce Daityas" (*tīkṣṇadaityavināśinī*): "fierce" (*tīkṣṇa*) because of her *tāmasa* nature; the rest is clear. (23) "The Giver" (*dātrī*): from the root *do* meaning "to cut," with the suffix *tṛc* and the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. She destroys the dullness of the skull-bearer (Śiva) and of the three worlds; she is the fierce Tārā, the one who protects (*trāt*) from that which makes sounds (*phetkāriṇī*). (24) "Devoted to giving" (*dānaparā*): [from the root *dā*] with the suffix *tṛc* and *ṅīp*, because she is intent on giving; or else, [she gives] fruits according to one's own actions.

From the statement in the Bhāṣya, "Because of giving according to one's disposition" (25), she is called Kālī because of her black color; as stated in the Mātsya Purāṇa and the Liṅga Purāṇa: "Then Rudra, consisting of vital breath, emerged from the mouth of the Lord, having become Ardhanārīśvara with a splendor like the rising sun, and remained there after dividing himself elevenfold."
With half of his own self, that Soul of All united with Śiva and Umā; and she then created Lakṣmī, Durgā, the excellent Sarasvatī,
Vāmā, Raudrī, Mahāmāyā, the lotus-eyed Vaiṣṇavī, Kalā, Vikaraṇī, Kālī, Kamalavāsinī, Balivikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, and likewise Sarvabhūtadamanī and Manonmanī.
Likewise, thousands of ignoble beings were created by her; here, the specific goddess Durgā is to be understood.

She is called "the destroyer of Daityas" because she brings about the destruction of the delusions of the Daityas—which are transformations of the quality of *tamas*—along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as well as their specific opposites. Thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is severed; all doubts are rent asunder."

And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both supreme and inferior (parāvara) is seen. (28) It is called *Padmā* because it has the form of Śrī (Goddess Lakṣmī), because she holds a lotus in her hand, and so forth;

[the name] *Padmāvatī* follows from the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs because it belongs to the *śara* group. Thus, in the section on the different forms of Tārā in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, after introducing the Great Goddess Padmāvatī, Mahānīla-Sarasvatī, and others, the thirteen Mahāvidyās of Tārā are described.

She is celebrated as "Kṛṣṇā. Because of her dark-blue color, the word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and the suffix *ṇa* denotes bliss (*nirvṛti*). The supreme Brahman, which is the unity of these two, is designated as "Kṛṣṇa" according to the Śruti. Thus, the meaning is that she possesses identity with Him at all times, or that she is eternally united with Him. Alternatively, "Kṛṣṇa" refers to Vedavyāsa; because she is his object of worship, she is "Kṛṣṇā. Furthermore, since even the omniscient Vedavyāsa—who, having been sustained by her, recites [the scriptures] and so forth—is [called Kṛṣṇa], she is likewise so named. This is the teaching of Bhairava.

In the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, it is stated: "Formerly, for the welfare of the worlds, the Goddess was propitiated by Dakṣa. For the sake of his purpose, she was addressed by the Lord Śambhu, saying, 'Divide yourself into a right [half] that is white and a left [half] that is black. Thus addressed, O twice-born ones, she became twofold—white and black. (31) Regarding the term "Puṣṭā" (the Nourisher): the root *puṣ* (to nourish) ends in the suffix *kta*; its meaning is the state of being eternally of a single form.

(32) *Tuṣṭā*: "Contented," as before, from the root *tuṣ* meaning "to be pleased. (33) *Vaśī*: "Mistress" (*vaśinī*), according to the Vedic usage. (34) *Ūrubhavā*: Because she was born from the thighs of Nārāyaṇa; she is called *ūrūdbhavā* because she was seen by the sage Narasara as a celestial woman (*surastrī*). The word is grammatically correct according to the *pṛṣodarādi* class. Etymological derivations such as "she desires (*vaṣṭi*) abundant (*prabhūtam*) thighs (*ūrū*)" and so forth are not elaborated here for fear of prolixity. (35) *Vajriṇī*: "The wielder of the thunderbolt."

By the rule beginning with *ṛjre* etc., the word *vajra* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*). In the term *vajrahastā*, the word *vajra* is placed after *hasta* because of the rule *praharaṇārthebhyaḥ pare niṣṭhā-saptamyau* (Pāṇini 2.2.36), which prescribes the posterior placement of the past participle and the locative case; thus, the locative is placed last. This is because the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states that Indra was given a thunderbolt (*vajra*) produced from a lotus-stalk. Furthermore, she is called *Vajrāyudhadhāriṇī* (Bearer of the Thunderbolt Weapon) in the section on the *Navarātri* festival, within the description of the characteristics of the worshipful form.

Regarding the *Śiṣyapurāṇa* (36): "Nārāyaṇī" [is explained as follows]: "The waters are called *nārāḥ*; the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara (*narasūnavaḥ*). They were his (*tasya*) former abode (*ayanaṃ pūrvaṃ*), therefore he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇaḥ*. This is the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *purāṇa*. According to the *Pañcarātra* and other traditions, it is explained that the word "Nara" refers to the *tattvas* (principles);

this should be understood (37). Regarding "Śivā," it has already been largely explained: either because bliss (*śivaṃ sukham*) exists in her, or because she makes her devotees auspicious (*śivayati*) and grants them happiness.

Or, by granting liberation in this manner, she makes [beings] into the very form of Śiva. She is called Śivā by the wise as the Goddess, the Supreme Self, the Lord, and the creator of that world; and her son is Purañjaya, according to the *Liṅga Purāṇa* (38). She is "Khaḍginī," meaning she possesses a *khaḍga*—for Amara states that *khaḍga*, *nistriṃśa*, *caṃdrahāsa*, and *asiriṣṭi* are synonyms for a sword—and this is due to her connection with the substratum of worship. Thus it is said in the *Devī Purāṇa*: "Gold, silver..."

Whether carved from clay, stone, or wood, the Goddess, when worshipped with swords and tridents, bestows the fruit of all desires. One should worship her with whatever weapon is prescribed for her; or, as Amara states, *gaṇḍaka*, *khaḍga*, and *khaḍgin* [refer to the rhinoceros], meaning she who possesses that [weapon] as her strength. With the flesh of the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) and likewise with the rhinoceros, Caṇḍikā certainly attains satisfaction for five hundred years—so says the *Kālikā*.

This is clearly stated in the *Purāṇas* as "with sword in hand" (*khaḍgahastā*). Likewise, it is said in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "She who resounds with the cry of a hero, beautified by a sword held in her right [hand]" (*khaḍgena dakṣiṇasyordhve śobhitāṃ vīranādinīm*). She is the bearer of the *kartṛ* and the *karpara*. The *kartṛ* is a specific type of weapon; the *karpara* is a skull, according to Amara. Regarding the form *karpara*, Svāmī and others state that the suffix *araṇ* is applied to the root *kṛp* due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), resulting in the substitution of *la* for *ra*. And it is said in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "With a sword and a blue lotus... (*khaḍgendīvara*).

Regarding "kartripharparabhujā" (41): the word *devāṅganā* is derived from the *aṅgakalyāṇe* sub-group of suffix rules (*anta-gaṇa-sūtra*) to express excellence, resulting in the suffix *na* after the group beginning with *vāma*. Alternatively, it refers to one for whom there is a *devāṅganā* (celestial nymph) in the courtyard of her house, because she has arrived there for the purpose of service. Or, the compound may be analyzed as "one whose body (*aṅga*) is joined with the gods (*deva*)," the meaning of which is as previously stated. Or else, *deva* means the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and *aṅgana* means the knowledge consisting of direct perception regarding those objects.

The meaning is that she possesses supersensuous knowledge, since the word "indriya" (sense-organ) here serves as an indicator for that which transcends the senses (*atīndriya*). According to the lexicon: "The word *deva* is used for the god of wealth, for a king, and for a sense-organ. [The form *aṅgana*] is derived from the root *agi* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *lyuṭ*. Alternatively, it means she whose "body" (*aṅgana*)—that is, her knowledge—is that of the gods (*deva*). In the first member of the compound, the genitive case signifies the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*), because even they (the gods) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. Thus.

In the *Brahma-sūtras*, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is indeed the existence (*bhāva*)—that is, the presence (*sattā*)—of the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman even for the gods, despite their lack of qualification for [the study of] the Vedas. For there is scriptural evidence (*darśana*) to this effect: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to it, he alone became that," and likewise, "Indra, indeed, went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from the Asuras."

(42) "ṇām" and so forth; (43) "devamānyā" has a clear meaning; (44) "devakanyā"—in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, there is this address to Bhairava: "Sometimes you are exceedingly beautiful, sometimes you are indeed the Guru, sometimes you are the son, and sometimes you are the disciple," and so on; (45) "pulomajā"—because she is the form of Śacī, [she is called] Pulomā, the daughter of the Daitya Puloman, as stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts; "muni" refers to Sāmya and others; (46) "sukhi".

The suffix *matvarthīya* [denoting possession] is used here because she is eternally united with *nīti* (the path/method), owing to her being the very nature of Brahman. (46) She is "the giver of happiness" (*sukhadātrī*) because, as a perfected science (*siddhavidyā*), there is an absence of the suffering associated with ritual means; the meaning is that she bestows heaven, liberation (*apavarga*), and so forth. Thus, in the *Muṇḍamālā*, following the description of the ten sciences (*daśavidyā*), it is said: "She who grants happiness and liberation, who is eternal, and who is not to be accomplished through effort—by whatever means possible, she will grant accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon the earth. And likewise:

"In this [practice], there is no dependence on perfected beings (*siddhas*) and the like, no consideration of constellations and so forth, no purification of time and the like, and no fault-finding regarding unfriendly planets and so forth" (47).

It is "that which increases all happiness" (*sarvasaukhyavivardhinī*); from the word *sukhapada*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "one who especially increases all happiness," or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. (48) Regarding "virtuous conduct" (*śīla*): it means she possesses such conduct; thus, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *arśas*. Furthermore, in the sense of purity...

"Cariteśīlam" according to Amara (49); "Śīlavatī" has the same meaning as before (50). Regarding "Sūkṣmā": "Sūkṣma" may mean pervasive, minute, or subtle; it is also used for the small, according to the Viśva-kośa. Furthermore, from the Prapañcasāra: "Even those who perceive the supreme form of the unborn [Brahman] do not truly know You, for they are composed of Māyā; yet these [beings] praise You as having a gross form" (51). "Sūkṣmākārā" means one whose nature is the subtle thread.

From the *Nīlataṃtra* (52): "She who is desired through austerities as the 'Bestower of Boons' (*Varapradā*)—he who is superior even to the gods is considered [the recipient]. Thus, the definition of a boon (*vara*) is that which is bestowed with excellence (*prakarsa*). Furthermore, this excellence consists in the nature of being a gift distinct from other deities.

(53) She is called *Vareṇyā* because she is chosen (*vriyate*) due to her being the most excellent; the suffix *-nya* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules (54). The term *Varapradā* is thus clearly established.

Regarding the word *vāṇī*: it is so called because the root *vaṇ* means "to sound" (*śabdāyate*), as stated in the *Vacanādhiṣṭhātridevatā-nighaṇṭu*; or alternatively, it refers to the daughter of the Asura Vāṇa, for she was adopted as a daughter by Rudra. *Śānanī*: She possesses excellent knowledge (*praśasta-jñāna*). Its excellence consists in having only the Real (*san-mātra*) as its object. Dholyā, Umā, Māyā, Auṣadhī, Dīpti, Viśva, Iti, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Bhadrakālī are declared to be the deities of the six rites (*ṣaṭkarma*); one should worship them at the beginning of the respective rites. Formerly, Fortune (Śrī) arose from the ocean; later, during the churning for nectar (*amṛta-mantha*), she was produced through the efforts of the gods and demons. That which arises from cows, humans, elephants, horses, buffaloes, boars, goats, and deer is declared to be the eightfold *mahāmāṃsa*, which causes pleasure to the deities, according to the statement in the *Yāmala*.
