(11) Regarding "bhavasya ṣṭā," [she is] the one made manifest (*ṣṭā*) by *bhava*, i.e., by births; for she is difficult to sing of (*durgeyatvāt*) due to her beginningless form. According to the scripture: "For the sake of the work of her worshippers, Brahmā assumes a form through the imagination of forms, though he is consciousness, non-dual, devoid of qualities, and the embodied soul. (12) Regarding "pāvanī," [she is] the purifier (*pāvaya*).

She certainly purifies; [this is derived] from the causative form *pāvayati* with the suffix *lyuṭ*. In the reading *pāvinī*, the suffix *ṇini* is used. Because the sight of a Śākta sacred field (*kṣetra*) serves as a cause for the purification of sin by acting as a substitute for the *kṛcchra* penance, it is seen in all Smṛti texts that the number of *kṛcchra* penances corresponds to the number of *yojanas* traveled when visiting all the Vaiṣṇava, Māheśvara, Saura, Śākta, and other sacred seats (*pīṭhas*). Thus, she is "the protector" (*paripālinī*).

He protects his devotees from all perils; likewise, the *cilu* scripture [states] "pāra" means protection, as in protection from thieves and the like. (14) Although it is indeed directly perceived by the mind even for oneself, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) that "it is to be seen through the mind alone," nevertheless, this statement is made here with the intention of negating [the perception] regarding the result and the activity. For this very reason, [it is said] "from which words turn back... and so forth.

"The [senses] return without having reached [the object], along with the mind," so says the Śruti. Alternatively, this prohibition refers specifically to the state of being an objective function (*viṣaya-vṛttitva*) with respect to pure Brahman (*śuddha-brahman*), because it is accepted by the Vedāntins that pure Brahman is not an object of mental function (*vṛtti*).

(15) "In its manifest form" (*vyaktarūpeṇa*): because it is made extremely clear through knowledge in accordance with the scriptures; as it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "By means of knowledge and the yoga of action..."

"O Great King, I am to be attained by you through austerity and worship, and not otherwise, even by millions of ritual acts. (16) [The form "dṛṣṭā" is derived from the root *dṛś* with the suffix *kta*; in the sense of completion (*niṣṭhā*) regarding the worship of deities and the like, there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution according to Pāṇini 6.1.15. Alternatively, because one accepts that the self possesses a relative dearness conditioned by its adjuncts (*upādhi*) through effort directed toward merging into the nature of the Self, [it is said: "Not for the sake of all [objects] does everything become dear; rather, for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

"Śruteḥ" means "increasing her own desired [state]," that is to say, she increases the excellence of her own devotees. Regarding the word *sveṣāṃ*, Hemacandra states: "Sva refers to one's own kin, to oneself, and to one's own wealth. "Acyuta" means that which is devoid of any alteration in its essential nature throughout the three periods of time;
for there are six modifications of being: birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay, and destruction.
Thus it was said by Vāryāpaṇi: "Because of the absence of the modifications mentioned by the Pāśupatas, [the term] *apracyutā* (unfallen/unswerving) is used;

the prefix (*pra-*) alone is the distinction. Alternatively, according to the Vedānta view, because Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, it is *prācyutā*—meaning it reaches its culmination in the form of the world without abandoning its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). This is to say that it is intended as the material cause. Furthermore, even in the Sāṃkhya system, regarding the relationship between cause and effect...

Because there is no difference between the two, even though [the world] perishes in the form of jars and so forth, Prakṛti is indestructible in its own essential nature. (20) *Prāṇā*: by means of this, beings breathe (*prāṇanti*) or live; it causes them to breathe (*prāṇayati*); or it moves (*aṇati*) in an excellent manner (*prākṛṣṭam*), or it sounds (*aṇati*). From the root *aṇ*, meaning "to sound," the suffix *yac* is applied. (21) *Prāṇadā*: she gives life (*prāṇān*) to her devotees; the sense is that she has attained a state opposed to those who are hostile to her. Or else, from that, I am all... [text ends].

"O gods, when there is no rain, I shall sustain the world with vegetables produced from my own body, which will serve as the support of life; at that time, I shall become renowned on earth as Śākaṃbharī. From the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (22). Regarding the title "Vāsaveśvarī": Vāsava is Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, according to the *Amara-kośa*, who states that he is the son of Vasu (*vasoḥ apatyam iti svāmī*). Alternatively, Vāsava is Pradyumna, the son of Nārāyaṇa (Vasu), as stated in the *Śaṃvara-vadha*. His [the Lord's]...

She is called *Vasu* because she is the abode (*kṣita*) [of all things], according to the lexicon which states: "Vasu refers to Nārāyaṇa, Punarvasu, and Viśvarūpa"; or else, it is so called because she bestows *vasu*, meaning a collection of wealth or objects.

(23) She is "born from the ocean," the repository of waters, because she was produced from the sea in the form of Lakṣmī; or alternatively, the word "repository of waters" (*apāṃ nidhi*) here denotes a lake in its etymological sense, as she is the blue lotus in the lake that is Mount Meru. The rest is clear. The source for this is found in the *Prākṛta*... [text truncated].

Or rather, it is presented as being of the nature of the shore (*velā*); for the Lord Rudra is the ocean, and [she is his] daughter, the princess of the lord of mountains on the shore, according to the *Liṅga Purāṇa*.

(24) She is called *Dhāriṇī* because she necessarily supports (*dhārayati*) the worlds; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity, meaning she is the substratum of the effort that prevents the falling of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). (25) She is called *Pratiṣṭhā* because she is renowned throughout all the worlds. *Pra*... [text ends]
(26) *Tiṣṭhā* is the power previously mentioned; it is called *asaṃjātā* because nothing has been born from her, or because she is the *tāraka* (savior) like the Sun.

Or, as for *udbhavā*: everything arises from her, because she is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe in the form of Brahman; in the Nyāya system, the meaning is merely that of an efficient cause (*nimitta*). (27) *Kṣobhiṇī*: through a specific meditation, she certainly agitates the enemy; likewise...
She agitates [the world], for it is said in the *Matsya-sūkta*: "having thoroughly agitated" (28). She is "secure" (*kṣemā*) because she performs what is auspicious (29).

She is "the womb of glory" (*śrīgarbhā*) because she possesses great luster; or else, because her mantra is joined with the *śrī*-seed syllable. According to the *Matsya-sūkta*, when ignorance—which is the departure from the *śrī*-seed syllable—is removed, then glory (*śrī*) faces every direction (30). She is the "Supreme Sovereign" (*parameśvarī*); "supremacy" consists in being the agent of creation and so forth.

Although the word *īśvara* ends in the suffix *ac* (as in *stheśabhāsa...*), the feminine suffix *svī* is applied here due to its connection with a masculine noun (*puṃyoga*), for otherwise the suffix *ṭāp* would have been required;

thus, it means "she who possesses the great medicine of auspiciousness placed [within her]. Alternatively, according to the rule *aśuṅ karmaṇi varaṭ* from the Uṇādi-sūtras, the suffix *varaṭ* is added, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel and its following consonant are elided, resulting in *īśvarī*; or else, it is derived from the root *īś* with the suffixes *kvanip* or *vanip*.

Thus, it should be understood that the word *īśvarī* is formed by the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *ra* for the *e* in the root *īś*, caused by the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

(31) Regarding *karālā*: the *Viśva* lexicon states that *karāla* means "terrible" or "frightful. *Ka* is the sun, and *ra* is fire; she whose ornament (*ala*) consists of these is [Karālā]. Or, as the text says, [she who is] "therein" (*tatra*). (32) Regarding *puṣṭadehā*: according to the *Rudrayāmala*, *pīna* and *pīvarā* mean "full-bodied"; alternatively, *puṣṭa* may be used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).

(33) *Kāriṇī*: because she is the cause of growth (*vṛddhi*), she possesses the activity of bestowing nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and movement (*īhā*). Or, (34) she is *Kāriṇī* because she necessarily acts upon the worlds and causes them to act likewise, by means of setting them in motion through Brahmā; or [it is derived] from the root *kṛ* meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*). Or, (35) she is *Kaṃjocanā*: *kaṃja* means a lotus (*padma*); this is a clear example of an elided simile (*luptopamā*) where the common property (*dharma*) is omitted within the compound. (36) *Śaraṇyā*: the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of "one who is fit for that" (*tatra sādhuh*).

"Kamalati" means she whose abode is the lotus-lake Kamalā; "mātsyam" [is derived from] *matsya*. (37) "Prītā" means she who is pleased; it is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) from the root *prī* meaning "to please. Alternatively, from the word *prīti*, which emphasizes the state of being, the suffix *ac* is added according to the rule for words beginning with *adarśa* to form a noun denoting a quality. She is called "Pulastya" because she is the wife of Pulastya;

she is "the beloved of the moon-crested Lord" (*śaśabhṛnmauli-prīti*), as stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "She is the beloved of the wielder of the Pināka bow. (38) "Vimalā" means she who is devoid of all defects.
Because [she is] "Vimalā" and "Puruṣottamā," this is the *Mātsya* [Tantra] (39). The title *Ānandavardhinī* has its meaning made explicit; likewise, in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*:

"If, after chanting the root-vidyā, one should chant these [mantras], one attains the fulfillment of all siddhis and shall roam upon the earth like a god. (40) Regarding *Kapardinī*: the *Amara* [Kośa], in the section on Śiva, states, "He who has a mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*) is *kapardī*"; and Halāyudha says, "The fierce one is *kapardī*."

In the word *padmapiñchra*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because there is no connection with a masculine [stem], since that [rule] falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "thereafter" (*tatra*). Nevertheless, by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word *kaparda* refers to his matted locks (*jaṭā*); thus, when the suffix *a* is applied, one must explain that the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs according to the rule "from words ending in *ṛt*" (*ṛnebhyiḥ*). This is the [correct] interpretation (*kalpanā*). The word *kalpa* may mean dissolution (*pralaya*), method (*nyāya*), scripture (*śāstra*), or the day of Brahmā (*brahmadina*); this is according to the *Viśva* lexicon. [The form *pralayakara*] is derived from the causative (*ṇyantāt*) of the root *kṛ* with the suffix *lyu*. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows: *kā*...
Because it consists of that [nature], so it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* in that context: "The power of that source of the entire world is renowned as Māyā;

the Lord, the Illusionist, the Supreme Person, causes that state to revolve" (42). [She is called] Kadrū because she was born to Kaśyapa as the thirteenth [wife], according to the Purāṇas; thus she stands in the midst of them. Alternatively, she is Kadrū because she is the support (*dru*) for happiness (*ka*), like a tree (*vṛkṣa*); or because her matted hair is tawny in color.

Because of the scriptural statement, "One should meditate on her as having a single, tawny, fierce matted lock" (43); [the word] *sumanā* is derived from the root *man* with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134, resulting in the form *manaḥ*; thus, the meaning is that she increases the bliss of those whose nature is right-mindedness (*samyag-manana*). (44) [The term] *udīrṇā* is a form of the root *ṛ* preceded by *ut* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), meaning "sovereign" (*svacchandā*); she is eternal due to being devoid of any modification in her conscious nature (*cit-svarūpa*).

Or, because she has been purified (*pacitatvāt*), she is "Adornment" (*bhūṣaṇā*); [the suffix] *yac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas* (Pāṇini 5.2.127), meaning "she whose adornments are complete. She is "Bhavyā," meaning one from whom existence (*bhava*) arises;

such a form is the form of Brahmā or Viṣṇu, and she is that in whom this exists—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the causal ablative (*hetu-pañcamī*). According to the *Nānārthakośa*, the letter *a* is Vāsudeva and the letter *ā* is Pitāmaha (Brahmā). Thus, the meaning is "she who gives birth to both of them. (47) Surasene.

Thus, she is Devasenā because she is the wife of Skanda; for it is stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "She who is the six-faced one, the destroyer of the cities of the enemy [Tāraka], and the beloved of Devasenā. Alternatively, she is so called because she performs the work of the army (*senā*) by slaying the Daityas. Or else, the meaning is that her husband is one who possesses affection for the Asuras. (48) Regarding the term *Sureśvarī*, the meaning is explicit: she is the sovereign (*īśvarī*) over the *surās*—that is, the gods, humans, and those characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*).

(49) According to the *Viśva* lexicon, the word "pāvaka" means both "restraining" (*niyāmaka*) and "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*). (50) She is called "Śrīmatī" because of her eternal possession [of Śrī], hence the suffix *matup*.

(51) Regarding "Śiśirā," Amara states that starting with "suṣīma" and "śiśira" meaning "cold" (*jaḍa*), there are seven words of various genders; she is so called because of her gentle form (*saumyarūpatvāt*). (52) She is "Anantā" because she has no counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); or else, due to the predominance of the abstract state (*bhāva-prādhānyāt*), she possesses infinity (*anantatvam asty asyāḥ*). Thus she is Anantā.

(52) From the *Harivaṃśa*: "She is the remover of the suffering of those who enjoy [her grace]. (53) She is called the "Daughter of the Snowy Mountain" (*Śiśirācalakanyakā*) because she was born from that mountain after Satī’s abandonment of her body;

regarding the word *śiśira*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the context of the divisions of seasons, it means cold or frosty. (54) "Worthy of the gods" (*Suramanyā*) is clear. (55) "Best among the gods" (*Suraśreṣṭhā*):

among the gods, she is the most excellent, the most praiseworthy; here the suffix *ya* is substituted for *iya*. (56) "The Eldest" (*Jyeṣṭhā*): because she is the embodiment of a particular power (*śakti*), she is everything.

Alternatively, because she is the Supreme Reality (*tattva*), or because she is remembered as "Mahatī" (the Great One) on the eighth day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Virgo and the moon is in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā—for the purpose of warding off misfortune (*alakṣmī*)—one should worship her as Jyeṣṭhā; she is the deity of the vow mentioned in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*. (56) She is called "Prāṇeśvarī" (Mistress of Life); according to Amara, "life-breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*) refers to the earth and progeny.
Because she is the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), so says the Śruti: "No mortal lives by the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or the in-breath (*apāna*); rather, [he lives] by another."

In whom these two are supported while living, or rather, who is the mistress of the well-known vital breath (*prāṇa*) because she is the cause of its activity, according to the Vedic scripture: "The breath of the breath, the eye of the eye" (57). She is *sthirā* (the Steadfast), because she is ultimately real by virtue of being the nature of Brahman (58). She is *tamoghnī* (the Destroyer of Darkness), because she destroys darkness consisting of delusion through her own knowledge (59). She is *dhvāntasaṃhaṃtrī* (the Total Annihilator of Obscurity), because she completely annihilates *dhvānta*, which is ignorance.

The meaning of *gvadartha* is that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the purpose in both cases. (60) Regarding *prayatātmā*: *prayata* means free from evil; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "one whose self is Brahman. This is because of the Śruti: "The Self is free from evil... ancient, pure, unaging, and unpierced" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23). (61) Regarding *pativratā*: there is no separate sacrifice or vow for women, nor is there separate meditation (*upāsana*), according to the Smṛti. Thus it is said: "When the husband is afflicted... (*Ārttārtte*).

(62) A woman who is joyful when her husband is near, distressed when he has gone abroad, and emaciated when he is absent—she who would die if he were to die—is to be known as a *pativratā* (devoted wife). (63) She is "Pradyotinī" because she shines intensely (*prakṛṣṭena dyotate*) or illuminates the world. According to the Sāṅkhya system, this is because she is the manifest form (*vibhava*) of this principle; or it is because of the Vedic scripture: "When He shines, everything shines after Him; by His light all this is illumined. She is "Rathārūḍhā" (mounted on a chariot); for "ratha" refers to a vehicle (*spandane*).

The term *kāye* means "in the body," because [the Lord] presides over the regions in the form of the Self (*ātman*). This is supported by the Śruti: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. And it is also stated in the Śruti: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself. Alternatively, at that time, during the afternoon on the ninth day, she was seated upon a chariot.

The well-known meaning is: "The King himself, bearing the title 'Viśva' (the All), should cause Bhavānī to revolve within the kingdom. (64) Alternatively, she is called *Sarvalokaprakāśinī* ("Illuminator of all worlds"), because of the statement: "By her light, all this shines. Or else, "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) are those by which objects are perceived and enjoyed, namely the sense organs; she is their illuminator because she is of the nature of the Self (*ātman*). Just as fire is the source of heat and water of cold, so too the mind, eyes, and other senses are of the nature of non-awareness (*abodha*).

[The sense organs] function depending on that which is of the nature of the Self (*ātman*), being immovable, one, and eternal; for it is said that "I am the Self whose nature is perception. Since the sense organs, by virtue of being instruments like an axe and so forth, are necessarily dependent upon an agent, the existence of the Self is established. (65) *Medhāvinī*: [This is derived from] *medhā* with the suffix *vini* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Alternatively, she is *Medhāvinī* because she protects the intelligence (*medhā*) of her devotees. (66) *Mahāvīryā*: [This is the name].

Because He is the cause of the production of various worlds and because He is the Lord of all, so says the Śruti: "He is the cause, yet He is beyond the cause; He has no progenitor, nor is there anyone who is His lord. (67) The word *haṃsa* occurs in the Viśva lexicon as meaning: "a species of bird, the sun, a particular kind of iron, the different types of yogis and measures, and the Supreme Self, as well as envy. In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, [the author] says: "Out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, we shall describe the practice known as *Haṃsa*."

By the mere knowledge of whom one truly becomes omniscient; [one] always conquers the Blessed Lady who is of the nature of the *Haṃsa*. Or, because she is the specific form of the mudrā called *Haṃsī*, three mudrās are prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homa*): namely, the *Mṛgī*, the *Haṃsī*, and the *Sūkarī*, according to the statement in the *Yāmala*. (68) She is the "Savior from Saṃsāra.
For Pārthasārathi Miśra states that "saṃsāra" is proclaimed to be the experience of pleasure and pain. [Thus, by her grace,] one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

From *tharvaṇāt* (69): the excellence characterized by an excess of devotion and faith is expressed by the prefix *pra-* in the sense of "removing the suffering (*ārtihāriṇī*) of living beings who bow down. She whose nature it is to remove (*harati*) the affliction (*ārti*) of pain is so described. *Daityanāśinī* (70) has a clear meaning; alternatively, *dainya* is the state (*bhāva*) of one who is cut down from the beginning—the suffix *yañ* being used in the sense of an abstract state. She bestows (*āśayati*) that [freedom from wretchedness] because of her unbroken form or because she protects her devotees. *Ḍākinī* (71) is so called because of the *bhūmi-tattva*. *Mi* [is the seed-syllable].

This is stated in the *Kāre-vī-tathā-ḍākinī-tāriṇī-ka-vaca-prastāva* as spoken in the *Gandharva-tantra*: "And it is said in the *Kula-cūḍāmaṇi*: 'The Ḍākinī on the left side is like ten million suns and fire. Or else, because she is of the nature of a specific type of liquor (*surā*), so it is said in the *Muṇḍa-mālā*, beginning with: "O Goddess, liquor is of three kinds: *Sphāṭikī* and likewise *Ḍākinī*," and then proceeding to describe the Ḍākinī.

By merely [reciting] this, one will certainly become the subduer of all. (72) In the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said: "One should worship Śākinī, and likewise Ḍākinī, Śakinī, Brah- mākinī, Kākinī, then Śākinī, and Hākinī, according to the sequence starting from the west. This is stated in the *Caitanyakalpa*. Here too, regarding the specific thirty-two-syllable mantra, [the deities are] Kulikā, Kāminī, Jñānā, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and then Kākinī.
Because it is said, "So be it, O Śākinī and Hākinī," likewise in the *Yogaratnāvalī*: "Śākinīs are considered to be of two kinds, due to the division into Khecarīs and Bhūcarīs.

I shall describe their locations and forms according to the tradition: in gardens, divine regions, and great mountains, the divine goddesses play as great Mālās; the Bhūcarīs are in the city grounds, while the Khecarīs, assuming various forms and visible [to the eye], bestow excellent siddhis."

Having somehow come to dwell in the world of mortals due to the curse of Rudra, they are seen endowed with various wonderful qualities, yet without auspiciousness. In sacred fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), villages, cities, districts, and towns, these *śākinīs* always dwell in many forms, remaining unperceived. O Goddess, [the *Gandharvatantra*] states that she is called *Śākinītāriṇī* because she resembles the orb of the moon, and *Śīlā* because she repeatedly performs the acts of creation and so forth.

Or, "she who is to be served by all the lords of arts" (74). Regarding the phrase "bearing the excellent *khaṭvāṅga*," the word "excellent" (*vara*) refers to its mudrā; as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "The *vara* and *abhaya* mudrās, O Dear One, are like [the gestures] of granting boons and fearlessness. The *khaṭvāṅga* is a specific type of weapon. Here, the bearing of the boon-granting gesture (*varadhāraṇa*) applies to Bālā Tripurā, according to the *Prapañcasāra*: "Holding a rosary, a book, the *abhaya*, and the *abhīṣṭa* [mudrās]. Now, regarding Kāmeśvarī:

According to the *Kādimata*, she holds in her hands a jewel-bowl filled with nectar and bestows boons; or else, according to the *Jñānārṇava*, one should meditate on Bhairavī as the constant bestower of great prosperity, supreme in granting boons. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well. The holding of the *khaṭvāṅga* (skull-topped staff) is to be known as being in the right hand, based on the recollection in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "The trident and the *khaṭvāṅga* are in the right. [She holds] a variegated *khaṭvāṅga*.

In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, [the Lord] is described as being adorned with a garland of human heads (*dharānara-mālā-vibhūṣaṇa*). Alternatively, in the meditation on creation (*sṛṣṭi-dhyāna*), he holds a lotus flower and a garland of flowers in his hands along with the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhīti*); whereas in the meditation on dissolution (*saṃhāra-dhyāna*), he holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a pestle (*muśala*) in his arms. These variations are stated in other Tantras. (75) Regarding the *Kaumudī*: "Know that splendor which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in fire—that splendor is mine."

Because of the statement [in the lexicon], "caṃdrikā, kaumudī, jyotsnā" [are synonyms for moonlight] according to Amara; or because of her gentleness (*saumyatva*), she is like that. (76) Regarding the term *kumudā*: they rejoice and are delighted by even slight objects, thus they are *mudrāḥ*—the suffix *kap* is added to a root with an *ig-upadha*, meaning those intent on desirable activities.
