(5) "She is a beautiful agent" (*sukartrī*) means she is an excellent agent; the expression is used because she wields weapons, or else it means she is both beautiful and an agent. Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in possessing an effort directed toward a material cause (*upādāna*) within the scope of an action. And "excellent" (*śobhana*) refers to that which pertains to every produced effect.

(6) The word *su* is to be understood as signifying that the suffix *-matup*, which expresses the sense of "possessing," takes on the meaning of "entirety" (*sākalya*) with respect to the "effect" (*kārya*), which is a part of the referent of the word *kṛti*.
(7) It is called *vimālā* because it specifically attains (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), or because it brings [the mind] under its own control;

this is due to its captivating nature or its being the very form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (8) It is called *amalavāhinī* because it possesses a flow (*vāha*) that is stainless (*amala*); that is, it has the form of a horse (*aśva*).

Because it ends in *ḍha*, the suffix *cha* is applied even from a *karmadhāraya* compound according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, it is a compound meaning "she who is both stainless (*amala*) and a river (*vāhinī*).

Thus, in the *Parameśvarī-dhyāna* of the *Prapañcasāra*: "Mounted upon a horse, holding in her hand a golden cane-staff. (8) Regarding "stainless" (*nirmalā*): it is that from which impurity (*māla*), or ignorance (*ajñāna*), has departed; or, it is that which has emerged from *mā*.
The compound [miti-tir-ādayaḥ] is formed with the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) in the sense of "having transcended" (*krānta*), etc. He accepts the poor among worldly beings;

that is to say, he favors them because [the state of poverty] serves as a cause for both [worldly experience and] the knowledge of reality (*tatvajñāna*). (9) Regarding "Bhāskarī": according to the scriptural statement, "That light which resides in the sun," or because it takes the form of a specific channel (*nāḍī*), the moon is situated in the *iḍā* and the sun flows through the *piṅgalā*, according to the science of breath (*svaraśāstra*).

She is called *Sūrya* because she generates the light of the sun, for the Śruti declares: "The sun resorts to that splendor" (*tattejo 'śritaḥ*). She is called *Bhīmā* because she is the form of a particular Yoginī; or else, she is *Bhīmā* because beings fear her greatly, as the Śruti says: "From fear of her, the fire burns," and so forth. The form *Bhīmā* is grammatically correct according to the rule *bhīmādayo 'pādāne*. Alternatively, she is *Bhīmā* because she measures out (*māti*) or does not abandon (*na yāti*) the fear (*bhī*) produced by saṃsāra and other such things.

Or rather, it means that which generates such knowledge as culminates in devotion (*bhakti-niṣṭhā*)—that is, the knowledge which produces a specific state of devotion, the object of which is that very form of devotion which is the cause of generating [such] knowledge. This is because it serves to dispel fear;

or else, "fear" (*bhī*) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), and "place of fear" (*bhīti-pada*) is formed with the suffix *aṇ* (yielding *bhāya*), with the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.
Thus, it is that which generates the aforementioned knowledge. It is the object of that knowledge in the form of devotion which generates the specific knowledge culminating in devotion.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the specific knowledge, it should be understood as having the scripture as its object and reality (*tattva*) as its object. (11) "Destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura":

this is derived from the root *han* with the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of the root itself, followed by the suffix *ṇini*. (12) "Kālindī": according to the *Padma Purāṇa*, she is named Kālindī because of her connection to Kaliṃdarpa, the son of the Yamunā; or else, *ka* refers to Brahmā and others, and that which is joined with them is *aliṃda*, which is the middle [term].

The compound *padalopī-samāsa* (elliptical compound) is as Amarasimha states: "The door of a house is called *aliṃda*. This [river] belongs to that [house], thus indicating a relationship of owner and property (*svasvāmibhāva*). Because she dwells at the door of the house of Brahmā and others for the sake of service, this indicates her supreme sovereignty. (12) Regarding *Yamunā*: she is the sister of Yama; according to Amarasimha, "Kālindī, Sūryatanayā, Yamunā, and Śamanasvasṛ" are synonyms. Alternatively, she is so called because she restrains (*yamayati*) him.

Because he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the mind (*manas*): [the word] *yamunā* is derived from the root *yam* with the suffix *una* by way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*). Alternatively, it means "he who knows" (*eti jānāti yaḥ*), according to the principle that roots meaning "to go" also mean "to know. From the root *iṇ* (in the sense of "going"), the suffix *ac* is applied; the substitution of *yaṇ* for *i* occurs by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*. He makes [the mind] like a sage (*muni*); thus, from the causative form *munayati*, the suffix *ac* is applied, and the *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*. [The name is] *yamunā* because of this [action].

The compound *tisamāsaḥ* has as its implied meaning "one who acts in a manner similar to a sage possessing self-knowledge. This is because of the statement: "He who possesses renunciation (*sanyāsī*) and yoga (*sayogī*) is liberated, and he is a knower of Brahman" (14). Regarding *vṛddha*: Amara states that *vṛddha* means "advanced in years" or "an elder" (*pravayas*, *sthavira*). Svāmī explains it as "one who has grown" (*varddhate sma*), derived with the suffix *kta*. The intended sense is that [the elder] existed at a time prior to the mere youth. (15) Regarding *yuvati*: [it refers to] a young woman. *Punar* means "again. *Tiri*... [text fragment].

The suffix *tit* is applied, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. Alternatively, it may be derived from the root *pū* with the suffix *satṛ*, or from the root *yu* (meaning "to mix" or "to not mix") where the sense here is "not mixing. Even though there is a connection between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) arising from ignorance (*avidyā*), no taint of that defect attaches to Brahman, according to the maxim: "As in the case of light and so forth; it is not so in every respect. Just as the light of the sun and other luminaries is limited only by obstructions such as nets and the like...

The meaning is as follows: just as one possessing limited power (*juvakratvādimān*) perceives sound only through the limitation of the ear, even so, the state of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) belongs to the Lord only through the limitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). (16) In the word *bālikā*, the suffix *ika* is used in its own sense; thus says the Śruti: "Thou art woman, Thou art man; Thou art youth and Thou art maiden; Thou art decrepit, moving with a staff; Thou art born, O All-pervading One."

The syllable *khaḥ* indicates that in all three of these [stages], women are said to possess the nature of a deity (*devatārūpatva*), since it is understood that the mere state of being a woman (*strītva*) is the defining characteristic for their worshipability. As stated in the *Kālītantra*: "Having paid homage to one who is a girl, or one intoxicated by youth, or likewise an old woman, or a beautiful woman, or even one who is despicable or very corpulent, one should meditate [upon her]. Or, as stated in the *Kāmaśāstra*, regarding the age of a girl: "A girl (*bālā*) is one up to sixteen years of age. This refers to the worship of the messenger (*dūtī*).

From the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "By means of the sixteen-year-old [vow], one [attains] a young woman with full and dark breasts. From the *Jñānārṇava*: "The Goddess Tripurā is threefold; hear first of Bālā. (17) Regarding "Kauśalyā," the suffix *nyap* is applied according to the rule "after *vṛddha*, from *kuśala* etc.
[Pāṇini 4.2.80]. From the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "All of you, beginning with Brahmā, have arisen from the state of being my own portions (*mad-aṃśa*)."
Because of her word, having led the son of Rāma [to her], and because she possesses the form of Aditi and is the daughter of Satyaśravas;

you are the husband of Ruṣā, Kaśyapa, and the son of Brahmā. Kauśalyā is Aditi, formerly the illustrious mother of the gods, because she possesses the power to create the world through meditation (*adhyāna*); or else, *kauśalya* is the state of being skillful (*kuśala*), according to the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*.

That [suffix] exists for this [word], or rather, because it is the cause of the festival of the moonlight (*kaumudī*), the moonlight itself, and Kārtika, it is so called. And thus it has been said: "There Śaṅkara was conquered and Pārvatī obtained the fruit of her recitation.

Regarding the form *mādrī*, by the rule *ataśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.173), which prescribes the elision of the *tadrāja* suffix *kāra* in the feminine, the form *mādrī* alone is correct in such cases as *mādrīsuta*.

In the *Ṭhitipadamālā*, having assumed that [the word] begins with *bharga*, Dīkṣita refutes the view that it begins with *prācya-bharga*. In the long reading (*dīrghapāṭha*), one must either accept the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "self" (*svārtha*) after the root *agha*, or alternatively, interpret it as "this [goddess] belongs to *madra* (happiness) by way of the relationship of being its producer"—that is to say, she is the producer of happiness for those born in Madra. (20) She is called *rundhatī*, meaning she obstructs the suffering of her devotees; this is according to the definition.

The suffix *śatṛ* [is used] as in "śayānā bhuñjati" and so forth. (21) Regarding the word *aruṃdhatī*, there is a statement concerning her in the *Dānadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*: "I stand immediately after my husband, supporting (*ruṃdhatī*) the earth (*dharām*), the sustainer (*dharitrīm*), the source of wealth (*vasudhām*); know me as *Aruṇdhatī* because I do not obstruct (*na ruṃdhatī*) my husband's mind. Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* it says, "O *Aruṇdhatī*, you are the foremost among virtuous women," and in the *Matsya Purāṇa* it says, "You are *Aruṇdhatī* because of your state of being a virtuous wife (*satītām*). [The text ends with: *aruṃdha*.
Regarding these [names], it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*: "The elders call Umā the mother of the *ūrjas*"; and in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "Vasiṣṭha is Maheśvara.

It should be understood that when they are synonyms, as heard in the texts, they apply directly to the subject (*prakṛti*), whereas when there is a distinction, they apply through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). (22) She is the "housewife of Purāri" (*purārigṛhiṇī*); *Purāri* is Rudra, because he is the destroyer of the three cities (*tripura*). (23) She is "Full" (*pūrṇā*), because there is no other excellence superior to her own.

"Āptakāmā" (one whose desires are fulfilled) means, according to scriptural tradition, being distinct from one who possesses a desire for the absence of their own pleasure or pain; or it means "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*), which is either unimpeded desire, or—alternatively—it is used because the tenth stage is designated as "Full" (*pūrṇa*) and that [stage] belongs to the *Kaulika* tradition. (24) "Of full form" (*pūrṇarūpā*) means because she is of one and the same nature at all times. (25) "Payasvinī" (the milch cow): since the word *payaḥ* can mean both milk and water...

"Tomorrow for him," and likewise, having commenced the *tarpaṇa* rite, [it says]: "with various fragrant waters mixed with the liquid of black aloe-wood" (26); and "like the full moon"—here, in the compound, the word *dharma-vācaka* is elided;
or else, she whose face is like the moon and whose speech is the form of the Vedas, because she favors all through her instruction on injunctions and prohibitions.

And so says the Śruti: "In this manner, from Him who is the Unslain Being, there issued forth as His breath the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgirasa," and so forth. Alternatively, because He causes the production of excellent poetry for His devotees, [the name] is a *bahuvrīhi* compound used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe bahuvrīhiḥ*).

Or else, it refers to her by whom the full face of the moon was protected—that is, its stability—[derived from the roots] *vad* (to speak) and *gam* (to go), meaning the stability of speech and movement respectively. Of this... [the word] *vākṣa*.

(27) According to the Vedic scripture: "O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand supported by the *rasanā* (the central channel). (28) [The term] *bālacaṃdrasamaprabhe* means that because her complexion is red, she possesses a luster equal to the young moon; or else, it means she whose splendor is like a digit of the moon—possessing an excellence of form free from defects—and whose nature is knowledge, as she is the substratum of valid cognition regarding all objects. (29) She is called *Revatī* because she is of the nature of the constellation Revatī, or because she is the beloved wife of Balarāma, or because she is a *grahī* (a seizer).
Or, because it is of a specific nature, so it is stated in the Āraṇyaka-parvan regarding the birth of Skanda: "They call Aditi Revatī; her planet is Raivata.
That most terrible great planet indeed afflicts children. [Viśva-kośa states: "Revatī occurs as the name of a wife, as a variety of star, and among mothers.
(29) She is called *Ramaṇī* because she causes delight, owing to her bestowing all perfections (*siddhis*) upon the Blissful Brahman.

Or, according to the Vedic scripture, "The wise man fears nothing from anywhere," she is *citrā*. Regarding the word *citrā*, the *Viśva* lexicon states that it denotes ṛkṣa, apsarā, hibha, and karbura. Alternatively, because she is the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the scripture says: "The one unborn [goddess], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar forms. Although [the qualities] such as *rajas* are indeed red...

The Sāṃkhyas say that although there is no such color [as blue], it is metaphorically designated as such because of the similarity in their qualities of coloring, clarity, and obscuring. The Vedāntins, however, say that this refers to the deities of the unmanifested state (*avyākṛta*), because of the similarity between fire, water, and food in having red, white, and black colors respectively. (31) "Possessing variegated and excellent ornaments" means she whose garments and ornaments are of various kinds; *ambara* means clothing or the sky.

According to Amara, "pariskāra" means ornament (*vibhūṣaṇa*). Alternatively, *citram* refers to the wonderful garment, which is Brahman—the space (*ākāśa*)—since Brahman is established as being denoted by the term "space. She has that very [Brahman] as her ornament because she is of its nature; furthermore, the qualification "wonderful" (*citra*) is intended to indicate that she is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), thereby excluding the material ether (*bhūtākāśa*). (32) Regarding "vīṇā": *vī*...

"Two kinds of lutes are proclaimed, characterized by the Śrutis and the Lord," so says the *Saṅgītadarpaṇa*. And it is stated in the treatise on music (*Saṅgītaśāstra*): "The staff is the form of Umāpati; the glorious Karabhaka is Mukuṇḍa himself; the gourd is Padmabhava himself; and the dwelling upon the string is Girīndraduhitṛ herself.
(33) Because she is the very form of Mātaṅgī, [the poet] addresses her as Vīṇāvatī, saying: "O Mātaṅginī, who is strumming that sweet-sounding lute..."

"May it pierce the heart," according to the *Śāradātilaka*. Alternatively, because she is a specific form of Nīlasarasvatī, the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi* states this after reciting her thirty-four-syllable mantra: "She who bears four arms, who is gentle, and whose habit is the playing of the lute," and so forth. [The word] *vidyā* means knowledge; it is twofold: *aparā* (lower) and *parā* (higher). The first is of the nature of ritual action (*karma-rūpā*), having prosperity as its fruit; the [second] is Brahman.

It is clearly stated in the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* that [the knowledge of Brahman] has knowledge as its cause and liberation as its fruit; likewise, there is a statement in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* of the Atharva Veda:

"Therein, the lower [knowledge consists of] the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda, as well as Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa. Beyond this, however, that which is unseen, ungraspable... [and so forth].

"Ptam," etc. (35). "Yaśodā": according to Amara, *yaśas*, *kīrti*, and *samajñā* are synonyms. She is so called because she bestows fame upon her devotees, or because, as stated by the Blessed One, she was born in the house of the cowherd Nanda and emerged from the womb of Yaśodā, or because she is his daughter (36). "Yaśasvinī": this is well known due to her universally renowned majesty; as it is said: "Know Him alone as the Self, and abandon words beyond that."

"Arising from fresh flowers" (ti) means "fresh," that is to say, not stale. According to the statement, "with flowers that are not stale, sprinkled with water, and free from insects," she became filled with intense joy by means of those flowers prepared according to the ritual rules;
this is the sense of "joy. For the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states: "The Supreme Light is pleased by the flower itself, as it has entered into the flower. (37-38)

Regarding the term *navapuṣpotsavā*: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to the menstrual flow of women (*kusuma*). Thus, it is one for whom there is a festival (*utsava*) of female menses. Alternatively, by the *bahuvrīhi* compound *navapuṣpā*, the woman herself is indicated; likewise, it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one for whom there is a festival. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Gandharvatantra*: "Seeing the Earth in the grip of death, they daily recited the thousand names; then the Siddhāntas were destroyed, and the [demons] were slain."

One should go to the *titala* [temple]; even the *Kālītantra* states: "The man who, having seen the vulva (*yoni*) of a woman in her menses, recites [the mantra] ten thousand times with a steady mind, [attains success]," and so forth. In the *Kalpalatā*, it is explained that by the word *pṛthvī* (earth), the temple of Smara (Kāmadeva) is intended.

(39) Regarding *utsavā*: she whose sacrifice (*yajña*)—consisting of excellent *sava* (libations) such as recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*)—is *utsava* is called *utsavā*; or else, *ut* means she who abandons (*tyajati*).

This [word] has the vowel *a* as its penultimate (*upadhā*) when the suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Pratyāhāra-āhnika*. From the root *sū*, with the suffix *ap*, the form *sava* arises; one who performs the act of letting go (*uttyāga*) is a *sava*. That which has such a *sava* is *utsavā*; because it is beginningless, it is devoid of birth (*janma*). (40) Regarding "a garland of fresh flowers" (*navapuṣpasrajā*), the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to lotuses, in accordance with the grammatical number (*vacana*).
Based on the vision in the Upaniṣad, "She who shines with a garland of blue lotuses," according to the opinion of Bhāguri, *āp* [is used] for *mālā*;

thus, she bestows (*lāti*) *mām*, that is, Lakṣmī, upon her devotees. Furthermore, since the verbal root *lā* in the sense of giving also exists in the *Candramata*, it is so called. Alternatively, she adorns (*alati*) or beautifies *mām*, which is Śiva. Or else, because of her extreme loveliness, she is like a garland (*māleva mālā*), serving as an ornament of garlands (*mālya-bhūṣaṇa-bhūtā*).

"She is white" because she is adorned with a garland of heads; she is beautified by a great garland of fifty [heads]—human skulls freshly severed, dripping blood, serving as crimson ornaments, their hair interlocked with one another, and hanging from her lotus feet—as stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*. Furthermore, according to the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, "she possesses the life-force of fresh flowers," and thus, having plucked a flower from a creeper...

Likewise, one should extract the pure leaf of *nāgavallī* from its stalk, smear it with the creeper [juice], and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) ten thousand times, a thousand times, or one hundred and eight times with diligence; thus one shall bring the three worlds under one's control. She who rides upon a corpse and wanders like a doe will manifest herself before him. For, by the grace of the *kula*-flower, such delight as this arises when one is intent upon the fresh flower.

According to the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* (45): "Consisting of fresh flowers" is stated to indicate her extreme dearness; or rather, it means she whose form is that of a woman during the period of menstruation. As it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

"Having approached one who is joined with the flow [of blood], and having worshipped the chosen deity upon her body, one should mutter the mantra for three days at the dead of night; the fruit of a hundred thousand recitations is bestowed."

One obtains [this] here; of this there is no doubt. (46) Regarding the term *puṣpa*: based on the etymology "she who possesses flowers (*puṣpa*)", she holds a blue lotus in her hand, according to the *Phetkāriṇītantra*, which states: "She has a sword, a blue lotus, a trident, and a skull-bowl in her hands. (47) The meaning of the word already explained as "adorned with a garland of flowers" (48) is that she is "endowed with the qualities of fresh flowers," because she is possessed of qualities directed toward those [flowers], such as desire and so forth.

"Adorned with fresh flowers" (*navapuṣpopaśobhitā*) has the same meaning as before. Regarding its perceptibility, it is stated in the aforementioned passage that she is "adorned with fresh flowers. This is clear: she is one whose beloveds—the heroic practitioners (*vīrasādhaka*) who take pleasure in flowers—are objects of her delight, being characterized by freshness (*nava*) and novelty (*anūtana*). Alternatively, she is one whose beloveds are those for whom fresh flowers are to be accepted (*upādeya*). She is "pleased" (*prītā*); [the root] *prī* means to please.

*Prī* means "that which satisfies the hunger of the foolish" (*jādin*); it is derived from the root *prī* with the suffix *kvip* in the agentive sense. The meaning is that [the Lord] has been attained by them through devotion alone, according to the statement: "Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this *māyā*" (Gītā 7.14), and according to the forthcoming statement from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Having meditated upon Me, the Reality... (52). The word *pretamaṇḍalam* means "the circle of the departed"; as Amara states: "*paretāḥ pretasaṃsthitāḥ*". There are corpses and *muṇḍās* in the four directions.
"One should meditate upon the Goddess in their midst, adorned with embers and bones, according to the yoga of meditation as described"—thus from the *Gandharva-tantra*.

[The term] *Kula-śāstra-pradīpa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that for which the *Kula-śāstra* is a lamp," because otherwise its feminine gender would be untenable. (54) Regarding the phrase "increasing the path of *Kula*":

the prefix *pra-* is used to indicate its excellence, such as its being non-disclosable (*aprakāśya*), its being seen by those who are not base (*apaśyaka*), and its granting of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). [The word] *Kula-puṣpa* refers to the *Kula*...

One should never, under any circumstances, disclose the substance, the worship of the *kula*, the *kula* itself, the Guru who is the Lord of the *kula*, the *kula*-garland, the *kulākula*, the *kulacakra*, or the meditation on the *kula*. This is according to the statement in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*. (55) As for "Śmaśānabhairavī," she is so called because she dwells in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
In the section on Kālī in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "She of terrible form, the Great Fierce One, the resident of the cremation-ground abode... Śma... [text fragment]

Beginning with "Śāna, Sthoma, Mahāraudra, Mahākāla, Digaṃbara," and continuing with "Viparitaratāṃ tatra Kālikā-hṛdayopari," and so forth, and according to the *Pañcarātra*: "One should install the terrifying Bhairava in cremation grounds, forests, or open spaces. And from the *Devīpurāṇa* in the *Kalpataru*: "O Goddess, when installed on a riverbank, at a crossroads, in streets, or in forests, she becomes the bestower of the accomplishment of all desires and purposes."

(56) *Kālabhairavī*: Because she is connected to the *Vīra-tantra* which begins with "Bhairava Kālabhairava, the lord of the cremation ground," it is stated in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: "Since she always subdues death (*kāla*) for those dwelling in Kāśī, she has attained supreme renown under the name Kālabhairavī. (57) *Bhairavapriyā*: As it is said in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, she who is always [devoted] to her devotees...

His messengers are extremely fierce; because they have attained the highest state of terror (*bhīrutā*), he is therefore remembered as Bhairava. Likewise, you are capable of sustaining the universe; because of this sustaining (*bharaṇa*), you are remembered as Bhairava. In the *Śrī Hayagrīva-pañcarātra*, it is said that formerly, when Hara was requested by the gods for the destruction of the Dānavas, he assumed the form of Bhairava, who is saluted by both gods and demons. In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, it is stated that one should meditate upon the self as the nature of Bhairava and Bhairavī whenever [one desires].

"O God, when I am intent on such thoughts during the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), at a wedding, while giving gifts, at the time of bathing, or during the worship of the limbs, may you be gracious toward me; of this there is no doubt.

Or rather, [I seek refuge in] those Bhairavas whose beloved is she—namely Asitāṅga and the others. They are described in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: 'Caṇḍa, Asitāṅga, Kapālī, Krodhana, as well as Unmatta-Bhairava, and likewise Saṃhāra and Bhausaṇa in sequence. Or else, [I seek refuge in] the ten Grāsas mentioned in the *Jñānārṇava*."

O Great Goddess, within that circle of the Mothers (Mātṛ-maṇḍala), one should worship ten Bhairavas: Hetuka, Betāla, Tripurāntaka, Agnijihva, Kālānta, Kapālin, Ekapāda, Hemarūpa, Acala, and Hāṭakeśvara. Alternatively, Vaṭuka Bhairava may be taken;
for it is said in the Kulārṇava: "O Queen of the Gods, as long as an offering is not given to Vaṭuka, all the deities remain unsatisfied."

She is satisfied even by mere remembrance (58). She is *Guṇānandabhairavī*, meaning that Ānandabhairava exists as a quality (*guṇa*) within her. Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the section concerning the ritual vessel (*kalaśa*), it says: "One should worship Ānandabhairava with these mantras," and so forth; here, the formation of the feminine form is established because of its presence [in the compound]. Alternatively, she is *Ānandabhairavī* because she belongs to Ānandabhairava; that is, she is connected to him as his attribute, characterized as being subordinate to him.

(59) *Nānandabhairavī*: This is a compound formed by the division of the yoga [of the words]. (60) Regarding *Dhyānabhairavī*, "meditation" (*dhyāna*) has already been explained; therein, she is called *Bhairavī* because her form is described as terrifying (*bhīṣaṇa-rūpa*), as it is stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "She is the Great Terrifying One" (*mahābhīmā*). (61) Regarding *Purabhairavī*, likewise in the *Varāhapurāṇa*: "That goddess is proclaimed as the Destroyer (*saṃhāriṇī*), she who is Kālarātri. Indeed, those gods who are her attendants... [the text continues with] *asaṃ...*.

By the passage beginning with "khyātakoṭi," [the text] describes the speech of Rudra regarding the request for that food: "O Lord of Gods, they shall dwell there, as well as other Jātahārikās, in houses, fields, ponds, lakes, gardens, and at shrines (*caitya*)," and so forth; or else, through a specific application, by causing agitation in cities and such places. As it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "There is loss of wealth in the house of wealth, but in the middle of the village, there is its destruction," and so on.
Remaining there, one should act without agitation, according to the words of the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "One should practice desire.

Because it brings about the power of illusion (*māyā*) through the specific application of desire in the form of Lalitā and others, it is stated in the *Kādimata*: "O Goddess, with one's body adorned with red perfumes, garments, ointments, and garlands, one should worship the Goddess while meditating upon her in a secluded garden."
Through these—white water-lilies, campakas, aśokas, pāṭalas, and śatapatras—along with these perfected substances, the *māyās* (illusory powers) of the virtuous are accomplished.

By obtaining the grace of these, a man becomes capable of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpa*). Alternatively, *māyā-jñāna* refers to that [knowledge] which has Bhairavī as its object, because it is the domain of the knowledge of the *Aśakaja* (the Unborn). "The knot of the heart is loosened, all doubts are severed, and his karma is exhausted."

Regarding the phrase "when that which is superior and inferior has been seen," it is so stated in the Śruti. The term *saumyabhairavī* refers to a specific division of Nīlasarasvatī; the meaning is that she is both gentle (*saumyā*) and *bhairavī*. She is called *bhairavī* because the word denotes a goddess in connection with a male [deity].
Thus, it is said in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi: "The gentle one who bears four arms," and so forth. *Lokabhairavī* is the cause of the creation of the world.

Therefore, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said: "O Dear One, O Great Goddess, the creation of the power of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa-śakti*) arises from Power; thus, without doubt, Brahmā is born from a Preta. (65) [She is called] *Suvidyā-bhairavī* because she is the cause of that. This is stated in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "For one who thus worships the goddess Mahānīla-sarasvatī, his speech, consisting of prose and verse, becomes like the Gaṅgā..."

As stated in the *Kālītantra*: "The practitioner who, seeing the naked-clad creeper, recites [the mantra] ten thousand times, shall immediately become the beloved of the Vidyā herself. Merely by the sight of her, disputants are rendered tongue-tied; his speech becomes composed of both prose and verse," and so forth. (65) *Nītibhairavī* means that *nīti* is guidance (*nayana*).

"Attraction" (*karṣaṇa*) refers to the state [of being drawn], as it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Having performed the recitation of the *Kula* and *Akula*, one brings [the woman] together at that very moment—even one dwelling on a river or mountain a hundred *yojanas* away, or one protected by ramparts and the like in thousands of other islands. Because she is the cause of all qualities such as the *vidyā* known as *Guṇabhairavī*, one who studies this [text] [attains] logic and so forth.

From the *Ārṣa-brāhmaṇa* (67), it is stated that one becomes a sovereign of speech through [the practice of] *mapurāṇakāvyādi*. It is called *Saṃmohabhairavī* because it produces delusion (*saṃmohana*) and so forth; likewise, it is said in the *Uttara-tantra*: "Attraction, subjugation, killing, eradication, as well as paralyzing, deluding, causing flight, causing wandering, eloquence of speech, wealth, and even the possession of many sons—and much more."

He becomes beloved by all beings, and he indeed attains the state of a sky-walker (*khecaratva*) as well as divinity. (68) Regarding "Puṣṭibhairavī," the meaning is that the goddess Bhairavī is of the form of nourishment (*puṣṭi*). With a sword in hand, of great form, bearing a shield and a mallet, mounted upon a horse, and rich in her own [divine] nature—such is Puṣṭī. This is from the *Devīpurāṇa*, in the sixty-fourth chapter on meditation. (69)

One should worship the goddess Tuṣṭi as Sṛṣṭibhairavī, who resides upon Kailāsa, who holds a noose, a goad, and a boon-granting gesture, who is gentle, and who bears a lotus in her hand—according to the Devīpurāṇa (70). She is called Sṛṣṭibhairavī because she is the cause of both [creation and maintenance]; for it is heard in scripture: "He who is the origin is indeed also the dissolution" (71). Thus, she is Sṛṣṭibhairavī. Saṃpa... [text ends]
Because she exists in the form of Tpradabhairavī, even though she is insentient, O Lord of Devas, she then became the worshipper of the deity Tripura;

for it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* regarding that Kalpa: "The Supreme Goddess became the agent of creation. She is known as Sthitibhairavī because she is the cause of the protection of the world-guardians.
Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the section concerning Rudrabhairavī, it says: "Having worshipped this Mistress of Devas, Mahātripurasundarī, [he attained] protection..."

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, although you are motionless even while in the state of a *preta*, O Goddess, through the guise of yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*), you became the power (*śakti*) herself for the sake of the destruction of that *preta* by means of meditation on him—namely, by the side of Kuvalaya. Alternatively, "stability" (*sthiti*) refers to the worldly order (*lokamaryādā*), because you are its cause;
and thus says the Śruti: "This is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Or else, it refers to the terrifying nature of Bhairavī, which produces fear.

It is heard [in scripture] that "from fear of Him the fire burns, from fear the sun shines; from fear Indra, Vāyu, and Death run as the fifth" (73). Regarding the term *puṇḍarīkākṣagṛhiṇī*: he whose eyes (*akṣi*) are like lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) is *puṇḍarīkākṣa*. According to Amara, *puṇḍarīkākṣa* refers to the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu). (74) The term *puṇḍarīkākṣavallabhā* is clear in both cases; [the commentary] Śrīkaṇṭha... [ends].

"O Gaurī, you alone have made your dwelling in my heavy heart, having established yourself upon the moon-crested Lord"—thus it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*. Alternatively, "Puṇḍarīka" means a tiger; she whose "house" (form) consists of that form which is the sense-organ (*akṣa*) in the nature of the mind (*manas*).

This is because, as the *Muṇḍamālā* states, "She is seated upon the back of a lion" due to her being mounted on a lion and because she is the abode of the minds of devotees. And the discus of the Goddess vomits blood.

One should show the lion, according to the *Mātsya Purāṇa*. Furthermore, by the term *puṇḍarīkākṣa* (lotus-eyed), the lotus seed is understood, as well as its suitability for that purpose, because of the prescription of those [seeds] for the rosary: "I shall describe the sphere of those situated in water, which bestows all perfections; one desiring prosperity (*śrī*) should perform recitation with lotus seeds and conch shells," according to the *Nārada Pañcarātra*. And the *Samayācāra* states: "For one who has fashioned a rosary of lotus seeds, both fame and fortune (*lakṣmī*) arise."

And from the words of the *Cāra* (the spy/agent), it is stated in the *Maṃtradevaprakāśikā*: "The lotus-seeds (*padmākṣāḥ*) bestow nourishment and fortune. Alternatively, the term "lotus-eyes" (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*) refers to the tiger (*vyāghra*), whose "eye" (*akṣa*) is its behavior in the form of an offering (*bali*); this is because [the Goddess] is fond of that. Thus, it is said in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*: "By means of the blood of a lion, a *śarabha*, or even one's own limbs, the Goddess attains satisfaction for a thousand years. Likewise: "A lion, a tiger..."
"A Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, give his own bodily blood to Mahādevī, nor should he kill a man, a lion, or a tiger;

having killed these, a Brāhmaṇa would go to hell. Regarding the word *puṇḍarīka*: "The white lotus, a white umbrella, and medicine [are called] *puṇḍarīka*; it is also [used for] a silkworm cocoon, a tiger, and the elephant of the fire-quarter," according to the Viśva-kośa. (75) As for *ānandaskaṃdarī*: now, [the text describes] the nature of the non-duality of Tripurā.

In order to express the state of being composed of the third division of *Ktvā*, the *Sundarī* is introduced by means of the manifestation of the essence of bliss; thus, "bliss" (*ānanda*) is desire (*kāma*). In this transmigratory world, which is as flickering as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, desire is the single essence and the sole happiness—so it is said in the *Kāmaśāstra*. By the etymology "she who is beautiful (*sundarī*) in relation to that [desire]," she is called the three-syllabled *Tripurā*. Accordingly, after reciting the mantra, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Goddess of Gods, one should worship her [as] Desire."

He shall become Kāmarāja, beautiful in all his limbs; this goddess is of the nature of Brahman, or rather, because she is of the form of Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is bliss, [and] bliss is the form of Brahman. (76) Regarding the term "Vīrasundarī," the word *vīra* refers to Nandin, since he is known by the name Vīraka. Herein follows a narrative from the Matsya Purāṇa: the Goddess, whose luster was dark, out of anger at the mockery of her own blackness, in order to abandon that [complexion]...
Having gone there to perform penance and having stationed the goddess of the mountain at the gate to prevent other women from entering,

Vīraka, by the power of Māyā, entered the presence of the Three-eyed Lord in the form of a jackal. Because she was ignorant of the true nature of the presiding deity of the mountain, Vīraka, provoked by her, cursed Hara’s vehicle, the bull, and reduced it to the state of stone.
Having heard the destruction of her wretchedness through that future prosperity which had arrived once more with the words "Pnuhi," he was moved by compassion and given the name Śailādi.
Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, concerning her deliverance: "Having worshipped Candra there, and thereafter Kāmarāja, one should abandon Candra and place [the mantra] in the mouth;
this is the method honored by Nandin. Or rather, she is the "Beautiful One" (*Sundarī*) for heroes because of their love for her; as it is said in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "And in a secluded place..."
"He should always dwell in a forest, on a mountain, at a crossroads, or in a cremation ground; this is the characteristic of a hero," and so forth.

(77) Regarding the phrase "Sundarī abides," the word "abiding" (*sthiti*) refers to speech (*vāk*), because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "The Supreme Lord created the names and forms of beings, as well as the setting in motion of their actions, from the very words of the Veda. This is because the Lord created the gods and others through the specific utterance of sounds. Thus...

And there is a scriptural passage: "Thus Prajāpati created the gods with the word *asṛgran*, humans with *asṛgram*, the ancestors with *indav*, the cups with *tiraspavitram*, the stotras with *āśavaḥ*, the śastras with *viśvāni*, and offspring with *abhisaubhāgya*.
This refers to the verse: "Asṛgran, indavaḥ, tiraspavitram, āśavaḥ, viśvāni, abhisaubhagā."

The meaning is that [the Lord], having remembered the gods and others by means of [specific] words, created them. (78) Regarding the term *guṇānandasundarī*: the root *aṃd* means "to smell" (*vaghraṇati*), and *aṃda* is derived from the root *ad* ("to bind") with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac); subsequently, there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Thus, *guṇānanda* refers to one who does not establish a connection with the qualities within himself—that is, one who is angry. For according to the statement of Hārīta: "When anger begins, even those [qualities] become unesteemed. And thus, by the force of the context, [it refers to] Durvāsas.

*Bhaḥ*. Thus, it is said in that context in the *Jñānārṇava* by Durvāsas: "O Goddess, in former times the Aparā was worshipped as Niṣkalā; or else, in the case of the Guṇas, the Guru-forms, and the various [deities], she who follows each respective name with the word 'Ānanda' is Sundarī, because her worship is performed for them in that manner. This is stated in the *Vīratantra*: "The Gurus, ending with the term Ānandanātha, bestow all accomplishments. (79) [The term] Kālasundarī refers to Saṃhāra.

By the word *kāla*, Rudra is intended; thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, beginning with "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the four-peaked [mantra] that bestows peace," it is said: "The great Vidyā of four peaks was worshipped by Śaṅkara; or rather, she is dark-colored (*kāla-varṇā*) and beautiful (*suṃdarī*). (80) Regarding the term *guṇasuṃdarī*: the "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are austerity, valor, and so forth; based on the etymology "he who possesses these qualities" (*guṇāḥ santi asya*), it refers to Agastya.

It is stated in that very same source: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the supreme form known as Lopāmudrā," beginning thus; and [it continues] that this is the knowledge (*vidyā*) worshipped by Agastya, which causes the agitation of the three worlds. Alternatively, the word *guṇa* (string) here refers to the taking up of the bow; likewise, in the *Māhiṣamardinī* [Tantra], it says: "The fish, the shield, the full bow, the noose, and the goad; the noose, the conch, the sugarcane-born [arrow], the bee-string, and also the goad."

Regarding the term *ṣpavāṇāni*, it refers to the meditation on the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhādhyāna*). The word *māyā* refers to *Suṃdarī*; she goes toward me, Lakṣmī, in the sense of being the object of a curse (*śāpaviṣayatva-sambandha*).

*Māyā* means Durvāsas; by him, Lakṣmī was banished from the three worlds (*trailokya*), as stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. From the root *yā* with the suffix *kvip*, [the form *yā* is derived]. By that [root], one assumes the distinction of its worship. This is stated in that very same [text] regarding the three peaks of the mantra known as *Kāmarāja*: [The verse follows: "In the three peaks of the *Kāmarāja* mantra..."

O fair-faced one, O Bhuvaneśānī who resides on the letter *ra*, divide [the mantra] into two parts. Devoid of the *bindu* and devoid of the *nāda*, she becomes Durvāsas-pūjitā. That knowledge which pertains to the deity Vāmā, he attains—that is, he reaches it—being one who knows the true form of that deity; for [this knowledge] turns away other desires regarding beautiful women. (82) She is called Saumya-sundarī because she belongs to Soma, as she is presided over by the Moon.

For it has been stated in that very same place, beginning with "She who bestows the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, having worshipped the deity [Candra]," that she is the one to be worshipped by Candra.

Alternatively, *aumyam* refers to the field of Umā (*umā-kṣetram*); by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of identity, it means "identical to that. She is *saumyā*—meaning beautiful—and thus possesses a lovely complexion.
Since the excellence of the flax flower (*atasī-puṣpa*) is also intended to apply to the field, she is called *loka-sundarī* ("the beauty of the world"). (83) *Loka-sundarī*. Thus.
Because Kautsyā is a guardian of the world (*lokapāla*), there is this reference to Indra. Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava*, beginning with the statement regarding the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja:

"This Vidyā, worshipped by Indra, bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; or rather, she is 'Sundarī' (the Beautiful One) among the worlds because she is the object of unconditioned love as the very form of the Self. (84) Regarding the term "Vidyāsundarī," [it is explained] as before: that which reaches the state of supreme knowledge (*vijñāna*).

That very [seed-syllable] is called the *agastya-graha*; it is stated in that same [text]: "O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the third syllable of the *vidyā* known as *Kāmarāja*, accompanied by the *śakti*-bīja, is the well-worshipped form of Agastya. Or rather, because she is the embodiment of Sarasvatī, she is called *Sundarī*.
This is because the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*, beginning with the words "He who has attained this syllable," states: "It should be known as the Great Heap" (*mahārāśi*). (85)

She is called *Nītisundarī* because, having been fashioned like the *Nītiśāstra*, she is the source of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja; for the *Jñānārṇava* states: "Having begun with the letter *ca*, the third [letter] ending in *ndra* should be made, O one worshipped by the sages. Alternatively, *nīti* means attainment (*prāpti*);
she is so called because she possesses that quality, owing to her all-pervasiveness, according to the Śruti: "And like space, she is omnipresent and eternal. (86) She is *Guṇasundarī*; the *guṇas*...

Because he possesses the nature of the three deities beginning with Satva, he is the Sun; he consists of the *Trayī* (the three Vedas), as indicated by the mantra-linga: "to the bearer of the essence of the three qualities" (*triguṇātmadhāriṇe*).

This has been stated starting from the passage concerning the lore known as Lopāmudrā: "O fair-hipped one, this lore was worshipped by the gods in the past. Thus, the twelvefold Sundarī has been described. It is said in the Jñānārṇava: "By these twelve... [The text ends here].

"O Goddess worshipped by the gods, by means of the well-known mantras, the Goddess who abides at the end of the twelve [syllables] is the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman; she is the Queen of all sciences (*vidyās*), served by all the *Āmnāyas*," and so forth. (8) (7) 12. Indeed, there are exactly twelve beautiful words here that possess the status of preceding terms;
however, those which are identical with her, designated as Tripurasundarī, have been shown to be of equal enumeration for one who delights in the *Māllikāhāra*.

Thus Halāyudha [explains] *mallikā-vivakila-vicakṣiṇī* as a compound where the word *hāra-pada*, although it generally denotes a string of pearls, here—due to its specific prefix (*upapada*)—has the meaning of a mantra; for it is stated in the section on prescribed flowers in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "One should offer *mallikā*. Furthermore, it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "He who, with devotion, worships Caṇḍikā with fragrant flowers, or with *mālatī*..."

One obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice by offering a *mallikā* flower; likewise, for each individual loose flower, the fruit is ten *sauvarṇikas*. By means of garlands, O King, that fruit becomes twentyfold. (88) The phrase "the necklace of *mallikās*" has been explained previously. Alternatively, *mallikās* are a specific kind of swan (*haṃsa-viśeṣa*); according to Amara, those called *mallika* are so named because they are made of *mallikās*. An offering (*hāra*) consisting of those [swans] takes the form of a sacrificial gift (*bali*).

Because it shares the common quality (*sādharmya*) of producing satisfaction (*tṛptijanaka*), she is "adorned by that," meaning she is insatiable (*asaṃtuṣṭā*). This is because of the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* regarding the section on offerings (*baliprakaraṇa*): "The pigeon, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the swan, the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), and the quail. Although Kṣīrasvāmin has explained [the term *mallika*] as "those with eyes like jasmine flowers, white-footed, and moving on white feet," nevertheless, the *malli*...

What word is used [here]? It is *vyasta* (dissolved). This is because the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon states: "The word *mallika* refers to a type of crane, as well as a clay vessel that resembles the root of a blade of grass (*tṛṇamūla*).

(89) "Possessing the hue of a fresh campaka" means she has a luster like the color of a fresh campaka flower—that is, its yellowish-orange (*piśaṅga*) tint; otherwise, the repetition of the word *varṇa* (color) would result in tautology. Furthermore, this should be understood from the *Navadurgā-mantra*: "Him whose crest is adorned with a heap of gold and a crescent moon. (pra)

From the *Pañcasāra*: (90) "Adorned with *nāgakesara*"; according to Amara, *cāṃpeya*, *kesara*, and *nāgakesara* are synonyms. According to Svāmī, it is so called because its flowers do not wither (*na priyāṇi na kesaravanti puṣpāṇi yasya*). Furthermore, according to the statement of the *Muṇḍamālā*: "The red flower, the *bilva* leaf, and the *nāgakesara* [are used].
(91) "Resembling the *javā* flower"; according to Viśva, "the *oḍra* flower is known as *javā*. [The suffixes] *-tulya*, *-saṃkāśa*, and *-nīkāśa* [indicate similarity]. *Uṣya*... [text fragment].
(92) Regarding the statement, "This staff, adorned with *javā* flowers," it is declared that it is a "deep red flower" (*tiraktapuṣpa*).

Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "By the offering of *javā* flowers, a woman with beautiful eyes shall be brought under control. (93) In the word "dear one" (*priyā*), the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *igupadhajñāprītikṛtaḥ kaḥ*.

Its meaning is "the essential nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*). (94) In the phrase "she who does what is dear to Viṣṇu," the suffix *khac* is applied according to the rule *kṣemapriyabhadreṣu khaḥ*. [She is] the sister of Vāsudeva.

Because it is said "She is," [she is] the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas; for *dānavas* are the offspring (*apatya*) of Danu, according to the suffix used in the sense of offspring. She is the Sovereign (*Īśvarī*) of Knowledge (*Jñāna*), that which is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death. Indeed, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* by the Blessed Lady: "O King of kings, without taking refuge in me, that auspicious nature which is pure by its own essence cannot be known; therefore, seek refuge in me."

"Vrajreti" means "the giver of knowledge. This is largely explained by the fact that one who knows is a "jña"; according to the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiriti kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied. She is the "giver of their *anaḥ*," which refers to the breath or, in other words, the life-force, because she is the cause of long life for her devotee.
As it is said in the *Phetkārīya*: "One obtains knowledge, the Vedas, fame, long life, and many sons; [she is] the abode of Śrī and Sarasvatī."

"Wherein one's own self is at rest"—this refers to the bliss born of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is liberation (*mokṣa*). Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the bliss of knowledge. The Vedāntins clearly state that its essential nature is Brahman. This has been stated in the Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa: "He who mutters, hears, contemplates, and upholds this [goddess]—who is without end, peaceful, wearing matted locks, the boundary of all the Vedas, and the giver of all objects..."

"One who worships the Yati-guru—[the one] whose name ends in 'Sra', whose parts are tranquil, and who wears matted hair—becomes a partaker of the fruit of the four aims of life, stainless, partless, free from duality, and devoid of fever," and so forth; likewise, it is stated by the Blessed One in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "For those who are constantly devoted to them, I destroy the entire darkness of the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva) by means of the lamp of knowledge before long; they, having shaken off all darkness..."

Through that single knowledge, becoming one with it, may they always be blissful and not be born again and again in saṃsāra. (99) Regarding the compound *guṇagauravasaṃpanna*, because of the usage by the author of the Bhāṣya and others where the prior member of the compound is predominant, Kaiyaṭa has explained that the prohibition of a ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa compound with *guṇa* is not universal;
thus, the compound *guṇānāṃ gauravam* is formed. The meaning is "the weightiness of the qualities related to Brahman. And so says the Śruti:

In the *Girijārthacintāmaṇi*, composed by Viśveśvara— the son of the scholar named Dharaṇīdhara, who was an ocean of words, authorities, and verses, and who possessed the knowledge of all that is to be known— this is the sixth moon (chapter). May the multitude of moons that are his toenails never abandon the mountain [of his feet], which dispels the darkness of the delusion of wealth through its supreme gift of light.
The inner self has released its lotus-feet from the clutches of the enemy. Now, regarding the sixth hundredth commentary: "Endowed with virtue and character" (*guṇa-śīla-samānvita*).

From the verbal root *śīṅ*, by virtue of belonging to the *saṃpadādi* group, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, the word *śī* refers to the state of being. *Guṇa-śīla* means that which takes or grasps the state of virtues. Thereafter, relying on the primacy of the abstract state, [the compound] *guṇa-śīlatvam* means that which destroys (*syati*) the absence of virtues.

The suffix *ka* is applied to the root *ṣoṃt-kṛ* (to perform the final rite) with the prefix *su-*, meaning "one who has attained the deity through the connection with the mantra. As it is stated in the *Phetkārīya*: "That man who performs the worship of this mantra becomes famous throughout the three worlds; he becomes endowed with beauty and youth. Here, "beauty" (*rūpa*) refers to a specific excellence of physical form.

Thus, O Devabodha, regarding youth (*yauvana*): it is *tāruṇya* (maturity). Since that [youth] exists as a single state at all times, it would follow that it is subject to modification (*vikāritva*) by attaining another state; therefore, the expression "endowed with fresh youth" (*navayauvana-saṃpannām*) is a mere sound (*phetkārīyam*). As for "adorned with the beauty of form and youth" (*rūpa-yauvana-śobhitā*):
it is adorned by that state of extreme excellence of form which exists beyond the diminution of its middle state. Alternatively, it is that which is beautiful (*rūpāti*) through its form (*rūpa*).

This multitude of young women possesses youth that is not subject to decay; according to the *Mahābhāṣya*, since the word *vati* is not included among the qualities such as "begging" (*bhikṣā*), the masculine form does not apply here. However, the term *yauvana* has been established and explained by another method, meaning "adorned by this [youth]. (3) Regarding *guṇāśrayā*: it means she takes refuge in the *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the others, by virtue of being the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*). (4) Regarding *guṇamayī*: it refers either to a modification (*vikāra*) or to an abundance (*prācurya*) of the *guṇas*.

In the alternative reading *guṇavatī*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used; however, the constant reading is *matup*. (5) Regarding the phrase "beautiful through the weight of her qualities" (*guṇagauravasundarī*), she is beautiful by virtue of the weight of qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomayī*) and "having the vital breath as her body" (*prāṇaśarīrā*); for it is observed that she is to be meditated upon by Brahmā on account of these qualities. (6) Regarding the phrase "famed as the lord of the shining ones" (*lasattārāpatiprakhyā*), the word *lasat* refers to supreme fullness, while *tārāpati* refers to the moon; the term *prakhyā* signifies a representative or likeness, meaning she is similar to [the moon]. In this sense, it conveys the idea of resemblance.

According to the *Prapañcasāra*, this [goddess] is Sarasvatī herself in the form of the teacher Daṇḍin, "white as the moon or a jasmine flower. Alternatively, she is one whose splendor is like that of Tārāpati (the Lord of Stars, i.e., Bṛhaspati); this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), meaning "she from whom a splendor equal to Tārāpati shines forth," because she bestows upon her devotees an intellect equal to his. (7) She is "adorned with two earrings" (*tāṭaṅkadvayaśobhitā*); *tāṭaṅka* refers to a type of ear-ornament for women.
In the *Uttaratantra*, within the section on the female messengers (*dūtī*), it is stated that [the goddess] "stands at the root of a tree" (*vṛkṣamūlasthitā*);

this is because the procedure for offering oblations (*bali*) to Graha and the others is prescribed beneath trees. Likewise, in the *Prayogasāra*, the trees of the Mothers (*mātṛvṛkṣa*) are enumerated in order starting from the east up to the northeast: the *kadaṃba*, the *karañja*, the *vibhītaka*, the *nimba*, the *aśvattha*, the *udumbara*, the *śleṣmātaka*, and the *vibhītaka*.

Those situated at the corners—having resorted to one of these, one should offer the bali-oblation as is appropriate; or else, one should meditate upon the Goddess seated beneath the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, because of the description in the meditation [as follows]: "(9) *Devī* means the female of the gods (*deva*); she is the goddess. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*. By her skill, that Rāma was previously drunk alone with ease. Bhara... [text ends].
Following such usages as "tastato bhūt" (he was here and there), because the relationship between the produced and the producer is inherent, [she] stands upon the branch of the tree.

This is according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "The trees have [birds] that are tawny, blue-necked, and deep red," or else because she resides above on the branch in the form of a creeper (*vallī*). As stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: "The god whose weapon is the trident is the tree; the beloved is the creeper."

Because it is not so stated [in the primary sense], [the phrase] "dwelling in the middle and at the top of the tree" is supported by the Śruti: "Two birds... Here, the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) is used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) to refer to the body; by this, her nature as both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is expressed. Regarding the phrase "residing in the middle of the tree," it has been said in another Tantra concerning these various forms: "In a grove adorned with *caṃpaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, and *kadalī* trees, she is mounted upon a swing, her face serene, surrounded by female attendants..."

"Vāritāṃ kumudvatīm": according to the *Viśvakośa*, "kumudvatī" refers to the wife of Aṅkuśa, who was born from a *kumudinī* (lotus pond). Alternatively, it means she possesses (*santi*) those who take delight (*ut-prīti*) in the base (*kutsitānām*), namely fools, the poor, and so forth, by virtue of her relationship as one who favors them.
(14) Regarding "kumudinī," the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *puṣkarādibhyaḥ deśe*. Alternatively, "kumuda" refers to the white water-lily (*kairava*).

"Ktapaṃkaje" according to the *Viśva* lexicon; "all deities are satisfied by a red lotus flower" according to the statement in the *Muṇḍamālā* (15). "Kumudā" because it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* that the Goddess resides in the Mānasa lake where there are water-lilies (*kumuda*); or else, because she possesses water-lilies (*kumudāni*), as stated in the *Śāradātilaka* in the section on Durgā: "One should subdue Brahmins with water-lilies and kings with lotus-homa" (16).

She makes a bed of white water-lilies (*kumuda*); that is to say, she has a lake of white water-lilies as her place of practice (*sādhaka-sthāna*), because it is stated in the *Vīra-tantra*: "In an empty house, a cremation ground, a temple, or a lake. (17) She is fond of safflower blossoms; for the *Viśva* lexicon states, "Safflower (*kusumbha*) means gold or great red dye. This is because it is generally prescribed that the Great Goddess is [worshipped] with red flowers. Or else, "Ke" refers to... [text fragment].

"O Śivā, by means of *laṃ* and golden flowers, one may paralyze the three worlds; within a single month, even the sins committed over seven lifetimes shall be destroyed, and one shall delude the entire earth encircled by the oceans"—so it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*. (18) Regarding the phrase "with heads as red as safflower": this is because, at the beginning of battle and similar occasions, the color of the face becomes red due to anger; or else, it refers to the heads associated with the garland being as red as safflower.

Because she is adorned with such a garland of severed heads (19), she is "resembling the *svayaṃbhū* flower. Since the *palāśa* tree is the *brahmavṛkṣa* (the tree of Brahmā), the term *svayaṃbhū* refers to that [Brahmā]; because she is red in color like the flowers associated with it, she is "resembling the *svayaṃbhū* flower" (20). She is called "bearing" (*dhāriṇī*) because those flowers are known to be used in worship. In reality, however, the intended meaning is the secret convention (*saṃketa*) accepted by the Kaulikas. That...

It is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "O Goddess, the self-arisen flower (*svayaṃbhūkusuma*) arises in three ways in this world: that which is obtained before the age of sixteen is the best, granting all accomplishments; that which is obtained by force increases enjoyment; and another, obtained through the power of the union with the *rajas*, is the lowest, bestowing pleasure. (21) Regarding the lake of the self-arisen flowers, it is because of the rule of not writing [the name] there; likewise, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

Having fashioned a yantra with substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, as well as with *svayaṃbhū* flowers, *rocanā*, lac, red pigments, saffron, and reddish sandalwood, one should perform worship there and then carry out the recitation (*japa*). Alternatively, according to the procedure for offering the *argha* water, as stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "By offering [worship] with *svayaṃbhū* flowers, one becomes a recipient of the six rites. This is because the word "always" (*sadā*) in the phrase "always possessing meditation" (*sadādhyānavatī*) has the sense of "constantly" (*pārṇārtha*).

The inclusion of his name within "Bhavāt" is more appropriate; likewise, another tantra describes her as the "Descent-bestowing One" (*avatāriṇī*), meditating upon him [Śiva] placed above a corpse, and above that, upon a skull-bowl (*kapālaka*).

She is intent on meditation at the tip of the nose, most terrible, and the bestower of boons. Śukrapriya—Śukra being the preceptor of the Daityas—caused the drum to be sounded. When the Goddess raised her trident against the ascetic, he attained the status of a son to the Goddess, and she [the Goddess] acted toward Śaṅkara as a father.

Thus, in the *Mokṣadharma*, because the Goddess was made her son at the time of the emergence of Śukra from the womb of Śiva; or alternatively, because the word "Śukra" refers to the seed (*bīja*), according to the statement: "by means of substances born from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*"; or because [the deity] grants that fruit through the fire-oblation (*ratā-homa*) of Śukra, as stated by Śātātapa: "The deities are on the earth, in the waters, likewise in fire, in heaven, and in the sun"; and because the ritual action (*kriyā*) is performed in the fire.

Regarding the phrase *tāṃ devā iti*: because the ritual procedure for worship consisting of oblations (*homa*) is prescribed there, [the term *śukra*] refers to semen. As Amara states: "The word *śukra* is used for semen, the planet Venus, the Nābhaṛga, the eldest [brother], and fire" (25). In the expression *śukramajjanatatparā*, the root *śuc* means "to grieve. That which moves away from grief is *krama*; one who acts like that is *kraman*, meaning "one who does not waver" (*avañcal*). Thus, *śukraman* means "one who moves through grief. Furthermore, *śukramajjana* refers to a person (*jana*) who is immersed (*majjana*) in that [grief]. Here, she is intent (*tatparā*) upon that [state].

The meaning is: "because of being intent on its extraction. Alternatively, it means: "O Body, you are immersed in the month of Jyeṣṭha, which is the best (śukra) for immersion and heating; that from which [merit] is extracted is the highest. A mantra is perfected by recitation (*japa*), not by mere offering (*āhuti*), and thus yields fruit"—this is the exalted praise of that [month].
As it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "Having recognized the time of spring, having constructed a supreme temple for Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Sun, or one's chosen deity..."

One should have a jar fashioned for us; on the first day of the month, one should place it upon the head of the deity according to this rite for four months. Thus it is said, and so forth. Alternatively, in the section on the offering of *argha*, the *Muṇḍamālā* states: "By means of the seeds of the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, one becomes a lord of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

That which is produced from union with a widow is the *kuṇḍa*, which bestows supreme prosperity; that which is produced from union with a widow is the *goḷa*, which bestows supreme accomplishment. (26)

Regarding the term *pūrṇā*: it refers to the full moon day (*pūrṇimā*). As stated in the *Harivaṃśa*: "O Indra among kings, the fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon (*amāvasyā*), and the full moon (*pūrṇimā*)—these are the sacred festival days (*parvan*), as is the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*).

Because worship on the full moon day is thus highly recommended, so too is it said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "He who at all times and in all places takes refuge in Caṇḍikā... [the rest of the verse follows].
Having ascended the boat of the garland of waves, O King Kuṃbha, one goes to the world of Brahmā and rejoices there for eternal years.
(27) Regarding the term *aparṇā*: it refers to her from whom the consideration of debt, wealth, and the like has departed, because she is a perfected *vidyā*. Thus, in the *Muṇḍamālā*:

"In this [practice], there is no dependence on the *siddhas* and so forth, nor is there any calculation of lunar mansions and the like; there is no purification of time and so forth, nor is there any defect regarding friends and the like. (28)

"Suparṇā": according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *parṇa* means "leaf" as well as "the *kiṃśuka* flower"; since worship is prescribed with those flowers—as stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "With *kiṃśukas*, *tagaras*, and so forth"—or else, because it is said that this creeper (*vilatā*) is born from a portion of the Blessed One, she possesses *suparṇa*, i.e., Garuḍa, as her purifier (*punatvena*). (29) "Niḥparṇā": since leaves are parts of a tree, by metaphorical usage (*upacāreṇa*), she is "without parts" (*niravayave*) [as she transcends material form].

The meaning is as follows: because it is of an indivisible nature, [the text] states "destroyer of sins" (*pāpanāśinī*) in order to indicate that the state of being sin—which has become pervasive—is the delimiting factor (*nāśyatāvacchedaka*) of what is to be destroyed;

this is for the purpose of obtaining the sense that [this rite] destroys all sins whatsoever, characterized by a specific intermediate genus (*avāntara-vaijātya*) produced by the killing of a Brahmin’s wife.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* it is said: "Even a mountain-like heap of sinful deeds, upon reaching Caṇḍikā, who is like a physician, is destroyed."

"Even a man who is like a malignant disease, full of malice in all conditions, or joined with all sins, reaches the supreme state after bowing to Durgā. (31) "Because it is endowed with the fragrance of wine, the world-mother Caṇḍikā, being enraged, [drinks] this excellent drink"—thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. And in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, beginning with "One should meditate on Kālī with a terrifying face," [it speaks of] wine.

Because of the performance of this worship, she causes the entire earth to tremble with her intoxicating laughter; and because she possesses the fragrance of intoxication (*mada-gandha*), that woman who moves slowly, stumbling from intoxication, is called *Sogrataretī*, as stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "She is considered the destroyer of sins.
(32) Regarding the term *madirāmodadhāriṇī*: she likewise bears the fragrance of wine (*madirāmoda*) which brings joy (*prīti*). Thus, [she is] the *Kula*...

In the *Cūḍāmaṇi*, it is said: "One should not perform the worship of the Vatsa-kula with liquor and meat; his merit earned over thousands of previous births is destroyed. In the *Śrī-Brahmasaṃhitā*: "One who is distinguished [by devotion] should offer that which is endowed with the five 'M' syllables (*makāra-pañcaka*) to the Goddess; without these five substances, one never attains perfection. (33) Regarding the phrase "the refuge of all" (*sarvāśraya*): the term *āśraya* emphasizes the state of being; it refers to the quality of being the refuge for all.

She should be the refuge for all, because she is the one to be resorted to by everyone; thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa in the words of Lomaśa: "She alone is to be served, chanted, and meditated upon by the wise, for she is the sole ferry across the ocean of worldly existence and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation (apavarga). She is the cause of the sprout of bliss consisting of all virtues. Here, "sprout" (kaṃdala) refers to her being the cause of the sprout of bliss consisting of all virtues—that is, the most excellent bliss in the form of liberation (mokṣa).

The word "pada" refers to the eternal state, according to the Vedic revelation: "All beings subsist on but a mere fraction of this very bliss. Likewise, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "He who always worships Durgā or bows down to her with devotion—he is a yogi, he is a sage, he is wise; liberation stands within the palm of his hand. And it is said in the *Nīla Tantra*: "A woman has life-breaths equal to a flower"; one should meditate upon the Goddess on the great *cīna* tree.

One should worship that [deity] with flowers produced from those trees, worshipping with a spirit of devotion. (36) The compound *nārīpuṣpasamutsukā* is a locative Tatpuruṣa compound where the locative case has the sense of "object" (*viṣayatva*). Thus, it is stated in the *Gandharvatantra*: "If one observes a woman who is in her menses and worships daily for a thousand times, then, having destroyed the established conclusions [of opponents], he shall traverse the surface of the earth. (37) [The term] *nārīpuṣpotsava*... [ends abruptly].

The festival of the Goddess is the cause of her delight; as it is stated in the *Śrīkrama*: "O Maheśānī, by offering as an *arghya* the substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, as well as the *svayaṃbhū* flower, one becomes a lord of all *siddhis*. (38) Regarding the word "woman" (*nārī*), those learned in the scriptures say that these are the female forms assumed by the Supreme Lord, who has taken on a form out of compassion for his devotees, beginning with Śrī Bhavānī. (39)

Regarding the phrase "delighting in the flowers of women," it is stated in the *Kālītantra*: "Having prepared the flowers of creepers, the wise one should take a hundred leaves; having consecrated them according to the rite with due honor, the excellent practitioner should then perform the oblation in the consecrated fire according to the rule. By that, O Śivā, ten thousand ages of worship are accomplished. (40) As for "mṛgī," the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *mṛgī* refers to a particular type of woman."

And likewise, Bharata, having begun with "one whose belly, navel, nose, calves, and thighs are lovely," and so forth, concludes by saying: "the angry one is of mountain-like nature, while the woman is of deer-like nature. Alternatively, because it takes the form of a specific mudrā, it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:

"Three mudrās for the fire-oblation (*homa*) are taught: the Deer (*mṛgī*), the Swan (*haṃsī*), and the Boar (*sūkarī*). The Boar is the contraction of the hands; the Deer is when the little finger is released."
The gesture known as *haṃsī* is proclaimed when the index finger is released [from the previous position] in three ways; likewise, in the *Aśokī*, it should be understood as the *mṛgī* [gesture].
(41) Regarding the four-armed form, it is stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "Four-armed, with a fist adorned by a piece of red flesh," and so forth.
(42) Regarding the ten-armed form, this should be noted in the case of Mahiṣamardinī; for it is said: "I shall describe the form of Kātyāyanī as ten-armed."

Regarding the statement that she is not mentioned in the *Purāṇas* (43): in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* cited by Hemādri, it is stated that Bhadrakālī should be made with eighteen arms and is enchanting; "she whose eighteen arms shine forth, plump and well-armed, as well as [holding] iron clubs.
Furthermore, in the *Vāmanapurāṇa*, there is a mention of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa as adversaries of Mahiṣāsura; likewise, in the context of the ten-syllable mantra (*daśākṣarī*), there is the *Muṇḍamālā*.

"She who has eighteen arms, is eternal, and is seated upon the back of a lion," and so forth; [it is also said] "she has two arms. Likewise, in the *Gaurīvivāhaprakaraṇa* of the *Hayashīrṣapañcarātra*, it says: "One should have the goddess made with two arms, adorned with all ornaments. Similarly, concerning Jalatārā, in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, after stating the twelve-syllable mantra, it describes her as blue-colored, three-eyed, and having two arms.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yad paṅkaje* (45): "six-armed" (*ṣaḍbhuja*) refers to her form as Kāmeśvarī; likewise, in the *Kādimata*, she is described as "six-armed, three-eyed, with a head adorned by the digit of the moon," and so forth (46). She is situated upon an eight-spoked lotus—that is, a lotus possessing eight spokes or petals—because this constitutes the ritual procedure for worship. This is stated in the *Ātharvaṇabrāhmaṇa*: "In the place of the full [moon]..."

*Oṃ tatsat*. Within [the maṇḍala] there is a six-cornered [figure] and an eight-petaled lotus. Alternatively, because she is of the nature of Kuṇḍalinī, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* concerning her: "She yawns and is offered as an oblation; she resides within the eight-petaled heart-lotus," and so forth. *Kauberī*:

This is because she is of the form of a Yakṣiṇī belonging to Kubera; or else, because of the relationship between the worshipped and the worshipper, since Kubera—the preceptor—possesses the sovereignty (*kauśa*) that holds the same respect as Indra.

From the *Śiva-kaṇḍa Purāṇa*, or rather, because she is the sole beloved of the North; as it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "In the division of the directions, the northern direction (*kauberī-dik*) is that which causes pleasure to Śivā. Or else, because she is the form of Kubera’s wife; for the *Liṅga Purāṇa* states: "The Lord of Yakṣas himself is the one with the crescent moon on his crest (*ardha-candra-mauli*), and Ṛddhi is remembered as Umā. Or else, because she belongs to the Northern Tradition (*uttarāmnāya*); as it is stated in the *Samayācāra*.

The Tārā-bheda-s, together with the Kālikā-bheda-s, are joined with Mātaṅgī, Bhairavī, Chinnā, and Dhūmāvatī; these are declared in the Uttara-āmnāya as bestowing fruits quickly. (48) She is called "Kauravī" because she was propitiated by Yudhiṣṭhira; thus it is said in the Mahābhārata: "As soon as King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, entered the delightful city of Virāṭa, he praised the Goddess in his mind."

Alternatively, it is called *Kauravī* because its sound is contemptible due to the division of parts as described in the *Avasantarāja*, or because its sound is contemptible since it brings about undesirable results in the absence of worship. This is according to the statement: "If one does not worship the Goddess who assumes the form of an animal in a secluded place with the howling of a jackal (*śivārāva*), everything of his will certainly perish quickly. Therefore, this belongs to her; hence it is *Kauravī*.

The meaning is "Śiva. As it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "One should utter 'Kālikālī'; therein she is of the nature of Śiva. She approaches in the form of a bound soul (*paśu*) together with her retinue of attendants. (49) Regarding the term *kaulya*: *kaula* refers to those who follow the *kula*-practice; that which is beneficial for them is *kaulya*. Alternatively, *kola* means a boar; as Halāyudha states: "*kola*, *kroḍa*, and *sūkara* are synonyms for *varāha* (boar). That which belongs to him is *kaula*; [the meat] of that...

It is excellent to use *saṃtatra* [the plant], because of the previously cited *Yāmala* statement: "That which arises from the boar (*varāha*), goat (*aja*), and deer (*mṛga*). Alternatively, one may use *kola* (black pepper), not anything else, as before. This is stated in the *Durgākalpa*: "By the oblation of black pepper (*marīca*), the enemy certainly meets his death. Amarasimha states: "*Marica*, *kolaka*, and *kṛṣṇa* [are synonyms for black pepper]. (50) Regarding "Kurukullā," likewise, concerning Dakṣiṇakālī, it is said in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "Kālī...
