Thus, in the Rudrayāmala, Brahmā asked the Lord of Gods, Viṣṇu, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds: "By propitiating which Vidyā is one called 'possessor of the four Vedas' (*caturveda*)? Viṣṇu [replied to him]...

He said to Hara, the Lord of Gods: "Ask Śaṅkara; the Great Vidyā Sarasvatī is established within the body of Śiva. Having heard those words of his, Brahmā asked Śaṅkara: "O Lord of Gods, tell us of that Nīlasarasvatī by name. Hearing the words of Brahmā, Maheśvara laughed and said: "Listen attentively, O Brahmin, to the Vidyā of Nīlasarasvatī, by obtaining whose grace one becomes a knower of the four Vedas."

"tvadiṣyasi," etc. (45). Regarding "cūrṇa," it refers to aromatic powders such as *paṭavāsa* and the like, according to the explanation by Svāmī and others; this is because she possesses the form of a messenger (*dūtī*). Thus it is said in the *Uttaratantra*: "One should employ that woman as a messenger in the ritual acts, having anointed her with red perfume, adorned with red garments, possessing fragrant red flowers, decorated with all ornaments, and fumigated with excellent incense. (46). "Caṃdrāsyā" refers to the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) with camphor.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Nīlatantra*: "Furthermore, by performing oblations (*homa*) with camphor, agallochum, saffron, and musk, the practitioner of mantra shall obtain all desired objects from Nīlasarasvatī. (47) Likewise, in the *Siddhasārasvata* regarding the meditation on Jalatārā: "I worship with my heart that Nīlā Sarasvatī, who possesses four faces rising upward and whose speech flows forth as a stream of poetic inspiration. (48) [The term] "calaccakoranayanā" is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The term *yagarbha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Alternatively, it refers to that [goddess] whose eye is the "bringing" (*nayanam*)—that is, the leading—of the *cañcala* bird, because it is to be offered as a tribute (*balitvena dātavya*), according to the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "The partridge, the fish, the sparrow, and the *cañcala* bird.

Regarding the phrase *calatkhañjanalocanā*, the compound is formed as before. Alternatively, it means she whose eyes cause the limping (*khañjana*)—that is, the obstruction of movement—of those who are moving (*calatām*) or possess motion.

The compound [locana-namaskārādi-rūpa-jñānasya] is a genitive-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhyanta-samāsa*) signifying "the object of that [knowledge] which consists of the forms of salutation to the eyes and so forth. Furthermore, according to the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra* and other texts, it is said: "In a field there would be a loss of crops; in a horse, a loss of speed" (50). Regarding the phrase *caladambhojavadane*:

alternatively, she is one whose face drives away (*calati*) the speed (*java*) or velocity (*vega*) of the great flow of water (*mahājala-pravāha*), which is moving water (*calad-ambhas*). Thus, she is *calad-ambhoja-vadana*. She is *conā*.

The mantra which begins with *namaskāra* is likewise ten syllables long. Having recited it, [it is said] in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "In this world, fear of water arises only through the grace of the Mother of the Universe.
And likewise in the *Siddhasārasvata*:

"Having performed the recitation (*japa*) in that manner, one should offer oblations (*homa*) with blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*) numbering one-tenth of the recitation; one should satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that [number]. The word "and" (*ca*) implies the inclusion of the student (*chātra*).

A *chātra* is one who possesses the characteristic of serving his guru; thus, because there is a prohibition against such a person receiving [the teaching] without his guru, this [practice] belongs to him. Likewise, it is stated in the *Mahogratārā-kalpa*: "But he who, having seen Tārā, the destroyer of sins, should receive [her mantra] by himself... (53). She for whom an umbrella (*chatra*)—that is, a parasol—is dear is *Chatrapriyā*. And so it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Pearls, stainless gems... and so forth.

"An umbrella with the luster of the moon," and so forth. (54) Regarding "umbrella" (*chatra*): from the root *chad*, meaning "to cover," and the suffix *tra*, it means that which protects (*trāyate*) or guards; thus it is called *chatrā* because it serves as a cause for protection on all sides. (55) "Adorned with an umbrella and a fly-whisk" (*cāmara*): it is stated thus in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Daughter of the Mountain, two fly-whisks white as the waves of the Gaṅgā [should be offered]. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, in the section concerning Durgā, it says: "To the God of Compassion, a fly-whisk adorned with a jeweled handle, with a handle made of gold, silver, or other materials... and so on. Regarding its [the handle's]...

Listen to the fruit of merit: surrounded by celestial women with yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*) held in their hands, one shall dwell for a long time in the city of enjoyment, situated in a great pleasure-palace (*vimāna*). (56) Regarding the word *Chinnamastā*: it is derived from *Satyabhāmā* [with the suffix *a*], where the latter part of the compound, beginning with *satyā*, is elided after the word *chinnā*.

For it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* that "even without a suffix, there may be elision of both the preceding and following members of a compound. (57) Regarding *chadiḥ*: it means "one whose neck is severed."

Regarding the visualization of her as "another [woman] drinking the stream of blood gushing from her own severed head due to vomiting blood," this is because it is seen in that very [scriptural] tradition that she is satiating the Ḍākinī with blood flowing from her own neck, which was just severed. Regarding the term "severed-headed" (*chinnaśiras*), it is because she is devoid of a head in that very form; for the *Viśvasāra* states: "She holds her own severed head in her hand."

Alternatively, "chinnośarodaityānām" means that she [cut off] the front of the army of the Daityas, just as their heads [were cut off]; for the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *senāgrabhāga* applies both to the vanguard of an army and to the head. (59) Regarding "chinnanāsa": it refers to her whose nose was distinguished in the middle because her loud laughter (*uṭṭahāsa*) had been severed; or else, it refers to her by whom the destruction (*hati*) of the devotees' noses was severed. In both cases, the form is derived from the rule: "After the roots *ṇas* and *ṇu*, when followed by *ṇi*, there is optionally [the substitution of *an*]."

Regarding the definition of *chala* (quibble) as "the deception consisting in the misinterpretation of words" (*drumapaṭhitābhyāṃ bhāva-cheda-chalāt tv iti*), it is so called because it involves the distortion of meaning through the application of one's own interpretation for the sake of rejecting the other's statement. According to the Nyāya Sūtra, there are three types of *chala*: *vākchala* (verbal quibble), *sāmānyachala* (generalization quibble), and *upacārachala* (metaphorical quibble).
An example of the first is as follows: when someone says, with the intention of referring to newness, "Devadatta has a new blanket" (*navakaṃvalo devadattaḥ*), [the opponent objects].

The statement that there are nine blankets (*kaṃvala*) refers to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of one; this is intended according to the third [category], *tejasvitva* (luminosity). When it is said, "Agni is Māṇavaka," it does not follow that he is not Agni because he is a non-burner. From the *Atharvaṇa*: "These are the tarkas and āgamas... (61).

Regarding *chalāḍhyā* (rich in quibbles): *chala* is the deception of people; by that, [the category] is "rich" (*āḍhyā*), because it causes the disputants to fall into error. Thus it is stated in the *Rudrajāmalam*.

One should speak even that which is impure for the purpose of causing laughter among the members of the assembly; furthermore, one should bring the disputant, the king, and the minister under one's control. The word "vādinam" (disputant) is to be construed with the preceding term. (62) Regarding the phrase "chalamantre stha": *chala* means "one who takes (*lāti*) the letter *cha*"; due to the rule of *bāhulaka*, there is an absence of the suffix *ka*. One who stands in such counsel (*mantra*) is [called *chalamantre stha*]. Likewise, the first letter of the word *chedanī*, which signifies a specific type of female messenger (*dūtī*), [is *cha*].
Because she possesses the form of Tvaritā—the mantra-deity who is the essence of the *pālikṣata*—it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "Having written *khecachekṣaḥ*... and so forth.

This Vidyā of Tvaritā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds; she is like the beautiful daughter of the *Vakula* tree, embodying the entire lion-throne. Alternatively, because the *bali-mantra* used as an ancillary to the ritual application is characterized by the letter *cha*, it is said in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "The Vidyā is *truṭi chiṃdhi* and *phaṭ*. (63)

"Chalarūpā" means she whose form (*rūpa*) is under the pretext (*vyāja*) of performing the duties of lay devotees (*upāsaka*); that is, for the sake of the duties of the lay devotees, there is the fashioning of a form by Brahmā. "Chalachirā" means she whose veins (*śirā-nāḍī*) are deceptive; likewise, according to the rules for stringing garlands, as it is said in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "A garland strung from the bones of human corpses grants all desires; the stringing of the veins should be done with a red garment, and not with a white one."

According to Amara, *ḍītu*, *dhamani*, and *sirā* are synonyms. Although Svāmin and others have explained that the word *sirā* begins with the letter *s* based on the rule *ṣij bandhane*, it is nevertheless authoritative as stated [in other lexicons], because the *Viśva-prakāśa* shows that *śirāḥ*, *śarāvaṃśaḥ*, and *śiraḥ* belong to the palatal (*tālavya*) class.

Furthermore, in the description of the letter *cha*: "The heart is the abode of the letter *cha*" (*chakāra-varṇa-nilaya*), meaning the heart is where the letters beginning with *ka* (the *kādi* group), indicated by the letter *cha*, reside; thus, the twelve-petaled heart.

The meaning is that [the Lord] resides in the region of the heart, according to the *Jñānārṇava*: "One should place the twelve [deities], beginning with Tpa and Dma. Furthermore, this is supported by the Śruti: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, the small space within it—in that is the goal;

that is what one should seek," and by the Smṛti: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings. This is also clear in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* (Brahmasūtra), in the section beginning with the word *dahara*.

The *Ekākṣarakoṣa* states that the root *chid* signifies "cutting. From the root *chid* in the sense of cutting, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *dhānyarthe ka-vihānam*. Here, "dullness" (*jāḍya*) is construed as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Thus, "Chakara" is the agent who effects the cutting of dullness. According to the *Nīlatantra*, this specific agent is the sword-wielding Kṛttikā. Alternatively, the suffix *kāra* may be taken as an abstract noun (*bhāvapratyaya*), meaning "the instrument for the cutting of dullness."

The meaning is "ḍhya. She is Ugratārā herself, who destroys the dullness of the skull-bearer [Śiva] and of the three worlds; thus it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*. (66) "Fond of deceit" (*chalapriyā*): "Deceit" (*chala*) is the appearance of even a qualityless person as if possessing qualities. She is "fond of" that because she is of the nature of *Prakṛti* (Nature). Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya tenet, liberation comes from knowing the distinctness between *Prakṛti* and *Puruṣa* (Spirit). (67) "The one who assumes disguise" (*chadminī*): *Chadma*...

Beginning with "That which deludes the world and which [deludes] even the minds of the wise" (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 68), up to the end of the verse "it bestows..."—regarding the phrase *chadmanilayā*: according to the Vedāntins, she whose ultimate dissolution (*nilaya*) or destruction occurs through *chadma*—that is, by means of a pretext or disguise, namely in the form superimposed upon Brahman, and not in her own essential nature; whereas in the Sāṃkhya system, it refers to the ultimate dissolution (*atyanta-laya*) occurring under the pretext of liberation from *prakṛti*.

Liberation, which consists in the absolute absence of the three kinds of suffering, belongs to neither [the self nor nature], because bondage and liberation are perceived as residing in the self and in primordial nature (prakṛti) respectively. As they say: "Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate; it is primordial nature, having manifold supports, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated. And so it has been explained by Vācaspatimiśra: "Even though enjoyment and liberation reside in primordial nature..."

The connection with the Puruṣa is established through the non-apprehension of discrimination (viveka). (69) "Dwelling in the abode of deceit" (chadmasadmanivāsinī): the meaning is that the "abode of deceit" (chadmasadma)—which consists of concealing one's family conduct—is the person who is its locus; it is because of his being dear to her. Thus, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

"One who is devoid of pride, devoted to Viṣṇu, and characterized by family worship and other such signs—whether walking, sleeping, wandering, or even stumbling—he is intent upon Viṣṇu, [engaged] in recitation..."

O Brahman, this mantra, which begins with *ṣṇoḥ* and consists of words for the sake of illumination, should be remembered by those of noble lineage in battle, in the forest, or by a body of water. (70) The syllable *cha* is the favorite of the Lord of the World; therefore, no wonder should be felt here. The Purāṇa says that the Lord of the World is deluded by Yoganidrā, yet he is not truly so.

(71) It is called *Jīva* because it gives life (*jīvayati*) to devotees; it is formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. It is *Ajapā* because its nature is that of the *Ajapā* mantra, consisting of the *Haṃsa* and *Ātmikā*. *Ambha*...

"Jīva worships him alone at all times," according to the words of Vīracūḍāmaṇi; or else, "Jīva" refers to Bṛhaspati, because he is the one to be propitiated, as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The Guru possesses the same respect as Śakra. The construction is: "that which was obtained through his worship. (72) "O Lord of the World, O Delight" is for the sake of clarity; or else, "the Lord of the worlds" refers to those wandering in saṃsāra, and "delighting therein" means delighting in their prayers, because he grants them—so it is said in the Phetkārīya-vidyāve.
One obtains self-control, fame, long life, and many sons; for it is there that the Sārasvata Manu resided, the abode of Śrī and Sarasvatī.

(73) Likewise, it is stated in the *Kaulāvalī*: "Where the Aparājita flower and the Java flower are found, or where the white or red Karavīra, or the Droṇa, stands—there the Goddess’s army always resides; that is proclaimed as her end. (74) Regarding the word "worn out" (*jīrṇa*): because it is beginningless, the state of being worn out belongs to Prakṛti.

In the Sāṃkhya school, since it is an unoriginated positive entity (*anādibhāvarūpa*), its being removable by knowledge constitutes the definition of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, the ignorance that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver is itself unoriginated. This view is indeed favorable even to the Vedāntins, who assert that this [ignorance] exists and maintain that ignorance is dependent upon pure consciousness (*caitanya*). For them, ignorance has as its object the pure Brahman.

(75) *Rājīmūtavalitā*: Because it was established by Indra, it will grant eternal abode on that best of mountains, Vindhya; thus it is stated by Kṛṣṇa in the *Harivaṃśa*. There is an alternative reading, *vanitā*, because it possesses the form of Indrāṇī there. (76) *Jīmūtairupaśobhitā*: Because the installation of Durgā on the mountain is well-known; likewise, in the *Devīpurāṇa* [it is said]: "Gaṅgā, Narmadā, the Vindhya mountain, Ujjayinī... [and so forth].

Alternatively, beginning with "On Arbuda, Himavat, Niṣadha, Droṇa," and so forth, it is established that, O Goddess, you grant the fulfillment of all desires and purposes. [Regarding the term] *mūta*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the sense of 'purpose,' [it is used for] Śakra, mountain, and *ghoṣaka*. (77) Regarding "bestowing boons upon the son-in-law" (*jāmātṛ-varadā*), the *Amara* lexicon states: "A son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) is the husband of one's daughter.
Thus, by means of a *homa* performed by a Brāhmaṇa acting as a substitute for the daughter, as stated in the *Śāradā*: "With parched grains (*lāja*) and the three sweets (*trimadhu*)..."

By this rite of offering oblations with *ropaṇī* [leaves], a maiden bestows [her hand]; according to this procedure, one obtains the desired bridegroom. It should be understood that, in relation to the father of the maiden, she acts as a daughter-in-law (*jāmātṛ*). Alternatively, due to the sense of "destruction" (*ai-kṣaya*), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the abstract sense (*bhāve*); thus, her mothers and kinsmen (*mātāro jñātāraḥ*)—because they do not desire her—she excessively (*atibhṛśam*) shatters (*saṃdyati*) those excellent suitors (*varān śreṣṭhān*). (78) *Jṛmbhā*.

Because she is the cause of yawning through her form as the wind named Devadatta, the *Prapañcasāra* states: "The *kṛkaloda* [Devadatta] causes hunger and performs the act of yawning" (79). Regarding the epithet "bearer of the twin *arjuna* trees": the word *jamu* begins with the third letter of the consonant class; the suffix *ja* denotes the state of being, and *mada* means eating.

She gives (*dadāti*) that which is endless (*antaṃla*), namely *jama*, because she provides for the welfare and security (*yogakṣema*) of the worlds. Alternatively, it refers to her taking the form of food offerings (*naivedya*) and the like.
The *maśana* tree bears [the fruit], and likewise the *arjuna* tree, which is the *kadamba*, supports it through its relationship as being worthy of worship;

thus there is a *karmadhāraya* compound of the two. This is because of the previously cited statement, "The *kadaiva* and the *karañja*," and also because of the statement to be cited later: "The *nimba*, the *aśvattha*, and the *kadamba*. (80) Regarding *java*: the root *ju* is used in the sense of "to go" according to the sūtra; *java* means movement or knowledge, and by connection with that, it refers to the *javākusuma*.

Or, according to the statement of Vīracūḍāmaṇi, "By means of *homa*, the deer-eyed woman shall be brought under control" (81), the term "possessing speed" (*javānvitā*) is a metaphorical designation for possessing velocity, based on the common property of being conjoined with a subsequent location due to its pervasiveness. Thus says the Śruti: "Without hands or feet, it is swift and a grasper. Another scriptural passage also states: "It is unmoving, yet swifter than the mind; it is unmoving, free from trembling."

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for the mind to be faster than even a swift horse, the venerable Bhagavatpāda explained: "The world-renowned speed of the mind is due to its knowledge of objects located at a great distance, such as the world of Brahmā; furthermore, because it first grasps the reflection of consciousness upon reaching [an object], it is said to be swifter than the mind. (82) Regarding "yawning" (*jṛmbhā*): it is so called because, like yawning, it is the cause of an excessive exertion of support; thus, in the case of a burden...

In the commentary (*ṭīkā*), it is cited that "by yawning (*jṛmbhaṇa*), indeed, the strength and splendor (*tejas*) of heroes increase; or rather, 'that by which one yawns'—this is a characteristic even in the state of reeling (*ghūrṇita*). From the *Matsya-sūkta* (83), with the realization that "she protects from reeling," [it says] "O giver of boons to Jambhāri. Jambhāri is Indra; as stated in the *Skanda-purāṇa*: "By whose worship, O Lord of Gods, Indra... [the state of lordship was attained].

The word *ptam* is to be supplied [to complete the verse]. (84) Regarding the term *jitā*: the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ji* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) to denote excellence (*utkarṣa*). As stated in the *Madhumaṅgala-vyākhyā*, "the root *ji* takes the suffix *kvip* in the sense of overcoming others (*parābhibhūti*) or excellence. Furthermore, since no specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is mentioned, this excellence is understood in relation to all things. This [excellence] belongs to her because her nature is that of Brahman. (85) Regarding the term *japitrī*: [she is the one who recites] against the wicked...

Because it is a verbal root (*bhāvaka*), the augment *iṭ* is applied due to its Vedic character; alternatively, the suffix *tṛn* is added to the root *ji* ending in *kvip*. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "To those who, having offered salutations, take refuge in Him during battles, difficult terrains, uneven lands, in combat, or in forests, He grants fearlessness. Alternatively, He bestows victory—that is, triumph—over their opponents upon His own worshippers and others.

She overcomes and utterly destroys the snares; "the giver of victory" (*jayadātrī*) is the clear meaning. Alternatively, "of Atri" is *ātrī*, due to the relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper. The suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of a cause or a characteristic, as in "giving victory. She is that very one—thus it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "she who is the giver of victory" (*jayadā*). According to the *Viśvakośa*, "victory" (*jaya*) means "to conquer" or "in victory"; she fills [or fulfills] the Victorious One (*Jayanta*).
In this context, up to the second [letter], because the emphasis is on the state (*bhāva*), it bestows lordship (*indratva*). Thus it is stated in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*:
"O twice-born ones, it bestows divinity, the status of Lord of the Immortals, the state of a Gandharva, the state of a Yakṣa or Vidyādhara, and likewise other states.

(89) Regarding the series beginning with the letter *ja*: *jhallarī* refers to a specific type of musical instrument; Svāmī [says] *jhallarī* and *tillarī* are two names for a small drum (*huḍukka*). The *Viśva* [lexicon] says: "The *mātṛ*... [text fragment].

Because that very state is [attained] through form (*rūpa*), and likewise, having described the characteristics of the *ḍhakkā* and *vālaka*, the *Gītaśāstra* states that "the seven Mother-deities were proclaimed by King Hammīra.

(90) From the *Atharvaṇa*, it is said: "In an empty house, in a cremation ground... Since the characteristic of the empty house is defined as being composed of *kriyā* and so forth, its ultimate intent is reached through the imitation of sounds, for that is what is dear to them. (91)

*Jhillī* refers to the sound of the *bhṛṅgārī* (the female bee) or the *cīruka* (a type of cricket); it is also said by others to be similar to the sound of a cricket (*jhillikā*). According to Svāmī, it is a specific kind of musical instrument (*jhillīvādya*), because its sound resembles that of the *kuṇḍalinī* in form, as stated in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "The *jhillī* is an indistinctly sweet sound that remains constantly resonating. There is an alternative reading, *jhallī*, in which case it refers to a specific [sound] within the *jhal* pratyāhāra.

The meaning is that it merges therein because it is of the nature of the *mātṛkā*s, as established in grammar (*ṣoḍvyākaraṇa*). This should be explained as follows: from the verbal root *rā* ending in the suffix *āya*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *itaśca*.

(92) Regarding *jharī*: *pravāhaḥ nirjharaḥ jharaḥ*—thus says Amara; its feminine gender is like that of *mṛṇālī* and other such words, because it is the locus of the means (*sādhana*) and is dear to Him. (93) Regarding *jharjharikā-tare*: *jharjharaḥ syāt kaliyuge vādyabhāṇḍe*. (Amara).

The *Viśva* lexicon states that *ḍana* means "giving. The suffix *ṭhan* is applied in the sense of "possessing this" (*matvarthe*). From the root *ata* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *ghañ* is added; since roots meaning "to go" also mean "to know," it signifies "desire for knowledge. Thus, it is one who bestows (*rāti*) the object that has become the focus of such desire. This forms a *karmadhāraya* compound of both [words]. Accordingly, having begun with the words, "Now we shall speak of those mantras which grant success (*siddhi*) in the Kali age," [the text proceeds] with *bhūtaḍā*.

"O Mother, Trijaṭā, Ekajaṭā, Kālī, Nīlā, Pūrvasarasvatī," and so forth—(94)—this is the section on words beginning with the vowel *ū*. Regarding the word *dhanuḥ* (bow), it is well known that its feminine form is *ṭāṅkāra*; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *ṭaṅkāra* refers to a bowstring and a bow. According to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "The entire Pātāla was agitated by the sound of the vibrating bowstring. In reality, however, the *ṭāṅkāra* [sound] is situated above...

Because it is situated above the *kartrī* which rests upon the seed-syllable of Krodha, it is likewise heard in the Atharvaṇa: "One should meditate upon a white lotus above that [Krodhabīja] from the sound *ṭāṃ*," and having begun thus, it continues, "Above that is the Mahāvidyā," and [further] "the producer of the sound *ṭīṭ*.
Here, the word *ṭīṭkāra* is intended as an onomatopoeia; or else, *ṭī* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) used by grammarians. And so says the Sūtra: "a..."

The meaning is that the technical designation *ṭi* applies to a word starting from the final vowel (*antyādacaḥ*) and including itself. Furthermore, *it* is a specific technical designation used in common linguistic practice, as established by the rule "upadeśe 'j-anunāsikaḥ" and others. *Kāra* is a specific type of suffix, because it is stated in the rule "varṇāt kāraḥ" that the term *kāra* is used when referring to a phoneme (*varṇa*). He causes those [phonemes] to be known—that is, he makes them known—because [this work] serves as a cause for the knowledge of grammar. (96)

"Holder of the Ṭaṅka" (Ṭaṅkādhāriṇī) is to be understood as a form of Vāṇī; likewise, it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "She holds the ṭaṅka, the rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting gesture, and has three eyes adorned with the moon; she is the pure digit of Vāṇī, and Īśvara is likewise. This is the sequence of words beginning with the letter Ṭa. Regarding "Ṭhakurākṣī," the word "ṭhaku" here refers to that which expresses or denotes the letters Ṭa and Ka.

The word *mṛdaṅga* is formed with the suffix *ka*, as it belongs to the *udarādi* (and others) group; for in that [group], the insertion of the letters *ṭha* and *ka* is prescribed. In the science of music (*saṃgīta-śāstra*), it is stated: "The *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, and the *ta*-group—excluding the letter *ja*—along with the letters *ra* and *ha*, joined with the vowel *u*, constitute the sixteen [syllables] of the *mṛdaṅgas*.
Therefore, the sages have declared the deity of the *mardala* drum to be Nandin, as it is said: 'The deity of the drums is Nandikeśvara. Its queen is Gaṇā."

Because he is the Lord of that, or else because it is a specific secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*) ending in *ṭhak*; by the rule "the suffix *ka* is applied after words ending in *taṅkāya* as before," it means "a heap of husks" (*tuṣāṇāṃ rāśiḥ*). (98) Regarding the section on the letter *ṭha*: *ḍamaruka*—one who sounds a *ḍamaru*, a particular type of drum; for its varieties, Amara states: "*ḍamaru*, *maru*, *ḍiṇḍima*, and *jharjhara*. According to the *Rudrabhairavī-kalpa*, the *jñāna* [mantra] is "triśūlaṃ ḍamarukha jham."

In the *Girijā-nāmārtha-cintāmaṇi*, composed by Viśveśvara—the son of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who grasped the ocean of words that are the authority of speech—this is the eighth moonlight-ray, which shatters the dullness regarding the eighth [chapter] on action. Now, as for the eighth hundred [of verses]: "Is Tāriṇī not also present within me, since even Umā [is so]?"—such is my conviction, as I hold a sharp-edged sickle. Now, the eighth hundred.

The word *ḍākvārī* is an explanation of the term *ḍātṛ*; she makes this sound because her nature is that of Śiva. Thus, in the fifth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*, it is said: "With banks formidable with the *ḍhātkṛta* roars of fierce jackals howling, accompanied by the *dhūtkāra* sounds of owls in the bowers of the forest... Jagaddhara notes that *dhūtkāra* and *ḍātkṛta* are imitative sounds (*anukaraṇa-śabda*). Furthermore, the phrase "fond of the *ḍamaru*" has a clear meaning; or else—

Because she has the form of a Yoginī, it is stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*: "One should worship the other Yoginīs who hold in their hands a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), a noose (*pāśa*), and a linga; they wear entrails as ornaments and are clad in red garments. Regarding the term *raḍhakkārava*: *raḍhakkā* refers to the sound of a musical instrument; *ḍhakitikā* is a specific mode of playing; and *ḍhakka* is the master [of the sound]. The sounds (*aravaḥ*) are the noises, and the state (*bhāvaḥ*) is that of the *ḍhakka*. The connection is with the opponent (*pratiyoginī*) of the *ḍhakka*. From that, by virtue of belonging to the *arśa-ādi* group, the suffix *ac* is applied. By implication, this refers to Brahmā. Vi. [End of section]

Because it is forbidden to play the *ḍhakkā* drum in the house of Śiva—since that drum is the cause of his destruction—and because the Śruti says, "He who ordained Brahmā first," the term *ḍhakkārī* means one who plays the *ḍhakkā* instrument; or alternatively, it means one who performs (*iyarti*) a specific rhythmic measure (*ḍhakka*) or a specific musical mode (*rāga*). Regarding *Tulasī*: by means of *Tulasī* blossoms, all desires and purposes are accomplished.

Because the *Trikālikā-purāṇa* prescribes the worship of Śiva with optional (*kāmya*) offerings, and because the *Śivadharmasamuccaya* prescribes the use of the *ketakī* flower—even though it is otherwise forbidden for the worship of Śiva—as a means for slaying enemies; and because the term "tālabhakṣikā" is well known to refer to the honey produced from palm fruits, as stated by Vācaspatimiśra: "The eleventh [offering] is that which arises from the palm fruit"; thus Pulastya says:

[The juices of] the jackfruit (*panasa*), the *saṃdrākṣa*, the *mādhūka*, the date palm (*khārjūra*), the palmyra palm (*tāla*), and sugarcane (*aikṣaya*) are called "molasses" (*guḍa*) because they preside over the divine scales; or else, because Viśvāmitra stated, "May Pārvatī be pleased with the molasses," and because the *Bhaviṣyottara* states that for saffron (*kuṅkuma*) the deity is Pārvatī, it is her presiding deity.

Regarding the commencement of the weighing of ghee and other substances, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* in Hemādri’s work states: "All [these gifts] bestow prosperity and bring about the destruction of sins."

He who gives a Tulā-gift to Gaurī shall attain the abode of Gaurī. If one should give even a single Tulā, consecrated with mantra, to the twice-born, he shall go to the most meritorious dwelling of Gaurī; neither sorrow nor misfortune shall ever reach him. (7) Regarding the word *tūli*: it is that which takes (*lāti*) a bed (*śayyā*) filled within with cotton (*tūla*); thus it is called *tūli*. A *tūlikā* is said to be a painting, or that which is curled like cotton (*tūla*). As for *yathorī*, it refers to the comparison.

This is the explanation of the meaning for that which ends in the suffix *ka* used in its own sense (*svārtha*), because this suffix *i* arises from the suffix *ṇa*. Thus, the suffix *ka* is added to that which ends in *ṇa* in its own sense.

Accordingly, in the section on the female messenger (*dūtī*) in the *Uttaratantra*, it says: "Having placed [her] in the middle of the *tūlikā* with fragrant flowers of various kinds, and having covered her with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and so forth, one should then worship the Mistress of the Kula. [The word] *tīrṇā*... [is used].

(9) Because she is included within the five, because she has the form of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), or because she resides in the pupil—according to the Śruti: "The person who is within the eye"—and because the Śruti states regarding the eyes: "These two are Vaiśvānara, full of splendor," it is clear in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* that the word *Vaiśvānara* refers there to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (10) *Tāriṇikā*: the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). "Nava-akṣara-manu" [refers to] the mantra of the Goddess Tāriṇī.

(11) It is declared that this Great Vidyā is extremely difficult to obtain even in heaven or on earth; it is said to be of a specific form, for she is known as the "Tantra-knower" (*tantravijñā*) because she knows the *mantra-śāstras*. This is because the Goddess spoke thus to Bhairava in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Sometimes [she appears] as a disciple. (12) She is called the "Essence of Tantra" (*tantrarati*) because she is expounded in the Āgamas.

(13) She is called "Tantra-knowledge" (*tantravidyā*). Regarding the word *tantra*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the context of a primary treatise (*śāstra*), it means 'established' (*siddha*). Because she is to be guarded [as a secret], she is [the Vidyā].
The meaning is that she has become firmly established. As it is said in the *Kulārṇava*: "The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas may be heard clearly like courtesans;

but the Vidyā of Śambhu is hidden like a noble lady of the Kula. (14) Because of this [statement], due to the protection from disclosure and so forth, and because the agent who prompts [the action] is also remembered as the cause of the action, the deities favor one who keeps the Kaulika conduct well-guarded; they grant success to those worthy of worship and destroy [the success] of others.

From the *Prakāśaka-nitikulārṇava* (15): [The word] *tāmitā* is derived from the root *tam*, meaning "to be weary" (*tamyati*), with the suffix *iti* added; the suffix *ta* is used in the sense of exhaustion (*glāni*). There is lengthening by the rule *anunāsikasya kvi-jhaloḥ*. By the rule *mono dhātoḥ*, there is the substitution of *na*. She whose waist (*trika*) is such is one with a slender middle—this is the meaning. According to Amara, "the *trika* is that which supports the backbone. Likewise, it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "Adorned, she has a slender body, and in her middle is the *trika*..."

(16) Regarding "valībhṛtā": by the rule *svatantraḥ kartā* ("one who is independent is the agent"), and because of the observation in the Mahābhāṣya that "this Brāhmaṇī is the principal [element] of the tantra," as well as due to the aforementioned fault, the meaning is that she is the primary *vidyā*. (17) Regarding "tantrasārā": based on the etymology "she whose essence (*sāra*) is the essence within the tantras," her state of being the essence is like [the expression] "Was Tārā not worshipped by the essence of the three worlds? and so forth; thus, she is the essence (*prītva*). (18) Regarding "tantraye": [This refers to] the triad of tantras.

Thus, regarding the word *tantra*: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, it means "a weaver" (*taṃtuvāya*) or "a specific disease. She is called *Tantrapālinī* because she destroys that specific disease; or alternatively, she is called *Tantrapālinī* because she "drinks" (*pibati*) the *tantra*—that is, the scripture—by virtue of its implicit causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇij-artha*), since she causes her devotees to understand it. (19) She is called *Tantradhātrī* because she maintains the *tantra*, which is the protective enclosure (*parichada*). (20) She is called *Tantrakārī* because she accomplishes the *tantra*, which is the intended desire of her devotees. In this context, the use of the short vowel [in *tantra*] is not a matter of primary importance (*ataṃtram*).

Because the word *tantra* is seen here to have its intended meaning [as "new cloth"], or else because Amara states, "An *anāhata* is a *niḥpravaṇa-tantraka*"—where the suffix *kap* is applied in the sense of "recently removed from the loom" (*tantrāt acirāpahṛte*)—the meaning is that she "attains" (*iyarti*) a *tantraka*, which is a fresh garment (*kañcuka*). (21) Regarding the phrase *tantraṇāvaratā*:

*tantraṇā* is "description" (*varṇanā*). By the rule "from the agent or instrument, in the sense of the root's action," the suffix *ṇic* is applied; then, by adding *yuc* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), we get *tantraṇā*. She whose excellence (*varatā*) consists of that [description] belongs to them.

Because it makes known its own greatness and because it is Vedic, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed even though there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*); it should be explained as "that which has 'Tārā' as its form" (22). Regarding the word *turu*: since it refers to another mantra indicated by the words *turu-turu*, the *praṇava* (OM) is extracted first; for it is stated in the *Gandharva-tantra* that this ten-syllabled mantra begins with "Tāre Tāre Turu. Furthermore, according to the *Kalpadruma*: "In the sense of granting what is desired, *tvara* [is used]; *turu* means speed or impetuosity. Thus, it is established.

The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *an*, which is listed in the *di-kṛt* group, according to the rule beginning with *pacādyac*. Thus, it is stated in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "May all mantras that have been perfected follow [the practitioner]; even one not perfected may grant its fruit as soon as it is grasped. Regarding the phrase "by the power of austerity" (*tapas-prabhāva*), because she is endowed with both [tapa and prabhāva], the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for *dvandva* compounds starting with *darśa*. Alternatively, it refers to her whose eminent states (*bhāva*) consist of austerity, which take the form of the *kaulika* conduct (*ācāra*). In the word *pra-*, [the prefix *pra* denotes excellence].

The exclusion of the auspicious [state] occurs because that side is inferior; as it is said in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Bhairava, listen: the state of Heroism (*vīrabhāva*) alone is being described by me.

Having become one whose mind is free from dualities (*nirdvaṃdva*), with the body of the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) in the heart, the excellent worship at night is always joined with [this] 'Hī' and so forth. Regarding the term "knower of the *tantra*," the word *tantra* refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and its meanings, according to the *Viśva* lexicon. In the creation of the world...

Because she is well-versed in the ritual procedures (*ritikarttavyatā*), she is called "the one who bestows the essence and fruit of the Tantras" (*tantrasāraphalapradā*). The "essence of the Tantras" (*tantrasāra*) is the Kula practice (*kulācāra*); she "bestows its fruit" (*phala*) preeminently. This is because of the statement in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Without the Kula practice, there is no attainment of success whatsoever. [The suffix] *-ī* is added to *ājñā* by the rule for the *ṛtikṛtya* suffix. Regarding *tapasyā*, since the root *tap* takes the suffix *kyan* when it has "asceticism" as its object, the suffix *ap* is added to that form, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

The meaning is "she who has this" (*sāsty asyāḥ*). The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) signifies the state of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), because austerity (*tapas*) is prescribed for the sake of attaining that [knowledge], according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahmins desire to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting.

Alternatively, *tapasya* refers to the month of Phālguna, because she possesses it; and according to the scripture: "Tapa and Tapasya are the two dewy seasons (*śaiśira-ṛtu*). Likewise, it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:

He who avoids salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna, and at the end of the month gives a bed equipped with all its furnishings, having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgya-vrata.

(27) Regarding the term *taulinī*: because they drag (*tija*) living beings due to their terrifying nature, they are called *tūlā*; these are the spirits, *piśācas*, and so forth, as well as the cotton-like (*tūlaka*) [entities].
O Sage, the suffix *ac* is applied here [to form *tūla*]. Alternatively, those such as the gods are called *tūla* because they satisfy (*tūlayanti*) or fulfill perceived objects;

the suffix is added as before to the root *tūl*, meaning "filling. A collection of these is *taula*, and this [city] possesses that, hence it is *taulī*. (28) Regarding the word *tīrṇā*: because she is situated in the middle of the ocean, she has been "crossed" (*tīrṇā*) by those two who have boarded the boat. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an action begun, such as the act of crossing or the ritual of consecrating the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), as she resides within the red ocean.

"Seated upon a red lotus that has not yet fully blossomed"—according to the *Prapañcasāra*, or else "one should meditate on her as mounted upon a boat situated in the midst of the ocean of milk"—this is because another tantra is seen to present this as a meditation on a specific form. (29) Regarding the term *tārttīyī* ("the third"), it is formed by adding the suffix *ṇic* in its own sense (*svārtha*), followed by the feminine suffix *ṣyaṅ* and *ṭāp*.
Because there is a threefold division into Tārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī, and because there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence, [the mantra] may be used for all of them.

Because he is the third; or else, because he is the third among the three sages (Munitraya) as established in the grammar of the three sages (*trimunivyākaraṇa*), Kātyāyana being the third due to his authorship of the *Vārttika* on grammar—therefore, the suffix *ṇa* is added in the sense of identity (*svārthe*). This [suffix] signifies that it exists in him. Thus, in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, in the account of the Goddess’s manifestation, it is said: "And that splendor of the most excellent gods, resembling the peak of a mountain, became one with Kātyāyana, who was without rival."
By that great seer, it was meditated upon and subsequently brought forth; and by the splendor created by that seer, she was enveloped, blazing like a thousand suns in radiant light.
From that [splendor] was born Kātyāyanī, who possessed large eyes and a body purified by yoga. It is also stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"The Goddess indeed assumed a form bearing that very splendor; kindled and worshipped by Kātyāyana, she is remembered as Kātyāyanī."

Therefore, [the term] "tulasī" is used in opposition [to its usual sense], by means of a lakṣaṇā indicating a possessive meaning, because of the prohibition of its worship; for the *Matsyasūkta* states: "With bilva leaves, maruvaka, and so forth, excluding tulasī petals. Alternatively, because tulasī is both prescribed and prohibited in the worship of Durgā, the *tilaka*, *mālatī*, *vāṇa*, *tulasī*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* may be both prohibited and prescribed for Śiva and Durgā, depending on the context.
(31) From the *Diti-bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Tuṣā" means she who is pleased (*tuṣyati*) and delighted (*prīyate*) by her worshippers;

thus [she is called] so, for the root *tuṣ* takes the suffix *ka* due to its inclusion in the *rigu* group. (32) "Tuṣārakara-pūrṇāsyā": she whose face is full of rays (*karas*) resembling frost—rays that are exceedingly pure and possess the beauty of laughter.
(33) "Lustārakaramaṇḍitā": although Akṣobhya is [the lord of] all beings... [text fragment].

According to the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, "She possesses the three forms through supernatural power and assumes the form of a serpent," and regarding the phrase "adorned with Akṣobhya on her crown," the Kalpalatā states that the explanation of the word "Akṣobhya" as referring to the imperishable crescent moon (*candrakalā*) is due to negligence; nevertheless, in the meditation for other mantras, another tantra states: "She has a moon-marked head and is three-eyed."

From this statement, it should be understood that by this [verse], the utterance of my venerable father—"May even a tiny fraction of the splendor belonging to the mass of matted hair [of Śiva] purify me"—is also explained. (34) Regarding the phrase "whose face is equal to the cool-rayed moon" (*tuhināṃśusamānāsyā*): the word *tuhināṃśu* refers to its digits (*kalā*), because there are sixteen of them;
thus, it means "she whose years are equal in number to those sixteen. This is according to the rule: "The words *hāyana*, *abda*, *śarat*, and *samā* [denote years]."

*Maraḥ* refers to one whose *āsyaṃ*—that is, *mukhaṃ* or face—is non-existent (*avidyamāna*). Likewise, in the meditation on Chinnamastā, it is said: "Always sixteen years of age, with full and dark breasts," which indicates a young woman of sixteen; this is also supported by the *Dūtī-prastāva* in the *Uttara-tantra*. (35) Regarding *tuhināṃśu-samaprabhā*: according to the *Viśva*, *aṃśu* means a small portion, a ray, or light. Thus, *tuhināṃśu* refers to the cool-rayed moon. Her radiance is equal to that of the cool-rayed moon.
She whose radiance is equal to lightning because she produces benefit and harm for those who exist and those who do not;
she whose limbs are like frost and crystal, and whose body—white in color—is like the moon, being the form of the deities of the heart and the head. Thus it is said in the *Śāradā*:

"The wise man should meditate upon the women who are the embodiments of light, possessing rays that are white as frost, crystalline, dark, blue, black, and ruddy, and who hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness."

By the same sequence [of the *te-cakra*], the deities of the limbs [are worshipped]. (37) "Tuṣārakarasundarī" means: she whose beauty (*sundarī*) consists of the cowherd girls (*gopikanyā*), who—like the moon (*tuṣāra-kara*)—bestow happiness (*sukha*) by beginning the worship during the winter season (*hemanta-ṛtu*). [The absence of the compound-ending suffix] is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). Alternatively, having formed a *karmadhāraya* with the preceding adjective [“moon-like”], it refers to the splendor (*lakṣmī*) of those [girls], because they grant the desired goal, which is the attainment of the Blessed Lord.

The elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *ka* following the word *tisundarī* is to be explained; and thus it is said in the tenth book of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, regarding the first month of the winter season: "O daughter of Nanda, the cowherd girls performed the vow of worshipping Kātyāyanī while eating *haṃviṣya* food, [saying]: 'O Kātyāyanī, O Great Illusion (*Mahāmāyā*), O Sovereign of the Great Yoginīs, O Goddess, make the son of Nanda the Gopa my husband! Salutations to you! and so forth. (38) [In the phrase] *tuṣāradhāmatu*...

The meaning is as follows: the word *lyāsa* has its place (*āsya*)—that is, its point of articulation (*sthāna*)—the same as the words *tukhāra* and *dhāma*. This is because the initial letter of the word *dhāma* and the final letter of the word *tuṣāra* share the same place of articulation; specifically, the *tavarga* (the dental class) has the teeth as its place of articulation. Furthermore, based on the etymology *āsyabhavam āsyam* ("that which arises in the mouth"), the word *āsya* denotes the places of articulation such as the palate and so forth.

This is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ...* (Pāṇini 1.1.9). Regarding the verse *tuṣāroṃ'śusamānena*: by means of its "frost-like" coldness (*tuṣāratvena śaityena*), it surpasses the sun (*aṃśuḥ*)—that is, the fire (*agni*) which possesses heat (*tajastvavantam*)—by abandoning its well-known property [of heat].
The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *tuṣārāṃśusātākarmaṇi*. Such is her devotion (*mānanābhaktiḥ*) toward the Fire; and they shall speak of her thus regarding Agni.

"By the recitation of this hymn, one surely produces coolness. (40) Regarding the term *tuhinādrisutā*: *tuhina* means "cold," signifying one who is devoid of the power to inflict suffering; *adrīsuta* means "the son of the mountain," referring to Yama, the son of the Sun (*sūryaputra*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a causal ablative sense, meaning "she whose [son] is the son of the mountain. Because he is the cause for the destruction of sins, the "son of the Sun" (*sūryaputra*) should be understood as Śanaiścara (Saturn), since he wards off the afflictions caused by the planets. Half of the verse... [end of fragment].

"Maśailārkā"—thus [it is stated] in the Amarakośa (41). She is called *nārkṣī* because she wards off the fear of serpents; for likewise, in the Brahma-saṃhitā: "If fear arises upon seeing a beast of prey (*vyāla*), one should mutter the mantra at the sight of the serpent: 'Vyālam vyālam,' and thereafter say 'Garuḍāya svāhā svāhā'; thus the fear of beasts of prey does not arise. This is the eighth variety (42). *Tālāṅgī*: she whose limbs or breast-forms are like the fruit of the palmyra palm (*tāla*); or else, *tāla* means a sword.

A *muṣṭi* is that which has a hand as its form joined with it; [as for] *tāla*, the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the context of the grips of swords and so forth, *tāla* refers to a type of tree and a kind of hand-gesture. (43) Regarding the phrase "devoid of *tāla*," it is likewise stated in the *Haṃsamāheśvara-tantra*: "By giving liquor to a Brāhmaṇa, one falls even from the status of a Brāhmaṇa. Also in the *Śrīkrama*: "A Brāhmaṇa should never give liquor to the Great Goddess; even a Brāhmaṇa who desires the Left-hand path (*vāmaka*) should not consume meat or liquor."

"Accompanied by the sound 'Tāra'" means: *Tārā* is so called because of her relationship as the mistress (*bhartṛtva*) [of Tāra]; *Tāra* is Bṛhaspati, and the word *sphara* denotes him. "Accompanied by that" (*tena sahitā*) means accompanied by what is beneficial (*hita-sahitā*). "Beneficial" (*hita*) refers to the devotion of her followers, and "accompaniment" (*sāhitya*) should be understood in the sense of being the cause [of that devotion]. Thus, the meaning is: she is the generator of the welfare of her devotees, characterized by the state of being denoted by the word *Bṛhatī*, which is rooted in the quality of possessing knowledge (*vidyāvatva*). In the scriptures of Vāgīśī and in poetry, [she is known as] Kāvyā.

Because it is stated in the *Maḥsmṛti-tibhairavī-tantra* concerning one who knows the mantra: (45) "Adorned with the sound of the *Tāra*"—for *Tāra* is indeed pure (*śuddha*), being unconfused (*asaṃkīrṇa*); [the syllable] *Haḥ* is the source of that, [and] *Vimarṣa* is its progenitor in the form of the *Bali*. Adorned by that, she is pleased. According to the *Kālikā-purāṇa*, she obtains satisfaction for twenty-five years through the blood of goats and sheep. By the word "pure" (*śuddha*), even ritual slaughter (*vaidhahiṃsā*) [is intended] for the person...

The refutation of the Sāṃkhya position that [non-injury] entails fault is as follows: the scriptural injunction "one should not harm any living beings" intends to prohibit only ritual injury (*vaidhāhiṃsā*). Now, regarding the sequence of letters beginning with *tha*: it is a compound of *tha*, *ka*, and *śra*—namely, *tha-ka-śra*. If one objects that, by the rule *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33), the vowel *a* should have been placed first [as in *atha-kaca-śra*], then the resolution is that this is due to Vedic usage (*chāṃdasatvāt*); or alternatively, [it may be explained] by means of the two *tha*s.

The compound *sahita-akāriti* should be explained as a *madhyama-pada-lopa* (elision of the middle term). In reality, its non-eternality is established by such usages as *sasauṣṭavaudāryaviśeṣaśālinīm*; thus, it should be understood that there is no fault in the *dvandva* [compound]. Regarding the form *thakaṃ*: due to the neuter gender resulting from the rule of singularization (*eka-vadbhāva*), and because of the short vowel, the form is *thakaṃ*. It is called *thakāraḥ* because it moves (*arti*) through the *thakam*. Alternatively, it may be expressed according to the order of the *akathaka* [roots], or in reverse order for the sake of the variety of stylistic modes (*prakāra*).

The statement is as follows: she whose abode is such a collection of stones (kūṭopalas) in the form of the Śrīcakra; for it is well known that within the triangle of the Śrīcakra, the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*, those beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*, and finally the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* reside in the center in their respective order. Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava: "The circle of letters (*varṇamaṇḍala*), beginning with *a*, *ka*, *tha*, and *da*, which bestows the perfection of the unbroken realm (*akhaṇḍalasi-ddhi*), shines forth within."

How do the bound souls (*paśu*) perceive the syllable *hakṣa* in Śiva? Likewise, regarding [the name] *Rākṣaramālinī*: the head of the letter *tha* is the first syllable—that is to say, *ta*. Through its connection with the vowel *ā*, *tā* is established. Following that is *rā*; she who possesses a garland (*mālā*) of these [syllables] is [called] *Rākṣaramālinī*.

By virtue of the relationship of denotation (*vācakatva*), the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule for the *brīhi*-class. This means she is denoted by the word *Tārā-rā*. Alternatively, it refers to the syllable *tha*.

The compound is *miti-samāsa* (a contraction), and its relationship is that of preceding [the subsequent term]; thus, the word *matha* is obtained, because the *prayoga-bali-yantra* consists of two words beginning with *matha*. Alternatively, it is because of the statement in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "At the crossroads, when there is fear, one should recite the eighteen-syllable mantra; having first extracted the *praṇava*, likewise the pair beginning with *matha*" (48). Regarding the series of *tha*-letters: *dayāvatī* is explained as preceded by compassion (*dayā-pūrva*) in the context of the *nitya-yoga* and so forth.

The distinction is that the suffix *matup* [in the previous verse] expressed identity (*tādātmya*), whereas here it expresses the state of possessing that quality (*tadvattva*). (49) Regarding "delighting in giving" (*dānaratā*): because they are devoted to giving, their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are purified, and since that [giving] is the cause [of purification], the principle of *māyā* has arisen within those who are constantly engaged [in practice]. Therefore, as stated by the Blessed One in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "I shall destroy that entire [māyā] without delay for them by means of the lamp of knowledge. [Regarding the word *dāna*: Viśva [states]: "The word *dāna* is used in the senses of the rut-fluid of an elephant, abandonment, protection, cutting, and purification. (50)

"She who destroys suffering and poverty" means she destroys the poverty that causes suffering; thus, according to the *Atharvaṇa Śruti*, "she becomes like Vaiśravaṇa. (51) "She who crushes misfortune and suffering": misfortune (*daurbhāgya*) is the state of having evil unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), such as being under the influence of planets that indicate it; she "crushes" or afflicts one who possesses the suffering born thereof, because she performs rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*) and so forth against such a person. This is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "Others... [text fragment].

The conjunctions of *piṭhādi* are indicators of what is undesirable. Because the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is the authority on this matter, one should not undertake rites such as killing (*māraṇa*) [during those times].

If the presiding planet (*sādhyagraha*) is malefic, as are the month and the year, then it is certain that one should not perform auspicious rites for that person. In the reading *dalinī*, there is an absence of the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). [The term] *daurbhāgyāpadanāśinī* means the destroyer of misfortune (*daurbhāgya*) and calamity (*āpada*). Misfortune... [text ends]

By the rule *dvandvāt cudaṣahāntāt samāhāre*, the suffix *ac* is added to form a compound denoting a collective; thus, *mahāpadma* means "great lotus. According to the *Kālīkulārṇava*, [it is said]: "In the case of great sins and the warding off of great planetary influences, it destroys them merely by being remembered at the beginning or the end. (53) She is called *duhitā* because she has the form of a maiden (*kumārī*); for it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "O Lord, I am indeed a maiden (*kumārikā*), and you likewise are a youth (*kumāraka*)," and so forth. Or else, *du*...

The word *haprapūraṇebhāvedhajrthekaḥ* means that she has become the daughter (*duhitā*) of *duh* [the root meaning "to milk" or "yield"] because of her fullness; as before, the word *duhitṛ* ends in the letter *ṛ*, but here it specifically ends in the vowel *ā*. (54) She is the "kinswoman of the distressed" (*dīnabaṃdhur*) because she dispels the demons (*daityas*). Alternatively, she is the kinswoman of the distressed because those who do not know Brahman are distressed, according to the Śruti: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is truly pitiable."

She is their kinswoman because she is the cause of self-realization. Regarding the term *dānaveṃdravimardinī*: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, the word *dāna* is derived from the root *dā*, meaning "to give" or "to stride. Thus, *dānava* refers either to those who give (*dātṝṇām*) or to those who are valiant (*vikrāntānām*). The suffix *ṇa* is used here as a possessive (*śaiṣika*) to denote "belonging to them. She is the one who specifically crushes (*vimardayati*) such an *indra*—the most excellent one—making him a locus of inferiority defined by her own established excellence; for she is thus the most preeminent of all. (55–56)

"Dānadātrī" means the giver of the ichor of the elephant; she is the cause of its breaking because she is the cause for tethering the intoxicated elephant. As it is stated in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "Then, having made this elephant firm with the five-syllabled mantra ending in the Bindu [namely] 'Gaṇeśvarāya', and with 'Oṃ Oṃ Svāhā'—this two-fold mantra for subduing the elephant is dear to princes. (57) "Dānavarā" means [the best among givers], because she was the primary object of the gift in former times.
Based on the statement in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Apart from action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action" (58), [the deity] is "pleased by giving and honor.

Because his nature is pure and enlightened (*śuddha-buddha-svabhāva*), he is pleased by these two: by "giving" (*dāna*)—which is equivalent to purity—and by "perfect knowledge" (*samyak-jñāna*). (59) He is "served by those beginning with dentals. By the force of the meaning, the dental is the letter *sa*; since it serves at the beginning of its own preceding part, it is the letter *ta*, which is one who serves those beginning with dentals.

Because this name of the Vadhū-bīja consists of the letter *ta* following the letter *sa*, or alternatively, because she is the one who serves the beginning of the word "Daṃtī"—that is, she whose [name] begins with *daṃtī*—therefore she is Raktadaṃtikā; for in the word *raktadaṃdikā*, the word *daṃtī* follows the letter *ta*. This has been stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, beginning with "Again, in an exceedingly fierce form... and continuing: "...those who praise her shall constantly utter the name Raktadaṃtikā."

The letter *ta* is the twelfth [consonant]; by that, she is "served at the beginning" because the word *tārā* begins with the letter *ta*. (60) *Dāntā*: those whose sensory activities have ceased are *dāntas*; she possesses them through her connection to being presided over by her own knowledge (*svajñānādhikṛtatva*). Thus it is according to the Vedic scripture: "One who is calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and full of faith, having become composed in mind, should see the Self within the self alone. Alternatively, she possesses a garland (*mālya*) made of teeth (*danta*), hence *dānta*. As it has been said:

In the *Kumārikā-tantra*, it is said: "With a rosary of teeth and bones, with the tooth of the King of Mountains [Meru] as the central bead (*meru*), one should recite ten thousand (*ayuta*) times the mantra of all the deities.

(61) The term *dāmodara-parāyaṇā* refers to her whose refuge is devoted to Viṣṇu (*Viṣṇu-parāyaṇa*). Alternatively, because she is seated upon five corpses in the form of a beautiful woman (*sundarī-rūpa*), the word *udara* is the final member of a compound in her name; thus, she is *udara-parāyaṇā*, meaning "one for whom the belly is the ultimate resort," which is a synonym for a serpent (*sarpa*). This is one interpretation.

Because the term *kodarapada* follows *udarapada*, and because the *Upaniṣad* shows that the word *suki* refers to the excellent girdle (*sumekhalā*) of the co-wife who has become the waist-belt (*kaṭisūtra*) of the slender-waisted woman (*drāmakaṭi*), [the phrase] "the boon of Dadhīci" means that Dadhīci is a particular sage and Rudra is his granter of boons; thus, having propitiated the Lord of Gods, the best of sages, Dadhīci, attained immortality and the state of being as firm as a diamond (*vajra*).

"From effort" (*prayatnataḥ*) is a mark [of authority] because it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*. Alternatively, *dadhy-añcati* means "he who moves toward the curd," that is, *Dadhyañ*; in that case, the phrase "in that person Dadhīci" (*dadhīcipuruṣe*) consists of separate words, meaning "O Giver of Boons" (*varada*). This is the form of the seventh case singular of the root *añc* with the suffix *kin*. As stated by Aṣṭaka in the *Tantratattvokti*:

"One should fill the arghya vessels with milk, or with curd, or with buttermilk, or even with water; each preceding one is more excellent than the next. (63) [The text continues: "Defective... (*duṣṭa*)...

The term *dānaveṃdravināśinī* ("the destroyer of the lord of the Dānavas") is derived from the root *dāp*, meaning "to purify" (*śodhane*), with the suffix *ki* added in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The word *duṣṭa* means "defect" (*doṣa*); it is derived from the root *duṣ*, meaning "to be corrupted" (*vaikṛtye*), with the suffix *kta* added in the sense of the abstract state. The word *ava* comes from the root *av*, meaning "to go" (*gacchati*). Thus, through a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), it refers to that which does not go toward purification—that is, the defect consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*). Consequently, the "corrupted Dānava" is the inner self (*antarātman*) enveloped by ignorance, which does not attain the state of being free from the phenomenal world (*niḥprapañcatva*).
The *Kalpadruma* states that *avratasneha* refers to a beloved woman; the *Viśva* lexicon states that *indra* refers to the husband of Śacī, a Vedic deity, the self, or the sun.

He [the Lord] specifically destroys that [ignorance] in the form of non-return [to saṃsāra], making one attain identity with Brahman, according to the Śruti: "He attains his own true nature. The word "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) serves to exclude the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), for in that state [ignorance] remains associated with nescience (*avidyā*).

"Long-eyed" (*dīrghanetrī*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the ablative case used as a cause (*hetau pañcamī*), meaning "she whose eye is long"—that is, an organ of perception whose range extends to objects that are past, future, remote, and so forth; in other words, she is the cause of omniscience. To the question, "How did those [sages] obtain the omniscient Lord?"—the answer is given by presenting this Vidyā, establishing her as the cause thereof.
"By the heart alone the yogi knows all," according to the Śruti (65). She is *Dīrghakacā* because her hair is long;

or else, because she possesses great luster (*dīptimatī*), since the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the suffix *dhañ* after the root *kac* (to shine); or else, because Kaca—the son of Bṛhaspati—is her progenitor through a non-physical connection, as the Viśva lexicon states: "Kaca is Bṛhaspati’s son; *kaca* [also] means hair and the preceptor’s son. Bṛhaspati... [text fragment ends].

The inclusion of the word *ti* [in the compound] indicates that she is the daughter of Bṛhaspati, who is long and eminent; thus, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) expressing cause. Alternatively, because there is a relationship of brotherhood between them, the word *kaca* refers to Gotama. This is because Utkatha and Bṛhaspati were brothers, and consequently their sons—Kaca and Gotama—were also brothers. The rest is as before. And it is stated in the *Phetkārīya-tantra*, in the section on the *yantra*: "In ancient times, this protection was bound by ignorance..."

"...by Arthagaṇa, Gautama, and others" (66). "Long-nosed" (*dīrghanāsā*) is for the sake of clarity; for it is seen in the *Tāriṇīkalpa* that there is a nine-syllable meditation: "long-shanked, long-limbed, long-tongued" (*dīrghajaṅghāṃ dīrghāṅgīṃ dīrghajihvikām*). (67) "Long-bannered" (*dīrghakā*)—the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense—because she possesses supreme greatness above all; for this very reason, O Goddess, although the immeasurable height associated with your body is such, nevertheless, O Parvati...

[She is] the one who destroys the poverty and suffering [of her devotees]. The meaning is that she brings about the destruction—that is, she brings under control—the wicked, uncontrolled "void" (*kha*) which is the sense organ in the form of the mind (*manas*), which is the cause of poverty. This is because tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are the specific qualifications for the seeker of Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*). [She is] the destroyer of the wicked *asuras*. [The word] *suṣṭu* means... [text fragment ends].

The gods (*surāḥ*) are so called because they utter the word *rai* (wealth); from this root, the suffix *kap* is applied. Those who act contrary to that are the *asurāḥ*. Thus, there is a connection with the distinction of being wicked in that regard, because they are the cause of fear (*a-śa*). Accordingly, in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, there is a statement addressed to Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa: "I gave the Arunmukha ascetics to the Śālāṣṭakas," [referring to] the non-utterance of words that establish Brahman.
The meaning is that he gave over his companions, who spoke words that tormented the vital organs (*paramarma*) of others, to the wild dogs of the forest.

Regarding this, it is established in the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā* (Vedānta) that there is no contradiction in Indra’s statement, "I am Prāṇa," because in the passage where it says, "I am Prāṇa, the self of consciousness" (*prāṇo'smi prajñātmā*), the word *prāṇa* refers to Brahman; thus, it was spoken by Indra while possessing the knowledge of his non-difference from the self-abiding Brahman. Therefore, that statement is a discourse on the realization of non-difference from Brahman.

Because he is the speaker; because the destruction of false speakers and so forth has Brahman as its agent. (70) *Dambhika*: the root *dabh* means "to drive away" or "to remove undesirable objects"; the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the agent. (71) *Dambhada*: hypocrisy is the performance of religious duties under a pretext; he shatters that [hypocrisy] by being the author of the *Nekheda* scripture. (72) *Dānta*: because he is endowed with self-control (*sāmarthya*). Thus it has been stated by Vācaspati Miśra in the *Bhāmatī*: "Self-controlled... (*dānto vṛ...*)

(73) "She whose power is supreme" is according to the Śruti: *parāsya śaktir vividhā* ("His supreme power is manifold"). (74) "Destroyer of the lords of the Daityas": those born from the Daityas are *dānavas*; the suffix *ḍa* is applied after the fifth case (*pañcamī*) with the root *jan*. The rest is clear. The section on the letter *da*: (75) "Beloved of wealth and grain": the word *dhana* refers to that which is beyond [ordinary] wealth;

she is beloved by those who desire it because she is the cause of its attainment. (76) "Fortunate" (*dhanyā*): she is *dhanya* because she is effective (*sādhu*) regarding wealth, or because she bestows it. Alternatively—

She is blessed and meritorious through her own superknowledge (*abhijñā*) and connection [to it]; likewise, he is blessed, wise, a poet, and a scholar, according to the statement in the *Kālīkulārṇava*: "O Dear One, whatever gain of this mantra may occur by the power of destiny... (76). She is the "Giver of Wealth" and the "Mistress of Wealth," for even Kubera, the lord of the treasury, is so described according to the *Bhairavītantra* in the section on the *Kavaca* (77). She is the one who possesses righteousness (*dharmi*).

Thus, because it possesses attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*), it is stated in the *Pañcapādikā*: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity—these appear as if distinct even though they are non-different from Brahman. (78) Regarding the word *dhārmikī*: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *dharma* means merit, restraint, and justice. The suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule *atin-ṭhan-au* to the word ending in a primary derivative (*svarthika-taddhita*) meaning "she whose nature (*dharma*) is this. (79) Regarding *dharmya*, [it is derived from] *dharma*.

Because this [knowledge] is the means of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and because it is established in the works of Vācaspati and others that the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) necessarily arises through sacrifices and the like performed with the aim of purifying the mind—provided they are not deviating from *dharma*, path, purpose, and justice—it follows that *dharma* is the quality of the person produced by enjoined actions, while *adharma* is that produced by prohibited actions; thus say the teacher Udayana and others. (80) Likewise...

And there is scriptural authority for this: "It is He alone who causes him to perform good deeds whom He leads upward from these worlds; it is He alone who causes him to perform evil deeds whom He leads downward. Nor should it be argued that this entails the presence of passion and hatred [in the Lord], because it is established that "one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action," since the goodness or badness of prior karma alone is the determining factor for the goodness or badness of subsequent karma. Thus it stands.

In the second chapter of the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* (the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*), [it is stated]: (81) "Dhaneśvarī" because she is capable of both bestowing and taking away wealth; (82) "Dharmadvāttrī" means that those who cut off or obstruct religious duties such as sacrifices are *dharmadās*; she is their devourer (*attrī*). [The term] *dharma* refers to the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and the actions that produce it. [She is called Dharmadvāttrī] because she consumes those who obstruct religious duties such as sacrifices—those who are *dharmadās*. Thus it is said.

The Mīmāṃsakas [derive the word] from the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *tṛc*, and then apply the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīṣ*. Thus, *dharmānandapravardhinī* means "she who increases the bliss born of dharma. Furthermore, this is supported by the Śruti: "Whatever is the bliss of the hundred Gandharva worlds, that is one unit of the bliss of the Karmadevas—those who attain the status of gods through their ritual actions. Those who attain the state of divinity through dharma are explained as the *Karmadevas*.

(84) According to the statement in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* previously cited, "She whose deity is the Lord of the Immortals" (*yaṃ-devatya-mareśa-tyamiti*). Regarding "Dhanādhyakṣā": she who does not fail (*na adhate*) to grant nourishment (*puṣṭim*) is *dhanādhiḥ*; the word *dha* has been explained previously. The form [of the name] ends in *ṇi*, derived from the roots *nātha* and *nādhṛ* for the purpose of protection, as it is an invocation for sovereignty and blessings.
This is because she is meditated upon by those desiring nourishment. (85) "Dhanaprītā": whether she be a *yati* or a *bhūyati*, may she be present at my worship.

Because it is stated [in the scripture]: (86) "O wealthy one" (*dhanāḍhye*), because she is eternally full; (87) "O you whose desires are attained" (*prāptakāme*), according to the scriptural revelation; (88) "O you who are satisfied by wealth" (*dhanatoṣite*)—since the word *dhana* has the same meaning as the word *nidhi* (treasure) or the word *dravya* (substance) which denotes the earth and so forth—it refers to the ninth (*navamī*) by virtue of its reference to the number nine. She is satisfied therein; thus says the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O Hero, he who worships the Three-Eyed One on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja..."

Hear the fruit of his merit: that hero obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) and a hundred *vājapeya* sacrifices, surrounded by hosts of gods in heaven. (88) *Dhīra*: she who bestows (*rāti*) wisdom (*dhī*), that is, distinguished knowledge, upon her devotees; or alternatively, she who impels the intellect (*dhī*) because her nature is that of the Supreme Self, according to the Vedic scripture: "May He who impels our intellects. (89) *Dhairyavatī*: possessed of steadfastness (*dhairya*). *Dharma*...

Bharata states: "Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is defined as the non-deviation from a resolve that is joined with purpose and desire, and endowed with both the auspicious and the inauspicious. Regarding the word *dhṛṣya*: it is derived from the root *dhṛṣ* in the sense of "to be bold" (*prāgalbhya*). The suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule *bhavya-geya-pravacanīya-ādy-artha-vacana-kṛtyāś-ca*, because this is a *kṛti-gaṇa* (an open class of words). This is made clear by the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakṛt*), who employs the term as a *karmapravacanīya*, thereby indicating its status as a *kṛti-gaṇa*. This has been explicitly demonstrated in the fourth [chapter] of the *Tātparya-śuddhi*.

According to the teachers: (91) "Resembling a white lotus" is because she is to be visualized as white in color due to her specific karma; (92) "Dhāriṇī" is so called because she sustains [beings] through both protection and support; (93) "Dharaṇī" is because she has the nature of the earth; "Dhariṇī" is an alternative reading, meaning she possesses "dhara," which refers to mountains, as her place of practice or abode—according to another Tantra, [she resides] on Mount Ujjara, or in a secluded place, or at a crossroads. (94)

Regarding the word *dhātrī*: this element (*dhātu*) is *dhātrī*; from that [word ending] in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus says the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Having worshipped the Great Goddess Caṇḍikā here on the ninth day, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others attained greatness. Therefore, this ninth day is highly meritorious and a destroyer of sins; it should always be observed with effort by all kings. Regarding *dharīśa*: *dhara* is a specific type of jewel (*vasuviśeṣa*). It...

The construction is as follows: "He is to be worshipped by them"—meaning by those who constitute the group [of the Vasus], namely the Vasus; for they are his lords (*īśa*) because he is their object of worship, according to the *Mahābhārata*: "By the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Sādhyas. (96) Regarding the term *dhavalāsya*: *dhavala* means beautiful, white, or a great bull; as the *Viśva* lexicon states, "Or *dhavalī* refers to a cow of the Surabhi breed. According to the *Amara*, names such as *śabalī* and *dhavalā* arise from differences in color and other qualities. The state of being the face (*āsya-tvam*) of those two... [is implied].

Regarding the fact that she is worthy of being praised for her generosity, it is stated thus in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*: "He who offers a bull marked with a trident to the Blessed Lady shall go to the abode of Mahādeva, along with seven generations of his family, up to the seventh [ancestral level]. Likewise: "And he who gives a beautiful cow with two faces to the Blessed Lady obtains that same fruit as one who has given the earth consisting of the seven continents. The word "gives" (*dadāti*) is to be understood from the preceding context. (97) Regarding the term "virtuous" (*dhārmika*), it refers to *dharma*.

Because [the performance of] rites is dear to Me, it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa in the words of the Goddess: "That Vedic ritual which has been remembered by those who know the meaning of the Vedas—those who perform that with diligence are dear to Me, and no others; for it is accompanied by Dharma. It is further stated in the same [text]: "In this manner, at My command, Manu, Vyāsa, and others shall establish the supreme Dharma of the Pitāmaha until the dissolution of all beings, provided it is free from the censure of the righteous. (98–99) It is said to be devoid of the reproach of the virtuous.

And so it is stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Lord of the Kula, two things are sinful and most contemptible, causing the destruction of the Kula: great censure within one's own family and union with another [woman]. Therefore, even greater than that sin is the arising of association with the uninitiated (*paśu*)," and so forth. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Always perform the duties consisting of caste and stage of life as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti, together with spiritual knowledge (*adhyātmajñāna*), for the sake of liberation. From dharma arises devotion; through devotion..."

Dharma, consisting of sacrifices and other rites, arises from the Śruti and Smṛti; it is held that no dharma exists other than this. For that dharma proceeds from the meaning of the Veda; therefore, one who desires liberation for the sake of dharma should take refuge in the Veda, which is my own form. This power of mine, known as the Veda, is ancient and eternal; at the beginning of creation, it proceeds forth in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. For the purpose of preserving these Vedas, the unborn Lord created the Brāhmaṇas.

Then he assigned them to their respective duties and enjoined them to perform that which they were to do; for whatever they performed was Dharma, and for that purpose was Brahman created. Beneath them, he fashioned the hells, beginning with Tāmisra and the rest.

This ninth ray [of the work] has been completed by Viśveśvara, the son of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who had crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative Vedic scriptures, in his composition titled *Girijārthacintāmaṇi*. [Salutations to] the one to whom the immortals bow...

Now, regarding the explanation of the word "navama" (ninth): the suffix *kha* is added to the word *nava* in its own sense; and although it is beginningless (*anāditya*), the suffix *pi* does not arise because of the presence of the vowel *i*.
