"She who has long ago abandoned the high and full breasts of ancient women," and so forth; or else, it is a compound with the negative particle *na*, meaning "she for whom no distinguished lord or controller exists," according to the mantra-text of the Śvetāśvataras: "She has neither progenitor nor master. She is called *līrā* because she arose from the center of the heart; or else, because she is devoid of passion (*rajas*), she is called *līrā*. She is called *rajas* because she speaks of darkness (*tamas*)—for *rajas* refers to that which ends in darkness—or because she speaks of the void (*ākāśa*).

The word *statheti* [is explained as follows]: the form ending in *kārā* (the suffix *ānac*) is derived from the root *niṃd* (to censure). According to the *Kalpadruma*, the root *niṃd* (*ṇiṃdic*) is used in the sense of "censuring" (*kuṃtsana*); furthermore, according to the commentary on the *Kāmadhenu*, it is also used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*). Thus, she censures (*niṃdati*) dullness (*jāḍya*) or carries away (*vahati*) the demons (*daityān*). Regarding the term *nimnanābhi*: *nimna* means "deep" (*gabhīra*), as stated by Amarasimha; this is because such a feature is mentioned in the *Sāmudrika* (science of physiognomy). Alternatively, it refers to her having seen her navel (*nābhim dṛṣṭvā*).

Because recitation (*japa*) is prescribed, and because of the statement in the *Matsya-sūkta*, "The lake of sesame flowers," the word "lake" (*sarovara*) is intended there to signify the Name. (4) Regarding "Nageśvarī": because she is the presiding deity over the mountains (*naga*), such as Pūrṇagiri and others, the word "mountain" (*naga*) refers to her breast.
Placing his hand upon that mountain-breast, even one who is fearless and whose mind is undisturbed attains poetic skill and also goes to immortality.

From the *Trigandharva-tantra* regarding the rules for recitation (*japa-vidhāna*): "She whose lotus-face is praised" (*nūtanāmbhojanayana*). [That is to say: one by whom there is no bowing (*nata*)—such a one is "not-bowing" (*no-nata*). The "lotus-face" (*ambhojanayana*) is Viṣṇu; she who possesses him is [the Goddess]. Regarding the lengthening of the vowel in the word *nūta* (meaning "praised"), it belongs to the *kuṭādi* class. For this very reason, the erroneous nature of Śrīdhara’s commentary—which asserts a long vowel in the *Bhāgavata* reading *pariṇūtākhilodayitī*—is stated in the *Manoramā*. [The text continues with: *navīnāmbho*...

She is called *Jasundarī* because of her exquisite delicacy. Alternatively, when intending to express a similarity of color, a blue lotus (*nīlāmbhoja*) should be understood; or else, she is the "beautiful one" (*sundarī*) of the Unborn (*aja*), that is, Brahmā, for whom water (*ambu*) was the first [element] at the beginning of creation. She is his beloved because she is to be worshipped by him, according to the Smṛti: "At the beginning of creation, he created those [waters] consisting of his seed. Furthermore, the primacy of water is established only in relation to the subsequent creation of the elements.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such [Upaniṣadic] passages as "From this Self, space was born" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*); thus it is established in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*.

(7) She is called *nāgarī* because she possesses urbanity (*vaidagdhya*); for it is stated in the *Uttaratantra*: "All noble women possess specific urbanity," and from the words of the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "She is not a courtesan (*gaṇikā*) nor a river (*nadī*)," etc., because she takes the form of a female messenger (*dūtī*). (8) She is the beloved of the *nāgara* kings; and likewise:

O highly fortunate one, you are worshipped in Bhārata by the Nāgas headed by Ananta, as well as by others such as the Takṣakas and so forth, who dwell in the depths of Pātāla. Even if the reading were *rājye* (in the kingdom), it should be understood through implication (*lakṣaṇā*)—just as in the word *śūri*—to refer specifically to those residing there; and the purpose of this is to convey that all of them are your worshippers. Furthermore, because the pouring of a stream of clarified butter (*ājya-dhārā*) is prescribed for one who has maintained the sovereignty (*rājya*), so too does the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* describe the *ghṛtābhiṣeka* (consecration with ghee).

O King, that wise ruler who, endowed with faith, should perform [this rite] for the Goddess on the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja using copper of fine grain, accompanied by songs, dances, gifts, and the sounding of conchs and musical instruments, as well as by keeping a vigil adorned with various flowers— he, liberated from all sins and consisting of divine splendor, rejoices together with Durgā and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

"Nagarājasutā" (daughter of the king of mountains) refers to Himavat, as stated in the section on kingdoms in the *Harivaṃśa*. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the causal ablative (*hetu-pañcamī*), meaning "she whose son is the king (Bhūpa) who has no poison (*gara*)—that is, the son of Brahmā (Aja). This is because she is called "the daughter of the Poison-Brahmā" (*viṣabrahmaṇaḥ putrī*);
that is to say, she is one who destroys the effects of poison. As the *Matsyasūkta* states: "She is the knowledge that destroys poison and bestows immortality. (10)

(11) "The gait of a nāga" (*nāgarājagati*): because the act of going to a mountain (*naga*) is an immaterial (*amūrta*) dharma, and in the absence of such [material] action, the quality of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is attained. Alternatively, since the word *naga* here ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing its own meaning, it means "the king of nāgas" (*nāgarāja*); thus, by "king of nāgas" one takes the *pārijāta* tree, for she possesses the gait of that very [tree] because it grants desired objects. (12) "Adorned with a garland of nāga-kings": because she is decorated with a garland in the form of the *mahāpadma* nāga; or else, [it refers to] the *nāga*...

*Rāḥ* refers to those connected with the body; for in such passages as "this small lotus within this city of Brahman," the word *pura* (city) is used as a designation for the body. *Ajāḥ* means the individual souls (*jīvas*). Their *mālya* is a garland, meaning a succession or lineage; she is adorned therein because her nature is pure Brahman. (13) *Nageśvarī*: because she is the presiding deity over the family trees (*kulavṛkṣas*) such as the *śleṣmātaka*, the *karañja*, and others. (14) *Nagārūḍhā*: [she who has ascended] Himavat, Kailāsa, and so forth.

Because it abides eternally (*sādāvasthānāt*), or because it is "not reached" (*na-gamyate*)—that is, not known—it is called *naga*. This is because the [entities] to be described hereafter are devoid of both ascent and non-ascent (*arūḍhārūḍhi-hīnā*), as they fall within its domain; and because pure Brahman cannot be reached by the power of words, since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by words is itself illusory, and that which is conditioned by such a modification lacks purity. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "From whence speech returns, along with the mind, unable to reach it. (15)

*Nagarājakuleśvarī* means the sovereign of that lineage which is preeminent among the Himalayan clans; or else, *nagara* refers to one who is free from defects (*doṣa*) and possesses the method (*vidhi*) of the *aja* (the unborn), wherein the word *gara* signifies the *lakṣaṇaka* (the one possessing the marks).

She is the sovereign of such a family—of the father and so forth—and is attainable by mere fortune even through one's own family. As it is said in the *Kālīkulārṇava*, cited in the *Rahasya*: "By the mere knowledge of the mantra, one may uplift ten million members of one's family; all the ancestors rejoice."
Singing this verse with joy, they said: "Will there be anyone in our family who possesses knowledge of the lineage? (16) "Navīneṃdukule" means in the family of the new moon;

or, because her breasts are adorned with the specific nail-marks known as *ardhacandra*—which are famous in the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*)—she is so called. Alternatively, it means that [the family] "takes up" or accepts the "navīneṃdu" (new moon-like) face, by virtue of being its progenitor. (17) "Nāṃdī" refers to a benediction, because it is a cause of auspiciousness; thus says Bharata:

Because it is always employed in connection with benedictory words for gods, the twice-born, kings, and others, it is therefore called *nāndī*. Alternatively, it should be understood as "the female descendant of Nanda" (*naṃdasyāpatyaṃ strī nāṃdī*). Regarding the phrase "beloved of Naṃdikeśvara," Halāyudha states that one who has been gladdened (*naṃddhaḥ*) is Naṃdikeśvara. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is said that she is equal to Śiva by virtue of being Naṃdin; the ellipsis to be supplied is "having obtained [this status] by propitiating her. In the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, it is stated that she attained sovereignty over all the worlds and over the Gaṇeśas.

And likewise, from the words of the Goddess: "O Lord of Gods, you ought to give me this son of Śailādi," [the name] *Nīraja* is derived as follows: he who possesses *irā*—meaning speech (*vāṇī*)—in an extreme degree is *nīraḥ*;

he who conquers or overcomes such an opponent (*pratipakṣin*) is *nīrajā*, because he is the cause of that opponent's defeat. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *irā* means earth, speech, liquor, and water.

(19) Alternatively, regarding the term *nīrajākṣī*, it expresses the sense of the genitive case; or, according to the *Viśvakośa*: "The letter *ra* signifies fire and sharpness. Here, *rā* refers to fire. (20) *Nīrajākṣī*. Or else... [text continues].

(21) *Nīrajaskaṃdākṣī*: "Skanda" refers to one who has emerged from the mud (*nīra*). She whose eyes are attached to him because he is the object of her affection as a son. Alternatively, it means she whose vision—knowledge—is free from the pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain, which are the effects of the quality of *rajas* (*rajoguṇa*); here, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) signifies the state of being an object. (22) *Tīraprasūtā*: The word *tīra* signifies sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*). She is so called because she has given birth (*prasūtā*) to such things as suffering; [this is formed with] the suffix *kvip*.

The compound *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.2.18) means that words beginning with *ni-* form a compound with a word in the fifth case when they convey the sense of "departed from" (*krānta*) or similar meanings; thus, *tad-abhāva-apa-prasūta-niḥkrānta-nirādayaḥ*. Regarding the term *nīrābha*:

those stars which have reached (*ati-prāpnoti*) the *nīrāṇi*—those which possess excessive radiance (*nitarām irā vāṇī yeṣu tāni nīrāṇi*)—are so called because such a placement (*nyāsa*) is highly praised. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Sūryārṇava Tantra*: "Having performed the great *nyāsa* beginning with Rohiṇī, the wise and best of men [becomes] the son of Rohiṇī."

One certainly becomes pure of speech and earth; his voice becomes composed of prose and verse, and he is born with a wife. He certainly becomes an expounder of scriptures never before seen or heard by others. If one should worship Tāriṇī without having practiced the *tāraka* [mantra], even if the mantra has been recited a hundred lakhs of times, it will not grant success. (24) She is called "Nīranirmaladehinī" because her body is as clear as water, or because of the performance of worship in water.

According to the statement of Śātātapa, "In the heart of the horse, in Agni, and in the Sun," and according to the statement of the *Yoginītantra*, "One should worship the Supreme Goddess whether she is situated in water or upon a stone," [she is described as] "rich with the sacrificial thread of the Nāgas. Here, "sacrifice" (*yajña*) refers to the connection with the Nāgas by way of being the cause of their destruction; "thread" (*upavīta*) means that which reaches or attains (*upaiti*); it is the cause of equality in all sacrificial sessions (*sarvasatra*), meaning it is the means for that. At the time of that traditional teaching, by Āstīka, that...

Because he causes the binding [of obstacles], or because he is the cause for the commencement of the snake-sacrifice (*sarpa-sattra*), he is grasped as such; for it was precisely due to the killing of Parikṣit by him that Janamejaya undertook that sacrifice.
He has attained this [state], and by him [the world] is enriched; for according to the *Upaniṣad*, Taksaka is present within his matted locks like a serpent in its hole.
(26) Regarding the term *nāgayajñopavītī*: the one-syllable lexicon (*ekākṣara-kośa*) states that the letter *ja* signifies Gaṇeśa; therefore, he whose nature is to protect Gaṇapati is [so called].
Thus it has been explained by Pakṣadharamiśra in the *Gavīti-śabda-khaṇḍa*: "By way of being the progenitor of Him. Gaya is Śiva; he who knows Him is a *gayajña*.

One who is the opposite of that is an *agayajña*, meaning one who does not recognize Śiva in the form of a child. There is no suffering (*duḥ*) created by Him; [the word] *aśiva* refers to that which possesses the affliction (*upadrava*) of the thunderbolt (*vajra*) fixed upon that [child]. Likewise, in the *Śatarudrīya* of the *Mahābhārata*, having placed the child upon his lap, He himself... [text fragment ends].

Furthermore, desiring to know Umā, he asked the gods, "Who is this? Then, as the powerful Śakra was about to strike with his thunderbolt, the Lord paralyzed that arm of the enraged one along with the thunderbolt itself.

After the gods had offered praise and inquiries regarding Brahmā, those gods then propitiated Umā and Rudra; and the arm of the wielder of the thunderbolt became restored to its natural state once more. [Thus ends the section on] the Nāgakeśara tree being satisfied.

"Thus, from the *Matsyasūkta*: 'The flower of the sage (*munipuṣpa*) has five stamens (*kesara*); that which arises from it is a serpent (*nāga*). That very [serpent] possesses stamens (*kesara*), and thus it is called *nāgakesara*, meaning 'lion' (*siṃha*). Because she is satisfied by that [flower], as it is her vehicle, she is described in the *Prapañcasāra* as 'mounted upon the shoulders of a lion' in the case of Śūlinī.
In the case of Mahiṣamardinī, it is stated in the aforementioned *Matsyapurāṇa*; and in this particular form, she is 'seated upon the back of a lion,' according to the statement of the *Muṇḍamālā*."

Alternatively, regarding the word *kesara*, it refers to the *vakula* and *puṃnāga* trees; by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *vakula* flowers alone, a man obtains good fortune. From the *Siddhasārasvata*: "One attains nourishment through *mallikā*, *jāti*, *puṃnāga*, and *kadaṃba*. And from the *Viśva* lexicon regarding the meanings of the word *kesara*: "In the sense of the *siṃhachaṭā* [flower], it also refers to *puṃnāga*, *kiñjalka*, and *vakula*. (28) Regarding the phrase *nāgakesaramālinī*: *nāga* means an elephant; its head (*kaṃ śiraḥ*) is the *nāgaka*.
The Lord moves there by virtue of possessing direct (aparokṣa) knowledge regarding the removal of that substrate; thus [is she] "Nāgakesara-haladantā-dṛti-saptamī-anuk-mālinī.

[The suffix] *ini* is applied according to the rule for the *brīhy-ādi* group. There is a *karmadhāraya* compound of the two [words]. Alternatively, she is called "Mālinī" because she is the daughter of a garland-maker (*mālākāra*), as it is proclaimed in the *Kumārikā-tantra*: "She who is nine years old is celebrated as a maiden (*kanyā*)," or because she has the form of a seven-year-old girl (*kumārī*), or because she is Mālinī herself through the seven [syllables].

Based on the statement of Ditiyāmala and the Vāmana Purāṇa— which begins, "Auspicious unguents fragrant with *mālinī* and *surabhī* flowers were applied by her two hands to the goddess who shone like gold," and continues, "When she had bathed in pure water on the mountain, she fashioned from her body a four-armed man with stout shoulders and endowed with auspicious marks, and released him onto the earth; he remained there, seated upon a throne (*bhadrasana*)"— it follows that in the variety of the *mālinī* meter, there may be a *mālākāra* (garland-maker).

"Even in a woman," according to the *Viśva* lexicon (29). "Worshipped by Navīnakenakīkunda-makaranda-prapūjitā": *Navīna* means that Brahman which has never been experienced before; *ita* means attained—that bliss (*ka*) which is Brahman, as taught by the fires to Naciketas in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* through the instruction "Ka is Brahman. One who desires that [Brahman] is *navīketakī*. By the suffix *kvip*, [the form] *navīketakī* is formed. She is worshipped (*pūjitā*) by such a devotee (*bhakta*) with *kunda* flowers, *makaranda* (nectar), and honey (*madhu*). Listen.

Having begun with the words, "O Śakra, I shall explain the chapter on flowers in brief," and citing from the *Devīpurāṇa* the verse, "With *kuṇda* flowers and *tirīṭaka* [flowers]," as well as the statement, "Combined with honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*"), the offering of honey is established as a constituent part. Alternatively, according to the *Matsyasūkta*: "Satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) with honey bestows the fruits of all desires; it directly effects the perfection of mantras and is the destroyer of great sins. (30)

(31) "Not even the heroine" means that according to Bharata’s statement, "The hero is Indra, but the heroine is Sarasvatī," she is regarded as Sarasvatī herself because she is the witness (*draṣṭṛ*) of that [performance]. (32) "Beloved by the hero" means that the hero is Śiva, and she is so called because she is the locus of his affection. (33) "Satisfied by the hero's love" means she is the object of the affection residing in the hero; for it is said by the theorists of poetics (*alaṃkārika*) that "in the beginning, there is passion in the woman. Ananta... [text fragment]

The description of the lover's passion (33): "O Tilaka of the Hero's Joy!"—according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *tilaka* refers to the central jewel in a necklace; thus, she is the one whose abode (*nilaya*) is Vārāṇasī, the source of the highest joy (*ānanda*), which is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Because she is the Great-Eyed One (*Viśālākṣī*) in Vārāṇasī, as stated in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*: "Those who desire all enjoyments even here in this world..."

Even beyond liberation, Bhavānī, the wife of Mṛḍa, bestows everything upon them incessantly and truly; she is the "Nāyakā-nandakāriṇī" (the one who causes joy to the Leader). "Nāyaka" means that which has no other leader—namely, bliss that is innate.

Such bliss is liberation. It is not a joy born from the attainment of the bliss of one's own nature—which, though already attained like a golden necklace forgotten around one's neck, is merely being realized as such.

The Vedāntins [hold] that its attainment is not real, because Brahman is eternally established. (35) "Accompanied by the lover's love" means: *āyaḥ* refers to fortune and happiness, which do not exist in the absence of the cause, since the effect does not arise without it; thus, she is one who possesses love directed toward Him, meaning she is compassionate toward the distressed. Amara states: "*ayaḥ* is a rite that brings auspiciousness. (36) "Satisfied by the lover's love."

A specific state of being (*bhāva*) called "love and devotion" (*prema-bhakti*) leads one to attain the Leader (*nāyaka*); for it is established in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other works that Rati alone is such a *bhāva*, as expressed by the phrase "Rati, whose object is the divine and so forth, is pleased by him. [Verse 37] Regarding the epithet "abode of the Leader's joy" (*nāyakānandanilaya*): the root *nī* with the prefix *ā* forms *nāyaka*. Those who lead (*nayanti*) or speak the truth are *nāyakas*; they are knowers of right reasoning (*yukti*).

That is to say, for those who know the scriptures, it reaches a state of unfathomable profundity that transcends ordinary joy; likewise, because it serves as the cause of the scholarship that generates delight in the wise among devotees, it has been said: "Even the gods are put to shame by his scholarship and the composition of his diverse verses, let alone the humans on earth"—thus it leads devotion to that which causes both distress and bliss. (38) It leads [devotion].

The leaders attain the state of being objects [of her grace]; she brings about the bliss that consists in the absence of the bondage of darkness for them. Thus it is said in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: "This great goddess, who is eternally worshipped by the three worlds, when remembered, releases from the fetters of the other quarters those who are situated in shackles. (39) "Delighting in the work of leather" means she is devoted to the activity of play for the sake of the world through her sport.

Having raised the objection— given that agency and so forth require a purpose through a connection with a desire for that purpose, how can God possess agency since He is devoid of the desire for a purpose?— the second Sūtra of the Śārīraka Mīmāṃsā, *lokavat tu līlākaivalyam*, [provides the answer]: even in the absence of a desire for a purpose, just as kings and others exercise agency in activities consisting of mere play (*līlā*), so too does God exercise agency in the creation of the world and so forth.
The meaning is that it is the absolute sport (*līlā*) whose agent is Śiva. (40) Regarding "eternal" (*nityā*): likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said:

"O Goddess, Mahāvidyā Mahātripurasundarī is called 'Eternal' (*nityā*), the supreme deity who is the essence of all parts. (41) Regarding "devoted to playful activity" (*narmakarmaparāyaṇā*): by "playful activity" (*narma*) is meant sport (*līlā*), which implies acting without depending on any external cause; she is the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇā*) of ritual acts (*karman*) such as sacrifices and the like.

The logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that God is established as the substratum of the direct perception regarding the causal relationship between sacrifices, heaven, and so forth. As it is stated in the *Kusumāñjali*: "Because valid cognition is dependent on other factors, because the creation and dissolution of the world are possible, and because there would be no confidence in anything else, no other means of proof is possible" (42). [She is] one for whom action performed without aiming at a fruit through sport is dear—this is the meaning of *narmakarmapriyā*.

"Furthermore, for the sake of liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence, one should go for refuge to Īśvara by means of knowledge, the yoga of action, or the yoga of devotion," according to the statement in the *Kaurma Purāṇa* (43). [In this context], "nāmī" is a word for the Lord (*nṛpa-dam*) referring to the Supreme Self (*para-ātman*). It denotes the direct realization (*sākṣātkāri-jñāna*) concerning Him; the form is derived by adding the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of being the locus (*āśrayatayā*) of that realization, followed by vṛddhi. Since individual souls (*jīvānām*) lack the direct realization of any other soul, [the term] refers to the Self of the Lord (*īśvara-ātman*).

"She is obtained as one whose primary devotion is to amorous play" (*narmakarmaparāyaṇā*): this means that amorous play alone is her uncommon activity, and she for whom such women are the desired resort; for *Śāśvata* states: "The word *parāyaṇa* is known to mean a desired resort. Because of the scriptural injunction: "One should offer to the deities flowers gathered by her hand, water gathered by her hand, and food gathered by her hand," [she is called so]. "Delighted by salutation" (*namapriyā*)—the opposite [of the previous state].

"Upon the heart, at the time of the end of dalliance," according to the words of the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*. Because she is intent on play (*krīḍāsaktatvāt*), there is "delight in jest" (*narmaprītā*); this is because she engages in playful banter with Śiva. Furthermore, regarding that context, there is the statement of Śiva in the *Purāṇa* concerning Himācala:

"Your mind [is distracted] by mountain peaks crowded with rows of clouds; likewise, your disposition [is drawn away] from those dense forests so difficult to penetrate. And in that very same context, there is the statement of the Goddess:

From the serpents [he received] his multi-tonguedness; from the ashes, his lack of oily attachment (*asneha-bandhana*); from the moon, the impurity of his heart; and from the bull, his inscrutability (*durbodhatva*).

(47) Regarding the phrase "devoted to jesting and dharma" (*narma-dharma-parāyaṇa*), this refers to the specific dramatic function (*vṛtti-aṅga-viśeṣa*) called *narman* in the *Nāṭya-śāstra*. Bharata defines it as follows:
"An action performed through deception, characterized primarily by jealousy and anger, joined with reproach and pathos, and intended for one's own benefit—that very thing is *dharma*."

The term "one who possesses qualities" (*guṇī*) does not refer to one who is merely wealthy, because even a subordinate quality (*aṅgaguṇa*) becomes a primary quality (*pradhānaguṇa*) through a traditional succession. In this context, the intended meaning is "one attached to that," which refers to the form of a *naṭī*. This should be understood as a *naṭinī* in the form of a *yakṣiṇī*, according to the statement in the *Bhūtaḍāmara*: "Gaurī, the enchantress of the three worlds, wearing wonderful garments, adorned with various ornaments, beautiful, and assuming the attire of a dancer. Thus, she is the embodiment of the *naṭī*.

In the *Kāveśya* [text], regarding the messenger (*dūtī*), it is said from the *Uttara-tantra*: "Accompanied solely by the act of sport (*narmakarma*). The act of sport (*narmakarma*) means an action for the sake of play; it is that which one "leaves behind" (*syati*) as primary (*eka*), meaning most important. This is derived from the root *syati* with the suffix *kap*. For him, she is beneficial through devotion (*bhakti*) that is entirely non-dual. As stated by the Goddess in the *Kaurma-purāṇa*: "Having resorted to my supreme state, worship me at all times through all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts; I am the deity of all. (49) Sport (*narma*).

"Karmaikapālikā" refers to her whose sole companion was the friend Mālinī through their playful activities; the suffix *ka* is applied to the word *pāti* (protector) in the sense of "one who has. At the time of the wedding, because Mālinī, a friend of Gaurī, acted in such a manner, it is stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Then Hara’s foot was taken by Mālinī for the sake of a gift; 'Why do you ask for my foot? You may go! said Hara," and so forth. (50)

"Delighting in the virtues of men and women": this refers to the virtues found in women, such as freedom from anger and so forth; she who delights in these is a virtuous wife (*kulastrī*). According to the *Yāmala*: "A practitioner should always avoid censuring a hero, stealing his property, showing malice toward women, and inflicting blows. (51) "She who bestows the boon of men and women": she who grants the boon of women in the form of men, by granting desired wives; or else, she is the mother of that particular deity.

Because she was born from Dharma through his gift of his own daughter, who possessed the form of a woman, to Dakṣa—since it has been stated previously that the daughters of Dakṣa were born from portions of the Goddess—she is called "the beloved of Nārāyaṇa. Among the various mantras, this five-syllabled mantra is declared to be the cause of all prosperity, according to another Tantra. [52-53] Regarding the term *ṇikṣa*: the root *ṇikṣ* means to kiss; and here, the word "kiss" refers to union.

The suffix *mātra* is applied after all nouns by virtue of their belonging to the *pacādi* class; through this, pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is obtained. (54) Regarding the term *niṣka-varṇa*: the word *niṣka* has the following meanings according to the *Viśva-kośa*: "a gold coin," "an ornament," "a measure," and "a weight. Alternatively, one should remember it as being like gold upon a pillar, according to another Tantra. (55) Regarding the syllable *na*: the single-syllable lexicon (*Ekākṣara-kośa*) states that the letter *na* is used for "welcome," "binding," "praise," and "tree."

That which involves the making of a prostration (*namaskāra*) is so called because it strikes [the enemy] by making prostration the cause for the destruction of the intended victim. O Great Goddess, he whom those whose forms are encased in the sixfold [mantra] worship shall immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles and fears him—therein lies the protection against the blue [demon]. (56) This is the section on the letter *na*. Regarding "fond of flowers" (*puṣpapriyā*): it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) in the feminine with the fifth case, meaning she for whom blossoming flowers are dear. [This refers to the word] *ātmarūpa*.

Through the distinction of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), various kinds of dearness manifest in wealth and other objects; for the scripture states, "But everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self's desire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8). [The term] *puṣparatā* means that bees (*bhramara*) delight in flowers; because she possesses them through the occasion of drinking honey, she is so called, as her body is not composed of those [ordinary elements].
This is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, beginning with "When he named Aruṇa... up to "...I shall slay the great Asura."

The commentators explain that "many" means "innumerable" because six [sins] are bestowed there. Thus it is said in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "When the great Asura named Aruṇa comes into being, then I, the goddess Hitā, shall assume the form of a large bee, destroy his life, and return again to heaven. (58) The word "pauṣpī" contains the term "puṣpa," as in the case of "bhīmā" and so on; here "puṣpa" refers to the *puṣparāga* gem. This [river] belongs to that [gem].
"Because it was fashioned like an image [of Viṣṇu], as stated in the Devīpurāṇa: 'as if made of the jewel-element' (59). Regarding the word *pāpaparāyaṇā*:

the *Ekākṣarakośa* states that 'the one who purifies is called *pa*'. *Āpamaya* means 'consisting of water'; since Varuṇa has water as his support, the term *parāyaṇa* is understood here with emphasis on the abstract state (*bhāva-prādhānya*), forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound. According to the Skanda Purāṇa: 'Varuṇa’s domain is mastery over the waters, and Vāyu’s domain is the wind. The syntactical connection is: 'that which was obtained through the propitiation of [him]' (60)."

"Pauṣpīpriyā" means she whose beloved [rosary] consists of a garland made of *puṣparāga* gems; for it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra* regarding the rosary for the attainment of health: "All [the beads] should be made of jewels. As for the formation of the word, since the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) indicating increase (*vṛddhi*) occurs in the sense of a colored modification (*raktavikāra*), the masculine form is prohibited by the rule, and thus the feminine form is established. (61) "Supuṣpejyā": here the prefix *su-* serves merely as a filler (*pūraṇa*), following the sequence of names beginning with the letter *pa*.

She who performs sacrifice to remove the fear of Yama; or, because she goes to the flower (*puṣpam ije gacchati*), she is the "Grasper of the Bee" (*bhramaragraha*). She whose bowstring consists of that [bee], whose noose is made of sugarcane, whose goad has the bee as its cord, and who possesses the five arrows—thus it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra* regarding the meditation for the installation of life-force (62). Likewise, in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "To a Brahmin devoted to the Agnihotra, who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, [she is] golden..."

O King, whatever fruit is obtained by giving a hundred gold coins, that same fruit one obtains by worshipping Caṇḍikā on the ninth day with a garland of bilva leaves and guggulu resin. O lord of men, the construction of the sentence is: "having worshipped Goddess Durgā with a bound garland and guggulu" (*mālābaddhena guggulena*).
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmāhnika*. One obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice by [offering] the leaves of the bilva tree, and likewise with garlands of karavīra flowers.
He who worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of *vakapuṣpa* flowers, having obtained the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Durgā.

He who worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of *kuśa* grass and flowers, having obtained the fruit of the *rājasūya* sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Śakra. He who worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of *śamī* flowers, having worshipped Āryā with faith, [obtains the same fruit].

Having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, he who worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of blue lotuses, or performs a hundred recitations (*japa*), having attained [the state of] Rudra, is glorified in the world of Rudra. Among all flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion and according to the rules, offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses to Durgā... [and so forth]. (63) This bestows merit.

"Thus, merit is utterly destroyed, or his karmas are exhausted upon seeing Him, the source of all that is high and low"—so says the Śruti. (64) Or else, it may be on the full moon day of the month beginning with Caitra, because of the statement in the *Triśaktiratna*: "The best of practitioners should worship Mahāśivā on the full moon days of the months beginning with Caitra according to the method to be described. Alternatively, it may be on the full moon of Pauṣa, since she is designated as a goddess (*devī*) and a mountain (*parvatā*) in the *Matsyasūkta*. (65)

"Meritorious" (*puṇyā*) means that merit (*puṇya*) belongs to her, because she is the intended object of its offering; for it is said in the *Bhagavad Gītā*: "O Kaunteya, perform action for My sake, free from attachment," and "This world is bound by action," [referring to] action performed for the sake of sacrifice (*yajñārtha*). (66) "Bestower of the fruit of millions of merits" means that through her worship alone, she grants the fruits of many actions; thus, what was previously sacrificed by the Great-Souled One through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha—
"By him who has performed infinite austerity, the Tārāṇī has been worshipped"—so says the statement [67].

Because the procedures (*itikartavyatā*) for worship are prescribed according to the Vedic, Tantric, and mixed traditions in the Purāṇas and Āgamas—[as stated] in the *Bhāgavata*: "Sacrifice is of three kinds: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed" [68]—and because she is pleased by the Purāṇas and Āgamas, that is, by those who have attained non-duality (*advaita*), through the recitation and giving of the scriptures...

"Because the *Devīpurāṇa* states, 'The Mothers are the givers of fruit to those who owe [debt],' (69) and because she is hidden within the Purāṇas and Āgamas, even though they have the Lord (*Īśvara*) as their ultimate referent, she is established through various modes of presentation. Thus, it is said in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*: 'This entire Veda has the Supreme Lord as its object:

as the Creator in the *Puruṣasūkta*; as [His] majesty in the *Rudra-hymns*; as the Word-Brahman (*Śabdabrahman*) in the *Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇas*; and setting aside the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [He is revealed] in the...'"

In the Upaniṣads, He is described through the proliferation of manifold forms as the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*); in the ritual injunctions of mantras, by the manifestations of His body; and in the narratives, as the object of worship—thus [He is present] everywhere.

(70) Because of the previously cited statement, "He is hidden in the Purāṇas and Āgamas like a protected woman of a noble family," the Purāṇa is defined by five characteristics: "Creation (*sarga*), secondary creation (*pratisarga*), genealogy (*vaṃśa*), the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantarāṇi*), and the history of the dynasties (*vaṃśānucarita*). (71) Therefore, because it falls within the scope of the Purāṇas, there is no mention [of Him] there, due to the worship performed according to the sequence of family customs.

(72) [The compound] *nāṭagocarapada* is a *bahuvrīhi* based on the predominance of the abstract state (*bhāva*). (73) Regarding the word *pūrvā*: since Pūrvāṣāḍhā is the family asterism (*kulanakṣatra*), while the other two [asterisms] are not considered families due to their irregularity; and according to Amara, "the words *yūḥ*, *strī*, *purī*, and *nagarī* all mean 'city'"; she reaches that [city] as her place of residence. Furthermore, in the section on the *Śākinīs*, it is stated in the *Pūrva-abhidhāna*: "The word *pūrvā* refers to female spirits (*bhūcaryaḥ*) and cities. (74)

The term *prauḍhāvināśinī* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both mature (*prauḍhā*) and indestructible (*avināśinī*). By this, it is also stated that she is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Alternatively, *prauḍha* refers to one who is free from childhood and old age and endowed with virility; she destroys such a person through her power. She is likewise forbidden for those who are children, the elderly, impotent, diseased, those with oozing sores, the weak, those with deficient limbs, those intoxicated by liquor, those whose sexual organs are aged, and those with discharging sores.

(75) Regarding the context of the *bali* offering, according to the words cited from the *Suparṇa*: "She who gladdens the heart of Prahlāda," because she is the cause of the manifestation of the power (*śakti*) of Nārasiṃhī; and likewise in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "Scattering the planets, lunar mansions, and stars with the falling of her mane, the exceedingly fierce Nārasiṃhī was born from the heart [of the Lord], the one possessing claws.
(76) "She whose conduct is meritorious" (*puṇyacāriṇī*), because she is the cause for bowing at her feet. (77) The section on the letter *pa*.

She is called *Phālgunī* because of the injunction for worship on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) of that month, as stated in the *Matsya-sūkta*: "The eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna. She is called *Phālgunapriyā* because of the statement in the *Triśakti-ratna*: "One should worship the Goddess in the month of Phālguna with [offerings] of gold or even silver," and so forth. She is called *Phālgunapremadhāriṇī*. Likewise, in the *Ananta-tṛtīyā-vrata*, regarding the monthly worship, the *Matsya-purāṇa* states: "With *siṃduvāra* or *jāti* [flowers]..."

One should also worship Umā in Phālguna; it is called "Phalgu" because it necessarily yields fruit. In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "In which [month] the cow, the wish-fulfilling cow, the water, and the earth bear fruit, and because the mind's thought contained within it bears fruit, that is the Phalgutīrtha, not fruitless. [The commentary explains: The river Phalgu, the cow, and the water are the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*); and the earth is the "gṛṣṭi," meaning a cow that has calved once. These three, when contained within the mind's thought, bear fruit.

Therefore, [the statement] "Phalgutīrtha is not fruitless" is found in the *Tristhalīsetu* (82). [The statement] "It yields fruit" is from the *Matsyasūkta*, which says: "In the case of the Guṭikāsiddhi, Vetālapātalī, Vaṭayakṣiṇī, and Parapurapraveśa, the attainment of mastery over commands (*ājñāsiddhi*) arises" (83). [The phrase] "Adorned by the King of Serpents" (*phaṇirāja-vibhūṣita*)—here the word *phaṇipada* refers to the lotus-seed (*padmākṣa*), and the word *bhūṣaṇa* refers to the anklet (*nūpura*). This is because the *Datyupaniṣad* states: "The lotus is dear to the one who wears anklets."* *(Note: The final sentence is a partial citation and interpretation of a passage concerning the symbolism of the lotus and ornaments in esoteric traditions.)*

(84) From the word *darśanāt* [is derived the meaning]: "She whose form is like a hood" (*phaṇākārā*) means she whose form is like a serpent's hood, impossible to release, and which has the nature of *saṃsāra*. (85) "Beloved by the Serpent" (*phaṇiprītā*): the word *phaṇin* refers to Patañjali. Regarding this, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states, beginning with "O subduer of enemies, those twenty-six principal ones are well-known," and continuing: "Kapila, Durmukha, and Patañjali are remembered. Thus it is said. Therefore... [end of fragment].

Vāgaurabhaṭṭa, however, says: "In both ways, 'Goṇikāputra' and so forth, this is the presentation of his own view in the Mahābhāṣya; and in the *Phaṇibhāṣya* (the commentary by Patañjali), that is its renown because he was worshipped by him. Furthermore, after stating the twenty-syllable mantra among its varieties, another *Tantra* says: "The seer (*ṛṣi*) is declared to be Patañjali," and so on. [Verse 86] "Adorned with the necklace of serpents" (*phaṇihāravibhūṣita*): one who carries away (*harati*) the serpents (*phaṇinaḥ*) is [a *hari*] in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*); and he is also *viḥ*.
And by the term "bird," there is the inclusion of Garuḍa; she is adorned by him because it was previously stated that she is born from a portion of the goddess Vinatā, and because Garuḍa is her son.

(87) The expression "she whose ornaments for all limbs were made by the Lord of Serpents" is a general statement; the word "all" refers to the specific limbs mentioned in other tantras. This is according to the maxim "the quality of 'all' is authoritative," just as in the phrase "by the final oblation, all desires [are attained]," where the word "all" refers to the subject at hand.

(88) *Phaṇivāhinī*: Because the Gaṅgā flows through three paths (*tripathagā*), it is the "carrier (*vāhinī*) of serpents (*phaṇin*)," meaning a river of snakes; this is because the non-difference between Gaṅgā and Gaurī has been stated. (89) *Phaṇiprītā*: The root *phaṇ* (from *phaṇa-gatau*, with the suffix *vica*) means "to know" or "to understand. Thus, *phaṇī* is the locative case ending (*saptamyanta*). It may also be analyzed as a separate compound using the *aluk* sandhi. (90) *Phaṇiratā*: The word *phaṇi* refers to the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī-tithi*) presided over by that deity.

(91) Regarding *raṃ*, it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta* that "on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārga," she is described as being on a mountain; furthermore, according to the *Upaniṣad*, it is seen that "she is adorned with a bracelet of serpents" (*phaṇikaṅkaṇabhūṣitā*), implying that the bracelet is indeed the serpent Śaṅkhapāla; and in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*, it says, "with a shining bracelet of golden serpents" (*suvarṇābhanāgollasatkaṅkaṇena*).

(92) Regarding *phaladātrī*: according to the *Ekākṣarakoṣa*, the letter *pha* signifies wind (*vāta*); that which takes (*lāti*) or receives (*ādatte*) that [wind] is *phala*. The suffix *vāti* is used to form a word meaning "born from" (*janyāpasarga*).

By the maxim "the word with its qualifier [negates] that [which it qualifies]," as in the case of "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī naṣṭaḥ*) and so forth, the connection of the negation applies to the qualifier alone. This is established by the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* passage beginning with "He is filled by the blow... (93). Regarding the phrase "unattached to fruits," there is the scriptural prohibition against the Supreme Self enjoying the fruits of karma, based on the statement: "Those who are unattached to fruits do not desire the fruit of action. Furthermore, the Śruti states: "None other than He beholds [the fruits]."

And regarding [the phrase] "adorned with ornaments of fruits" (*phalābharaṇabhūṣitā*): the word *phala* (fruit) here refers by implication to the *guñjā* berry; thus it means "reddened by ornaments strung with *guñjā* fruits," as stated in the *Tvaritādhyāna* and *Prapañcasāra*. Alternatively, it means "by the sound of battle (*raṇa*) which is characterized by the absence of fruit (*phalābhāya*)," that is, by a battle where no fruit is attained. Or else, it means "by such a 'battle' (*raṇa*)—that is, by sound—in the form of constant loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*), which grants fearlessness to the worlds," according to the statement in the *Upaniṣad*. [This concludes the section on] the letter *pha*. (94–95) *Phakāra*.

The syllable *pha* is called *phakūḥ* because it produces the sound *phak*; [this is derived from] the root *kuṅ* (to sound) with the suffix *kvip*, where *phakāra* means the sound *ṭa*. By that [syllable], she whose limbs consist of the mantra-form that destroys dullness (*jāḍya*) from all objects is [described]. Furthermore, in the section on *vāsanā*, a statement cited in the *Rahasya* says: "The sound *phaṭ* is the destroyer of all dullness; such is its nature."

*Śakam-phālgunānandavardhinī*: Arjuna is called *Phālguna* because he is swift (*jiṣṭari*), as stated in the list of synonyms for Arjuna in the Virāṭa-parvan of the Mahābhārata. She increases his joy through victory over his enemies; likewise, in the Bhīṣma-parvan, she makes the meaning of that [victory] manifest.
Alternatively, by virtue of a temporal relationship, she was born under the asterism Phalgunī; thus, she increases the joy of Śiva arising from their marriage. And so it is.

"Having entered into conjunction with the moon during the auspicious hour (muhūrta) under the asterism of Uttaraphālgunī"—as stated in the *Kumārasambhava*, since Gaurī’s marriage took place under the Phālgunī asterism; and likewise in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "Then the Seven Sages said to the King of Mountains:
'Listen, O Night! On this third day, there is a lunar conjunction with Uttaraphālgunī, which is endowed with the qualities of Mitra, auspicious, and highly meritorious.'"
The auspicious moment presided over by Maitra, which shall bring welfare and protection, is approaching; on that lunar day, Hara will take her hand according to the mantras.

(97) This section begins with names starting with the letter *va* belonging to the labial class (*pavarga*). The commentator has provided this title in accordance with that [convention]. In the word "Vasudevaratā," the syllable *va* functions as a simile (*upamā*), while in "Varuṇe," the *va* is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*); thus, it belongs to the labial class (*pavargīya*).

The word *viśvaḥ* [is from] the *Viśva* lexicon; *tanniṣṭham* means "devoted to that"; *sudevayā* means "by one whose devotion is characterized by excellence" (*praśastya*); the genitive case signifies the sense of possession (*viṣayatva*). According to the *Skanda Purāṇa*, *varuṇena* refers to sovereignty over the waters (*jalaiśvarya*). Regarding *vijñāvijñā*: the *Viśva* lexicon states that *viśreṣṭātītanānārthe* [is the meaning]. Those who know variously (*vividham*) are *vijñāḥ*;

those who perceive the phenomenal world (*prapañca-dṛṣṭayaḥ*) and possess the conceit of duality (*dvaitābhimāninaḥ*) are *avijñāḥ*. She is the one for whom they are ignorant (*avijñā*). It is said: "That which is unknown to the ignorant is known by the wise. (*avijñātam vijānatām vijñātam...*)
"Because of the scriptural statement, 'For those who do not know' (99), and because of such declarations as, 'It produces manifold knowledge for devotees;

thus his poetic flow arises as a succession of the essence of nectar' (900); this tenth [chapter], the Mayūra, has been completed in the *Girijārthacintāmaṇi* composed by Viśveśvara, the son of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who has crossed the ocean of words, authoritative statements, and grammatical forms."

May Śrī reside in your mind upon some object—be it the head of Speech (Vāc), the source of hearing (Śruti), or the ultimate limit reached by wandering through the various intermediate meanings—which serves as the primary cause for the cessation of false cognition, specifically in the Fourth State (Turiya). Now, regarding the commentary on the hundred [verses] beginning with "vīṇavatī":

although, in the rule *vīṇāsthūṇā-vīṇā* (*Pāṇini 4.1.64*), the word *vīṇā* is derived by relying on the application of the root *vī* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and so forth, the word *vīṇā* [is used here].

The word *vīṇā* is well-established [in lexicons] such as the *Viśva*, which states: "In the context of a lute (*vīṇā*), a market (*vipaṇi*), and bamboo (*veṇu*)," it is *vīṇā*. Nevertheless, by relying on the irregularity (*nipāta*) of the verbal root *vaṇśabdi*, it is established that it begins with a labial (*pa-varga*).
Thus, the *Viśva* [states]: "It consists of a labial and a dental. Here, there is a specific distinction regarding the meaning of the root, such as "to place" (*dhā*) and so forth.
If it were composed of a dental and a labial, there would occasionally be a deviation here; for this [word] possesses a lute (*vīṇā*) and lightning (*vidyut*) as the correlates of similarity.

The meaning is as follows: according to the *Viśva* lexicon, "vīṇā" and "vallakī" both mean lightning (*vidyut*). The *Nīlatantra* states that she has a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning. (1) She is "crowded with cranes" (*balākīrṇā*); this is a form derived from the root *bal*, meaning "to kill" or similar, because she dwells in the midst of armies such as those of the Kumārīs. Alternatively, she is so called because her chariot has a crow-banner (*vāyasadhvaja*) in the form of Dhūmāvatī, according to the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "mounted on a chariot with a crow-banner. (2) She is "the nectar for the young" (*bālapīyūṣarorikā*), because she protects (*balate*).

*Kṣīrasvāmī* [explains] *prāṇitivālaḥ* as "having arms that are immersed" (*āplāpye*). According to him, both [words] begin with a labial (*pavargīya*), because they are both recited in that section in works such as the *Kalpadruma*. The word *pīyūṣa* refers to the moon by virtue of being composed of it; thus, it is said, "it shines like that. (3) Regarding *bālāvasumatī*: young women are "wealth" (*vasu*) belonging to her; this is the common property (*sādharmya*) of her extreme dearness. As it has been said regarding them...

One must never, under any circumstances, practice censure, hypocrisy, or unkindness, as these act as obstacles to success. (4) Regarding the phrase "free from the taking away of knowledge and ignorance": *vidyā* is the path of knowledge (*jñāna-mārga*), while *avidyā* is the path of action (*karma-mārga*). In this context, *hāra* means abandonment; thus, it is "devoid of that" because Brahman, being of a dual nature, is to be cultivated in both paths. Alternatively, *āhāra* refers to the bringing forth or giving of knowledge to disciples who desire it.

Therefore, because the word "aviśabda" has the meaning of non-existence, it is so stated in the Devīpurāṇa in the Hemādri [digest]: "He who constantly promotes the gift of knowledge in the temple of the Goddess shall become worthy of worship by all the worlds and shall attain the state of the worshipful. She is called "Vidyāvatī" because, in the form of Sarasvatī, she pervades that [knowledge]; thus says the Mahābhāṣya: "This collection of phonemes and this collection of sentences are both in flower and in fruit."
Kaipaṭa explains: "The mass of Brahman should be understood as appearing like a cluster of stars" means that the very form of Brahman appears in the form of sound.

(6) Regarding "Vaidyapradaprītāvaivasvatīratiḥ": [He] is to be known by the wise as one who gives a bird as a sacrificial offering (*bali*); because he employs a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in its own sense, he is "one who gives service" (*seva-pradaḥ*), meaning an excellent giver, since the giving of the *bali* excels other forms of giving. In that regard, she is pleased... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The term *tuṣṭatā* [is derived] from the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied after the word *prī*, with the substitution of the agent (*kartṛvyatyaya*). [The compound *vaivasvatīratiprītā* is explained as follows: according to the statement in the *Cāmuṇḍā-kalpa*, "She whose delight (*rati*) is in the southern [direction], that of Vaivasvata," and "The south is for exorcism (*abhicāra*)," she is both "pleased" (*prītā*) and "the delight of Vaivasvata" (*vaivasvatīrati*). This is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-elided) compound. (7) Regarding the form *vāṇīvilāsakariṇī*, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* due to its being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*), or it is derived from the root *vaṇ*.

The word *ṇī* begins with a letter of the *pa*-group (*pavargīya*). Its "uninterrupted" [form] is *ṇi*. There is the abandonment of that because it is the cause of it. (8) In the phrase *varāgasthāvarānaneti*, with respect to the letter *ba* of the *pa*-group, by means of the word *ra* which denotes fire, the third [letter, *la*] is taken; by the word *aṅga*, the sixth [letter, *ṣa*] is to be understood. The vowel *ā* situated there, followed by the letters *ma* and *la*, results in the form *mālā*. She whose face (*ānana*) is *vara*—meaning beautiful—is *ṇīmālāvarānanā*. *Ṇī*...

According to the statement in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, "She who has a terrifying mass of matted hair like a beautiful garland of blue lotuses," the word *viṣṇoḥ* [in the phrase *viṣṇorvakṣasthalastha*] is an imitation of the word *damu* found within the word *viṣṇu*. Thus, Viṣṇu is one whose name ends with the specific word *ṣṇu*; otherwise, because the word *viṣṇu*—derived either from the roots *viṣḷ* (to pervade) or *piś* (to enter)—is a word beginning with a retroflex (*antasthā*) letter, [it would not conform to that rule].

Because that heart is the very form of Śrī, or because it is the beautiful one mounted upon five corpses, its nature as consisting of auspicious fortune (*saubhāgya*) is seen through the indication of Satī’s birth; likewise, in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Formerly, when the worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and the rest—had been burnt, the auspicious fortune of all beings then resided in the navel. Having reached the Vaikuṇṭha creation, it remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu."

Then, after a long time, when the world was enveloped by egoism and possessed by the Primal Person (Puruṣa), and when rivalry had arisen between the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā) and Kṛṣṇa, there emerged from the fire an exceedingly terrifying flame in the form of a Linga.
From the chest of Hari, which was scorched by that flame, [a substance] issued forth; taking refuge in Viṣṇu’s chest, it established its auspiciousness within him in the form of essence (rasa).

Then it reached the surface of the earth, having been cast up into the sky by the wise son of Brahmā, Dakṣa. As soon as that which produces beauty and charm was drunk by Dakṣa, the supreme progenitor, great strength and splendor arose within him. That which remained fell upon the earth and was born in eight forms;

from these, the sugarcanes, the king of grasses (sugarcane), the niṣpāva beans, the ajājī seeds, and the dhānyaka herb were produced for the benefit of people, bestowing praised good fortune, as well as the various products of cow's milk.

Saffron is the seventh, and salt is the eighth; this is called the "Eightfold Saubhāgya" (the eight ingredients of fortune). When drunk by the son of Brahmā, who was a knower of the science of Yoga, she became his daughter, who is known as Satī. Because she surpassed all women in the world in her grace, she is called Lalitā. The wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva) married her, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds. A man who worships that Goddess, who consists of auspiciousness and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation— [The text ends here.]

"By devotion, what does she not know? (10) She is called Vāgvatī because she dwells on the Vindhya mountains; she is Vaṅgā because she causes the water of Varuṇa to bend toward her mouth due to her attraction of the Yamunā, according to Baladeva. She is Balavatī because she is the sister of Baladeva, as stated in the Harivaṃśa. Alternatively, she is Vāgādyā because the *Tantra* states that when this Vidya begins with the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāk), it bestows the status of Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśatva*). He who knows her as Vāgādyā, Kamalādyā, or Tāriṇī becomes a lord of song; indeed, he is Śiva.

According to the *Atharvaṇa* scripture, "she becomes speech" (*vāṇī bhavatīti*). [The name] *Vindhya* refers to that which "binds" or "dries up" (*viṃdhyati śoṣayati*); the suffix *vun* is applied to the root *vyadha* in the sense of drying. She who "dwells" (*vasati*) there is *Vindhyavāsinī*. According to the *Mahābhārata*, [the sages] Pulastya, Agastya, and Pulaha [reside there]. From the root *as* meaning "to shine" and so forth, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied; then, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed with the preceding term. Due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*), there is no change of gender to the masculine form. Alternatively, it is the abstract state (*bhāva*) of the word *vāgvatī*.

Due to its predominance, it is expressed by that [term] through the elision of the middle word (*madhyamapadalopa*), as in the compound *vaṃśa-vānīrataru-saṃsthā* (the state of a reed-tree on a bamboo). By the word *vaṃśa*, which refers to water, the ocean is grasped. That lotus has such a tree as its progenitor—the water being the cause for its production and maintenance on all sides—and because it rests upon a red lotus situated above the ocean, it is said in the *Āpyarvaṇa*: "There, one should meditate upon the letter Ā, which is pervasive, [and] the shore, etc. Then, that...

One should meditate on a red lotus through its connection with the quality of *tva*. Regarding the term *vānīrakusumotsūka*, although Svāmī explains it as "that which is impelled by water" (*vanitambuvāni*), and since the root *vanu* means "to pervade" (*saṃbhakti*) and belongs to the class beginning with the semivowels (*antaḥsthādi*), it would indeed follow that form; nevertheless, because the root *vanati* has the meaning of "begging" (*yācanā*) and so forth, its initial being a labial (*pavargīya*) is also authoritative. For this very reason, in that same context, it is stated: "vānīra, vānara, vacā."

"By offering *dūrvā* grass tomorrow one becomes long-lived; by [offering] *vetasa* reeds one becomes a giver of rain," according to the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*. (13) Thus ends the section on the letter *va*. *Bhītiheti*: This is the name of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). It is so called because it destroys (*han*) calamity (*īti*), derived from the word *bhī-bha* with the suffix *aṇ*. It is thus because it wards off the afflictions of the planets (*graha-pīḍā*), as indicated by the rule "the substitution of the neuter form does not occur when there is a cause for *vṛddhi*" (Pāṇini 7.3.20), and by the statement "in the case of a great planet or a great portent. (14) *Bhayadā* ("fear-giving").
As stated in the Bhairavī Tantra: "She bestows upon her devotee a supreme power that is the ultimate cause for the end of fear," as in the case of Durvāsas toward Śabara and others.

(15) Regarding the phrase "possessing a luster equal to the web of rays of the sun": although the word *aṃśu* (ray) is dependent on the word *bhānu* (sun), the compound is formed just like "the teacher’s son of Devadatta" (*devadattasya guruputraḥ*). This was stated by Bhartṛhari: "A relative term, being always dependent, is employed [in a compound] as if it were part of a sentence."
Even in the case of the activity of a serpent dependent on poison, it is not diminished. Thus, in the *Gandharva-tantra* within the context of the *Kavaca*, it is said:

"Having known [this], the highly effulgent Bhārgava Rāma slew the Kṣatriyas in battle; he, of great splendor, gratified the goddess Kālikā along with her hosts with offerings of flesh arising from the bodies of the Kṣatriyas and their blood. This is the worship of Bhṛgu. Furthermore, according to the *Mahābhārata*, [he was honored] by Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, and others.

Because of the power of the fifth [syllable] following the *bhṛgu* (ṅ), *yad* (ya), *daṃsaka* (sa), and *kara* (ra), and through its conjunction with the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*), the curse was removed. Thus, in the *Phetkāriṇī*, it is said: "The Goddess was propitiated by Vasiṣṭha, yet she did not grant immediate fruit; therefore, the sage bestowed a most terrible curse upon them. From that time forward, this vidyā has not granted fruit to anyone. Then, the seed-syllable of Śakti was joined above the seed-syllable situated within the triad. From that time forward...

This knowledge bestows fruit upon no one else; it is like a virtuous bride who carries within her the seed of the three powers. "O Bhāradvājī, support [your] sons, support [your] disciples, support the gods, support the twice-born, support your wife, and support your husband; O beautiful one, I am Bhāradvāja. A *dvāja* is a servant who goes to his master with both speech and mind (*dvābhyāṃ vāṅ-manasābhyām*). Having placed [the burden] upon the world (*aja-gatau*), [he is so called].

From the root *dhā* with the suffix *u*, *dhātuḥ* means "one whose understanding is stainless. His offspring is *Bhāradvāja*. According to the rule *ṛṣyaṇḍhakety-aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.114), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. In the one-syllable lexicon (*Ekākṣarakośa*), *bha* is proclaimed to mean a bee (*bhramara*) and a leaf (*dala*). Then, by the rule for feminine connection (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīp* is added; thus, she who possesses similarity to that [bee] because of her dark color is [called] *Bhā*. *Hi* has the meaning of a deer (*hariṇa*); she who possesses these [qualities] by way of being powerful (*balitva*)—the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *arśādi* (Pāṇini 5.2.127)—is *Hā*. In the sense of exhaustion (*kheda*), a deer (*hariṇa*), or a deer-marked [bow], *ha* and *śū* [are used]. *(Note: This is a commentary on a verse likely from the *Śabdaratnākara* or a similar lexicon, analyzing the etymology of the name "Bhānumatī," the wife of Rāma.)*

The term *liṅga* is defined as "that which marks" (*liṅgayati*) according to the *Ekākṣarakoṣa*. It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "light" (*jyotis*) and "that" (*hā*). This is because the *Sudhārṇava*, citing the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, states: "She [Kālī] is the one who knows all kinds of animals, even the divine ones. (20) Regarding the term *bhayasaṃpannā*: by the word *bha*, the circle of stars (*tārakā-cakra*) is intended. Those who move toward it and deliberate upon it are the *bhayāḥ*; from the root *pad* in the sense of "to go," with the suffix *kra*, the form *pannā* is derived, meaning "well-known" (*saṃyak-prajñātā*). Thus, she is the *Tārā* of Kālikā, the *Tārā* of the stars.

According to the statement in the *Yāmala*, "The wheel shall be auspicious" (21). Regarding the phrase "the beautiful one from the terrifying-shaped clouds" (*bhīmākārābhrasundarī*), "terrifying-shaped" (*bhīmākāra*) is an adjective qualifying "cloud" (*abhra*). Alternatively, if it were an adjective qualifying the deity, it would form a *karmadhāraya* compound. Or else, it means "that cloud from which the terrifying-shaped [bird] has departed," referring to the swan (*haṃsa*), because the description of the departure of the swans at the end of the rainy season is established by the oral tradition (*kāva-sampradāya*) of the Kaulas; for it is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "The pigeon, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, and the swan. (22)

Regarding the section beginning with *bhakāra*: the term *māyādharī* refers to the *Vidyādharas*, since the word *māyā* signifies *vidyā* (knowledge/spell). The meaning is that she is their object of worship. Alternatively, it may be understood from the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "The Vidyādharas possess incomparable knowledge, and their intellect is fixed on manliness; this is the duty of the Vidyādharas, namely devotion to Bhavānī. Or else, *māyādharah* refers to Śambara, and because she is cognizant of him, she is his object of worship.

And likewise, in the *Harivaṃśa*, there is the speech of Nārada to Pradyumna: "O son, this powerful mallet, the destroyer of enemies, was given by Pārvatī when she was well-pleased; it is unfailing in battle against gods, dānavas, and humans. (23) [The term] "māna-rata" [is used] because it is an object of mere cognition, since the manifestation of the self as "I am" arises for everyone; thus, it cannot be denied by this self.

As for what was indicated [in verse 24], "intent on the honoring of those worthy of honor" (*māna-saṃmāna-tatparā*): "those worthy of honor" (*mānāḥ*) are those who deserve such respect; "intent on their honoring" (*saṃmāna*) means devoted to showing them due care, because otherwise faults are heard [to result]. As it is stated in the *Kādimata*: "If, during a worship ceremony, the Guru arrives or anyone else likewise, one should simply say 'It is done' and not engage in silence with them. Alternatively: "O Lord, having invited the Guru and seated him like a deity, one should perform worship with garments, ornaments, gold, and so forth."

Having satisfied one's own guru, as stated in the *Puraścaraṇa* [section] (25); for there is a one-syllable lexicon (*ekākṣarakośa*) stating: "Mādhava, Ānanda, Da, Ma, Śiva, and Candramas are Vedhas. Since he is the husband of Mādhavī, and the suffix is used in its own sense (*svārtha*), he is called Mādhava. Furthermore, because he bestows happiness through the performance of her marriage, so it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra* after describing Gaurī’s marriage: "The merit that is obtained when this is performed... [the rest of the sentence follows].
O Grandfather of Awakening, one shall dwell for a long time in Rudraloka in Laṅkā, possessing ten million-fold the fruit of a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeyas;
this is because of the performance of the Damana-pūjā in Vaiśākha. Likewise, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā it is said:

"The three months beginning from Caitra, and both fortnights, bright and dark—[the word] 'mā' [in the verse] has the sense of negation (mā = na), meaning that there is no other [time] than this which is of the nature of Brahman."
Because it is devoid of distinctions—whether of its own kind (*sajātīya*) or of another kind (*vijātīya*)—it is explained in the passage "one alone, without a second" as being thus [non-dual].

(27) Regarding the word *madirā*: from the root *mad* in the sense of "to know" (*manujñāne*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*). *Iḥ* means desire; *tūrāt* means she who gives that [desire].

Thus, *madirā* [is derived], with the reversal of the order of words being Vedic (*chāndasa*), or else there is an elision of the middle term (*madhya-pada-lopa*), because knowledge (*jñāna*) is the ground and support of *harā* (the destroyer). (28)
"Madirekṣaṇā" means one whose eyes (*īkṣaṇa*) are as beautiful as wine (*madirā*); [the suffix] *ra* is applied according to the Uṇādi rule "iṣimadimudi-".

Alternatively, it means one whose vision (*īkṣaṇa*, i.e., perception) is delightful (*mya*). "Endowed with the quality of great enthusiasm" (*mahotsāhaguṇopetā*) means those who possess the quality of great enthusiasm;

for others, even the attainment of the states of the sense objects results only in distraction. Mastery over the Maheśvaras, wealth, and further, the abundance of wives and so forth—these are considered inferior accomplishments (*siddhis*).

"Because of the statement: 'The first stage of practitioners has been declared; he whose mantra is perfected is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt' (30). It is called 'great' (*mahatī*) because it transcends all [others] (31). The compound *mahadadbhuta* is to be understood as "a marvel even for the great. Otherwise, there would be an undesirable consequence (*atyaprasaṅga*). Kaiyaṭa states that 'marvel' (*adbhuta*) is the cause of wonder, and thus it takes the gender of the qualified noun (*viśeṣyaliṅgatva*). [End of commentary on verse 20]. "Nala was born from the earth... [End of verse 21].

Because of the observation [of the text] beginning with "not from wonder" (ṇādbhuti), etc. (32). "Intoxicated by the fragrance of wine" (*madirāmodabalitā*): *mada* means musk; that which possesses this is *madī*, meaning fire.

By implication, it refers to one who is endowed with the joy of the fragrance resulting from the oblation of musk. This is because of the statement: "The oblation consists of camphor, agallochum, saffron, and musk" (33). "Delighting in immersion in wine" (*madirāmajjaneratā*): as it has been said regarding the offering of the *argha* libation with wine to the Yoginīs.

She should be beloved (*bhavet-priyaḥ*); [this is] the section concerning the letter *ma*. Because she is called *Yaśasvatī*, even though there is the designation *bha* [by Pāṇini 1.4.18], the substitution of *ru* (the *r*-sound) occurs as a Vedic (*chāndasa*) word-formation (*pada-kārya*), resulting in *yaśo-viyā*. Alternatively, it is because she is the cause of that [fame], or because she is the form of Kīrtīśvarī. Thus, after stating the thirty-two-syllable mantra division, another tantra says, regarding the introduction to the enclosure (*varaṇa-prastāve*): "One should worship the goddess Kīrtīśvarī," and so forth.

"Yaśodānandavardhinī" means she who increases the joy of Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda-gopa, because she is the cause of his joy by being his daughter; or alternatively, it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "Yaśodā and Nanda," and she is so called because she makes them exalted by increasing their joy through her birth. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, it is said that she herself was the Great Goddess Kālī, born from the womb of Yaśodā, who, having placed her foot upon the head of the demon Kaṃsa, departed; from that time forward, [she became known as] Dē... (the text continues).

(37) Having worshipped Tyaghrī, Yaśodā, and Nandinī on the Vindhya mountain, I have once again initiated worship. (38) Regarding the phrase "white as the camphor of fame" (*yaśaḥ-karpūra-dhavala*), since fame is conventionally established by poets as being white, there is a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) in which fame is the camphor;

yet, because there is no decisive reason to determine whether it is a *rūpaka*—namely, "fame is camphor"—or an *upamā* (simile)—namely, "fame is like camphor"—there is a *saṃdeha-saṃkara* (blending through doubt). Yaśodā.

Regarding the phrase "not adorned" (*mavibhūṣitā*): here, there is indeed a metaphor (*rūpaka*), because that which resides in the ornament is a sublater of the simile (*upamā*). (39) As for *yamārājasvasā*, Amara states: "The sister of Yama is Śamanī. Svāmī explains it as "the sister of Yama" (*yamenarājati*). Alternatively, this refers to her form as Yamunā; or else, because she is beneficial to those who have self-restraint (*yamavatām*) like a sister. Thus, in the *Bhūtaḍāmara* during the section on the Yoginīs, having heard that, the best of practitioners...

One should meditate upon the sovereign Mother as one's mother, sister, or wife with a spirit of affection (40). She is the "increaser of the bliss of the path of Yoga," for according to the *Pātañjala Sūtra*, "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ*), and she is attained through that very [cessation]; or else, because she is the cause of various fruits according to the method of practice (41). She is the "giver of the bliss of the Yādavas. Thus it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*: e...

Men on earth called her Kāñcanā, the daughter of Yoga, who was difficult to overcome; and for the sake of protection, all the Yādavas honored her as the garment of Keśava. Like a goddess with a divine form, she by whom Kṛṣṇa was protected—she who is called the "Increaser of the Yādava Joy" because she protects the Yādavas when they are distressed or perishing.
This is also a statement explaining the meaning of her name: *avati* (she protects), from which the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).

The compound *yātāṃ-avati* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound); she is both that [the protectress] and the increaser of bliss (*ānanda-vardhinī*), according to the indicative mark of the mantra: "intent on the protection of those who have come for refuge and those who are miserable and distressed. Alternatively, because she is the cause of happiness for the protector of those who have sought refuge, as stated in the Smṛti: "Fearlessness has all the gods as its deity" (43). Regarding the phrase "pleased by Yaśa," it is said in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "I shall explain the state of the bound soul (*paśu-bhāva*); listen, O child, with concentration."

Having proceeded thus, [the word] "yajñamayī" refers to the Vedas, as they are engaged for the purpose of Vedic sacrifice, according to the passage beginning with "faith in hearing the Purāṇas... the abandonment of the meaning of the Vedas and Vedānta. Furthermore, from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "This ancient power of mine is known as the Veda. Also, in the phrase "yajñakarmavibhūṣaṇā," the word "yajña" refers to Dakṣa; for one who performs the sacrifice is called "yajñakaḥ," derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *vic* and the addition of the syllable *guṇa*. He indeed performs (*kṛṇoti*) or destroys (*hinasti*) the sacrifice (*yajña*). Thus, the term "yajña" here is intended to denote the Veda.

Although there is the elision of the *vakāra* (v) which is a constituent part of the verbal root *div-*, there is no prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *na dhātulopārdhadhātuke* for the suffix *vic*, because [the presence of] *val* alone serves as the cause; this is clear from the works of Kaiyaṭa, Kaustubha, and others. And she, for whom such a Soma is the sole ornament (*vibhūṣaṇa*)—that is, the object of her passion—at the sacrificial ritual (*yajñakarma*), or rather, she for whom his state of being an ornament [is established]. Thus.

In the *Caśiva Purāṇa*, it is stated that Śaṅkara smeared his own body with the ashes from that funeral pyre through the yoga of supreme knowledge (*vidyā-yoga*), which transcends all [worldly] attachments.

(46) Regarding the section on the letter *ya*: "Rāma is dear" (*rāmapriyā*); the *Viśva* lexicon states, "Rāma may refer to a particular animal, or to Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni. Having abandoned the black antelope skin, the *Sudhārṇava* states that for the Kṣatriyas and others, there should be a *vali* (offering/ornament). This is recorded in the *Mahākāla Saṃhitā*; [the text continues with] the Kṣatriyas...

Because of the exclusion [of other animals] among deer by the term "the black antelope" (*daukṛṣṇasāra*); because Vālmīki was delighted by Rāma—Rāma being Dāśarathi—and because Sarasvatī belongs to him, as stated in the *Harivaṃśa*; and because she is intent on pleasing Rāma due to her manifestation at the time of the slaying of Rāvaṇa, it is said in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "For the sake of Rāma’s grace and for the slaying of Rāvaṇa, [she appeared] indeed at night..."

O Goddess! Having been awakened by Brahmā in the past, she then cast off her sleep and, filled with joy during the bright fortnight of Āśvina, quickly brought about the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. (49) She is called *Rājñī* because she is superior to all knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, even if there were a woman equal to you and a man equal to me...
"Umā is like Sarasvatī; she is Mandohrī," so it is said in the Bhairavī-tantra (50). "In the royal family (*rājakule*)":

because she is the deity presiding over that [family], she is worthy of worship in the family of King Candra. For it is stated in the Matsya-purāṇa: "And Umā is likewise [the wife] of the Moon. Alternatively, she is worshipped in the king's *kula*—meaning his body—or in his vehicles such as elephants and the like, since elephants, horses, and so forth generally belong to the king. Thus it is established.

One should bow with the thought that these are deities upon seeing a white garment, flowers, a king, a prince, elephants, horses, excellent garments and the like, fruit, a *kālīra* plant, and men; this is according to the statement of the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*. (51) Regarding "Rājarājeśvarī," Amara states: "Rājarājī is [an epithet of] Dhanīśvarī"; furthermore, according to the *Bhairavī Tantra*, Dhanādhipa is Kubera. Without knowing this armor (*kavaca*), whoever [worships] Śivā as Rājarājeśvarī...

"One should worship with the elders of the Yoginīs; there is no doubt that it should be consumed"—thus it is stated in the *Kulānandasaṃhitā*. Furthermore, such a practice exists in the *Sundarī* [Tantra] as well.

Alternatively, because she is to be propitiated by kings, the best of rulers, she is called "Dayā" (Mercy). She is the protection established in the city, for the sake of the knowledge of the goal, by Gautama and others, and by other earthly beings desiring victory in battle—so says the *Phetkārī*. (52) When the Vidyā begins with the Śrībīja (the syllable *Rām*), then...

Śrī is "facing in all directions" according to the *Matsyasūkta*; one should know her as Kamalā and others in the northwest wind, for she becomes Vaiśravaṇa according to the *Atharvaṇa*. She is "passionate" (*rāgiṇī*); these "passionate ones" (*rāgiṇyaḥ*) are well-known in the science of music (*saṃgīta-śāstra*), and she possesses that form. Alternatively, from the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "O Sage, Jyeṣṭhā is the daughter of Ena, red-limbed, with red eyes, adorned with red garments, and renowned among the passionate ones. (54) She is the "delighting one" (*ramaṇī*).

Thus, *rovahnistasya* refers to the crystal jewel (*maṇiratna*). Because it produces day through its connection with the sun, the word *maṇi* takes the feminine suffix *ṅī* [becoming *maṇī*]. This is supported by the *Naiṣadha*: "by the luster of the king's sapphire-jewel" (*nṛpanīlamaṇīgṛhatviṣām*), and by the statement of Svacchandabhairava in the section on yantras: "one should also employ a crystal [rosary], which grants all accomplishments" (*sphāṭikīm api yojayet*), as well as from the rule for rosaries: "even in the case of a great conch, if one is unable [to obtain others], one should join a crystal one" (*mahāśaṅkhe 'py aśaktes ca sphāṭikīm api yojayet*). (55)

She is called *Rāmā* because she delights (*ramati*) the mind; according to the *Viśva* lexicon, *rāma* means "beauty," "Lakṣmī" (the goddess of fortune), "the red Aśoka tree," and "Cupid. Alternatively, she is called *Rāmā* because she protected Pradyumna during his battle with Śambara, or because she is fond of Aśoka flowers, as stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Dhattūra, Aśoka, and Bakula are white, while Kṛṣṇā and Aparājitā are black. She is the "bestower of bliss upon women" (*rāmānandapradāyinī*) because she grants happiness to women; likewise, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states in the context of the *Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata* regarding a woman: [she who performs this vow becomes]... [end of fragment].

O Lord of Monkeys, even a young maiden who performs [this rite] obtains that same fruit, being cherished by the grace of the Goddess. Likewise, in the *Sudhārṇava*, in the section on the descent of the *Kulasūla*, beginning with "Mātaṅgī, Ugratārā, Kālikā, and Śyāmalā," it is specifically stated regarding women: "That woman who is separated from her husband, or who is auspicious and restrained in her conduct—may she too accept these [offerings]. Furthermore, it is said: "She who is devoted to me... [and so forth].
