"She who grants the three-fold joy"—thus from the *Brahma Purāṇa* (57). Regarding the phrase "she whose face is full like the moon": according to the lexicon, *janī* means wife, and *janī* also refers to a woman with a parting in her hair (*sīmantinī*). She makes the sound "svāhā" during the oblation (*homa*) and other rites; therefore, she is "full-faced" because of being satisfied by that. For it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "In the oblation and the satiation, [the word] 'svāhā' is uttered. (58) Regarding the phrase "she whose eyes are like red lotuses," the meaning is clear; or else:

She whose eyes are delighted by blood (*rakta*)—meaning fresh blood (*rudhira*)—and by an offering made with choice pieces of meat (*māṃsa*) and fat (*vasā*), as well as by the oblation performed with them;

likewise, it is stated in the *Kālītantra*: "One should offer clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked food (*bhakta*), meat, and blood; especially with black flowers and blood mixed with clarified butter. In this same manner, the wise one should also offer meat and other such things in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Or, "blood" refers to one who possesses passion (*rāga*).
The meaning is that he observed him specifically as a particular kind of Daitya; for, having recognized his illusory power (*māyā*), [the Lord] had already destroyed it.
Thus, in the fifty-sixth chapter of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa: "Mṛḍānī, while sporting, beheld the roaring Daṃbaka;
and by those two Daityas moving through the atmosphere, she was, as it were, glanced at with side-long looks by those who had arisen along with Death."

As the Creator moved about with his two hands known as *dala* and *utpala*, which by their own strength treated the three worlds as mere straw, he desired to seize the Goddess; thus afflicted by the god of love, he cast away his illusory power (*māyā*) and descended from heaven. Having understood that Śāṃvarī was indeed the one who shared half the body of the All-pervading One, he then [struck] simultaneously with that very same ball.

Those two of great strength, who had been concentrated upon by the Great Goddess with her ball, wandered about and wandered about; then those two wicked ones were destroyed. (59) [This is] the section on the letter *ra*: "Lāṅgalī is satisfied by love," and "nālikela is a *lāṅgalī*," according to Amara; Kṣīrasvāmī says it is so because its stalk has the form of a plow (*halākāra*). Likewise, [it destroys] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as treachery.

"Upon seeing an unworthy recipient, one should destroy all [offerings]"—thus it is stated in the *Bhairava-tantra*. From the *Triśakti-ratna*: "In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should recite the mantra with charming black-gram cakes; one should offer camphor mixed with coconut water. Furthermore, in the context of the libation (*tarpaṇa*), there is the statement: "For the accomplishment of all aims, [one should offer] water mixed with coconut juice and the waters [of the sacred sites], O beloved of Lāṅgalī. (60)

"Coconut water in a bell-metal vessel, honey, and cow's ghee placed in a copper vessel are equal to *sīdhu* liquor, excluding clarified butter"—this is from the *Kulārṇava*. Furthermore, "He who offers mango, coconut, dates, and citron to Durgā shall go to the supreme abode"—this is from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. Or, because of the injunction for *homa* (fire-offering), it is stated in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "In eight ways... [The text continues with the list of offerings].

The adept should perform the *rikela* oblation; by this, prosperity remains firm in his house like subjects [obedient] to a king. Or, because the serpent Śeṣanāga has a body as small as a child, he is his weapon; therefore, by wearing that [serpent] in his matted locks (*jaṭā*), it is said in the Upaniṣads, "He dwells within the matted locks" (*jaṭāsvananti*). (61) Regarding the phrase "red as lac," since the application of barley-meal (*yāvaka*) to the feet is prescribed among the sixty types of services (*upacāra*), [it refers to the feet]. Tṛ...

The compound is formed according to the rule *pītātatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* [Pāṇini 2.1.59], or alternatively, it is a compound according to the rule *upamānācceti sāmānyavacanaiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.1.55] because she possesses a red color like lac (*lākṣā*). One should meditate upon her as red in order to bring someone under one's control, according to another tantra. (62) Regarding the word *lalanā*: Amara states that *lalanā* means "a woman with shapely hips" (*nitaṃbinī*). She is called *lalanā* because she plays (*laḍati*) or is cherished (*lālyate*); *laḍ* means "to sport," while *lal* means "desire," according to Svāmī. In reality, however—
She sports and dallies with supreme excellence as a woman; thus it was said previously in the *Mātsya*: "Because she transcends the worlds and sports (*lalati*), she is called *Lalitā*.
(63) She is *Līlā* because she bestows speech through her play (*līlayā*); thus, according to the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī*, she is *Nīlasarasvatī*.
(64) She is *Līlāvatī*; as it is stated in the *Bharata*: "With speech, gestures, and ornaments that are interconnected and joined with delight, [she is like] honey..."

"Līlāvatī" is derived as follows: "Lāva" refers to a specific kind of bird; its state is "lāvatā. One who desires *lāvatā* for herself is [called] "lāvatī," formed by adding the suffix *kvip* to the word ending in *kyac*. Alternatively, it means "one who cuts" (*lāvā*). She in whom the playful movements (*līlā*) of that [bird] reside is "Līlāvatī"; this is formed by adding the suffix *ac* to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *lī*, and then appending the feminine suffix *ṅīp* (as indicated by "kṛdikārād..."). Regarding "raiḥ": it is the imitation (*anukṛti*) of a beloved person through the employment of playful gestures (*līlā*). It is the imitation of the beloved's [beauty] produced by the application of playful movements. Or, "lāva" is a type of bird; its state is *lāvatā*. One who desires *lāvatā* for herself—by adding the suffix *kvip* to the word ending in *kyac*—is "lāvatī," meaning simply "one who cuts" (*lāvā*). She in whom the playful movements (*līlā*) of that [bird] reside is "Līlāvatī"; this is formed by adding the suffix *ac* to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *lī*, and then [the feminine suffix]. From that, [the rule] "kṛdikārād... [applies].

There is elision of the *tiṅ* suffix because the verbal root *lī* is prescribed as having the *bal* designation. In the *Sudhārṇava*, [the term] *cakravākaṃ calāvakaṃ* is explained as *mahākalalaya*. She is so called because she "merges" (*līyate*), meaning that having cast off the form of the individual soul (*jīva-rūpa*), she becomes her pure essential nature (*śuddha-svarūpa*), according to the Vedic scripture: "She attains her own true form" (*svena rūpeṇābhisampadyate*). She is "delighted by the qualities of the Lord of Laṅkā," for Laṅkā is indeed the city of the Śākya branch.
According to the statement of Vīracūḍāmaṇi, "nīkulaṭā-suceti-vipat-vālaṅka-akulaṭā-tasyīśvara-pūjaka-gaṇikā-naṭī," etc.,

[the term refers to] the Lord of Śakinī, Skanda; or else, taking the sense of the word from the *Gāthākoṣa*— which states, "laṅkeśa-varadāyinī" (the giver of boons to the Lord of Laṅkā), and "laṅkā-śākhā-ateva-laṅkā-lāṇa-yuta" (endowed with the protection of the branch of Laṅkā)— it refers to both the Palāśa tree and the Rākṣasa.

This is clear from the *Ṣaṣṭhādvavaraṇa*. Here, "sācī" refers to that which is connected with the *bilva* tree and so forth, because it is to be worshipped by the Lord (*Īśa*); for it is prescribed in the *Navarātra* rites that worship is performed upon a *bilva* branch.

Thus, it is stated in the *Gauḍanibandha*: "The jujube, the pomegranate, grain, green mango, the *kañcu*, the *bilva*, the *aśoka*, and the *jayantī*—these are to be known as the nine leaves (*navapatrikā*). And it is said in the *Triśakti*: "She is pleased by the flower of the clove (*lavaṅgī*)."
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Great Auspicious One (Mahāśivā) with sandalwood, flowers, cardamom, cloves, *kaṅkola*, or other offerings.

(69) According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the suffix *tā* is applied [to form *lavaṅgī*] because it is a garland of clove flowers (*lavaṅgī-kusuma-sraj*). (70) Regarding the section beginning with the letter *la*: she is called "Bālā" because she is extensive (*balate*) or because she is spread out (*tatā*); this is based on the reading in the *Kalpadruma* lexicon within the section beginning with dentals and labials: "she is Bālā because she is powerful (*bala*)" or "she is spread out (*tata*). (71) She is the wife of Vivasvat.
This Vivasvān is that Āditya; he is the "expander" (*vivasta*) of day and night. According to the *Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa*, she is situated above the moon and sun.

In another system (*tantrāntare*), due to the meditation on the *Kālikā-bheda*, there is a *matvarthīya* suffix following a *karmadhāraya* compound [forming the name] *Vivasvat-premadhāriṇī*. This is stated in the *Nandikeśvara-saṃhitā*: "As long as the *arghya* offered to the Sun has not been presented, so long is it not [complete]. (72) *Vivasvat-premadhāriṇī*. Thus it is said.

She conquers Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Queen of the Asuras; she dispels darkness like the sun—this is from the Skanda Purāṇa. (73) Regarding the form *Śarakarā*: "Śara" means she destroys the wicked (*śṛṇāti hinasti duṣṭān*), derived from the root *śṝ* (to injure) with the suffix *yuc*. Alternatively, "Śara" refers to that which causes auspiciousness (*śaṃ kalpaṇam*), and "Karā" is a word whose cause is sound (*aṇaḥ śabdaḥ*) because of her auspicious renown. (74) Regarding *Śaralā*: she takes (*lāti*) or holds (*dhārayati*) the arrow (*śaram*); likewise, it is said, "she holds the spear and the arrow in her right [hand]."

(75) Regarding *mahiṣamardinīdhyāne*: it is stated in the *Pañcarātra*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *śalya* refers to a spear (*śakti*), an arrow (*śara*), a bamboo pole (*vaṃśa*), a sword-hilt (*kavika*), and a javelin (*tomara*). Thus, in her form as Kaumārī, she holds a spear in her hand. (76) Regarding *śaraṇya*: the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of "one who is fit for that" (*tatra sādhuh*). From the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "For those who have taken refuge in You and do not perish, having sought Your protection, they indeed attain the state of being protected. (77) Regarding *śrī*: [the suffix] *kvip* is applied in various senses.

By the rule *caprachītyādinā*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *śri*, and there is a lengthening of the vowel; thus some say "they resort to her" (*śrayanty enām*), while Haradatta Miśra and Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita maintain it means "she is resorted to" (*śrayati*). She is called "possessing the qualities of autumn" (*śaradguṇā*) because she is dear to the autumn season; for the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, in the context of the *Tvarātra*, states: "In every city, in every place, the Goddess is to be worshipped by people. Furthermore, during the autumn season, the Great Worship (*mahāpūjā*) is performed, which is [also] annual.

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the repetition "in every year" (*varṣe varṣe bhavati*) indicates its permanence, as understood from the commentary of Bandhakāri: "In every spring, [one should worship] Jyotiṣmatī. Furthermore, because the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) for that [deity] is stated there as: "Especially during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth [day].
(79) Her place of worship is within the center of the six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) of the *trākāra* group; thus, she is situated at the end.

From the *Atharvaṇa*: "A six-cornered [figure], an eight-petalled lotus," and from the *Gandharva Tantra*: "Then a lotus situated within a hexagon, followed by two terrestrial discs; in their center, one should worship the Goddess, as well as her vehicle, which is indeed a corpse. (80) Regarding the word *sampadā* (attainment): it is formed with the suffix *ṭāp* according to the rule *āpaṃ caiva halantānām*. Alternatively, it means "she whose foot is on all sides. She is to be perceived at all times in all beings, facing in every direction. Mā.

Because of the statement by the Goddess of Wealth (Śrī): "Adorned with modesty," since shame (*lajjā*) is the abiding wealth [of a householder]; and likewise the word of Śrī: "I avoid such a woman who delights in the houses of others and is devoid of shame; one who is skillful at the wish-fulfilling tree [of generosity], compassionate, possessing shame, fortitude, faith, splendor, renunciation, and gratitude—he whose virtues are these is called a preeminent householder. [The term] *kṣema* [refers to security].

Because she brings about the security (*yogakṣema*) of her devotees through the protection of what has been acquired and the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained, it is said in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: "Therefore, Bhavānī, who dwells in Kāśī, should be constantly served by those residing in Kāśī. Alternatively, she is so named because she is endowed with the power (*śakti*) designated by this [syllable *kṣa*];
or else, because the syllable *kṣa* contains *ī*, which is Lakṣmī, and *mā*, which is Sarasvatī, since the alphabet begins with *a* and ends with *kṣa*. (83)

The sixteen names are stated in the sequence beginning with *arthākāra*. First, regarding *Ādyā*: from the root *ad*, meaning "to eat," the suffix *kvip* is applied to form the state [of eating]; *ad* refers to devouring, that is, killing. She is called *Kālī* because she attains (*yāti*) that [state] through specific ritual actions, as she is the cause thereof; for it is said in the *Kālītantra*: "So too in killing and eradication. Regarding *Ājñā*: because she resides in the wheel located between the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya-cakra*) which bears this name; or else, because she is one for whom no [external] command (*ājñā*) exists.

The compound is formed with the prefix *a-* in the sense of negation; alternatively, according to the *Matsyasūkta* (85), "the accomplishment of the command (*ājñāsiddhi*) arises from making the region of the devotees free from obstacles" (*avyāruta-deśa*). Regarding the word *ijyā*: *i* is desire (*kāma*), and *jyā* is the earth (*bhūmi*); as Śāśvata states, "the bowstring (*jyā*) is made of *maurī* grass, and it is the bearer of wealth. One should meditate upon her, who is firm above the Mind-born God (Kāmadeva) attached to Rati, resembling a javelin (*java*). Thus [ends] the meditation on Chinnamastā.

Because she is not seen [by others], she is called *Īśvaravallabhā* (the Beloved of the Lord); this is clear from the meaning. From the dog, *Sārameya*, comes *Śvara* (Lord), as seen in the expression "the delightful one surrounded by a pack of dogs" (*śvayūthaveṣṭitam*). Because it is the cause of fortune (*bhāgya*), [the word *ūrṇā*] refers to the hair between the eyebrows, as Amara states: "The hair between the eyebrows is called *ūrṇā*, *meṣādiloman*," and so forth. This is because it is the object of all cognition as being colored (*uparakta*) by its own attribute, such as existence (*sattā*), and so on. (89) Ṛ.

Even so, one might argue that it would not be beloved by the people; therefore, he says: "By beauty" (*kāntyā*).

The meaning is that he gladdens all like the moon. He is Śaṅkara (the auspicious one) by virtue of his power and firm means, which possess the capacity to accomplish what must be done; and because he is not inferior to Śiva in any respect, the author says "śaurye" (in heroism), implying that he possesses both types of capability. Here, the poetic ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is the simile (*upamā*) in the phrase "equal to the Lord of Wealth" (*dhaneśvara-sama*), the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in "Vākyatī," and the contrast (*vyatireka*) in "embodied" (*mūrtimān*). Upa... [text fragment].

In the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, it is stated that when there is a non-exclusion [of the object] from pride and so forth, through the implication of similarity by way of identity—as in the phrase "embodied"—the distinction of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) from the object of comparison (*upameya*) is expressed; therefore, because these [figures] exist within a single sentence without depending on one another, the figure is *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling). Even though the identity [of the two] is possible merely by this much, the particle *eva* (only/just) serves to strengthen the superimposition (*āropa*).

In works such as the *Alaṅkārasarvasva-vivaraṇa*, it is stated that "the wealth of a Brahmin is poison" (*brahmasvaṃ viṣam ucyate*) and so forth; this has been accepted in that manner by authors such as Ruyyaka and Śrīdhara. However, Appayadīkṣita, in his *Kuvalayānanda*, accepted *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment) in instances such as: "This is not the moon, but rather the moon is the face of my beloved. According to his system, however, [the figure] occurs in the verse beginning with "śaṃkare babhūva," where the particle *eva* is used in relation to himself.

Since the superimposition of identity with Śaṅkara is understood by negating identity with one's own self, it should be noted that the same applies here as well; this should be seen in the *Pallava* section of the *Alaṃkāra-kaustubha*. May all be auspicious! This [twelfth] moon has reached its end in the *Girijā-nāmārtha-cintāmaṇi*, composed by Viśveśvara, who was born from the body of the scholar named Lakṣmīdhara, who had crossed the ocean of words, scriptures, and authorities.

Victorious is King Vājacaṃdra, who has illuminated the three worlds with the radiance of his fame— a moonlight that rivals the splendor of Śrī, who dwells upon the earth and whose lion-throne is crowded by the dancing crests of the crowns of all the gods.
While he was ruling the earth in accordance with righteousness, Viśveśvara [composed] a thousand names of the Mother of the World, suited to his own intellect.

Although there is not even the slightest trace of any new distinction here that has not already been made clear by others, nevertheless, O wise ones, do not ever abandon this work. For though the ocean exists in the world, it is a heap of worthless stones; does it ever yield even a single cowrie?
In the year 1942, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, on a Tuesday. May the venerable Supreme Deity be pleased. May there be auspiciousness!

this is the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Sahasranāmadīpa* of Tārā. [End of File: Maṃtraśāstra]
